skills.description: Use when modeling direct- or indirect-conversion x-ray detectors (a-Se, CsI) with a cascaded linear model and you need to trace how an upstream input approximation (e.g., attenuation-coefficient source) affects downstream noise metrics like NNPS.
skills.name: cascaded-linear-system-noise-propagation
skills.search_text: cascaded-linear-system-noise-propagation Use when modeling direct- or indirect-conversion x-ray detectors (a-Se, CsI) with a cascaded linear model and you need to trace how an upstream input approximation (e.g., attenuation-coefficient source) affects downstream noise metrics like NNPS. The analysis requires per-energy-bin propagation of signal and noise quantities, Fano noise, photoconductor discharge, Lubberts effect, or optical Swank noise — CASYMIR does not explicitly model these. The detector is a photon-counting system or involves temporal effects such as detector lag and ghosting, which are not included in this CASYMIR implementation. You need input-quantum-limited (input-labeled) DQE formulations, which are not included. Propagate x-ray detector signal through serial/parallel gain, blur, sampling, and additive-noise process blocks in CASYMIR to compute quantum efficiency, MTF, and NNPS, and quantify how upstream approximations (e.g., the attenuation-coefficient source) attenuate by the time they reach the NNPS. genomics/v1 10.1002/mp.18079
skills.summary: Propagate x-ray detector signal through serial/parallel gain, blur, sampling, and additive-noise process blocks in CASYMIR to compute quantum efficiency, MTF, and NNPS, and quantify how upstream approximations (e.g., the attenuation-coefficient source) attenuate by the time they reach the NNPS.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The analysis requires per-energy-bin propagation of signal and noise quantities, Fano noise, photoconductor discharge, Lubberts effect, or optical Swank noise — CASYMIR does not explicitly model these. The detector is a photon-counting system or involves temporal effects such as detector lag and ghosting, which are not included in this CASYMIR implementation. You need input-quantum-limited (input-labeled) DQE formulations, which are not included.

skills.description: Use when two dRNA-Seq datasets (case vs control, e.g. a modification-writer mutant vs wild-type fast5 raw reads) must be compared at single m6A sites to find sites with significantly altered modification stoichiometry.
skills.name: case-control-modification-site-comparison
skills.search_text: case-control-modification-site-comparison Use when two dRNA-Seq datasets (case vs control, e.g. a modification-writer mutant vs wild-type fast5 raw reads) must be compared at single m6A sites to find sites with significantly altered modification stoichiometry. Site coverage is below the min_coverage 50 threshold — the site will not appear in mAFiA.sites.bed and modRatio comparison is unreliable You need Ψ or motifs beyond the m6A DRACH subset covered by mAFiA classifiers — use the superseding psi-co-mAFiA model set instead You have no per-read modification calls (e.g. only bulk chemical-assay stoichiometry) — this skill requires read-level MM/ML tags from mAFiA modBAMs http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Compares per-site m6A stoichiometry (modRatio) from mAFiA between a case and control dRNA-Seq sample — e.g. Arabidopsis thaliana vir1 mutant vs col0 wild-type — to identify transcriptome-wide down- or up-regulation of m6A at otherwise highly modified sites. genomics/v1 10.1038/s41467-024-47661-2
skills.summary: Compares per-site m6A stoichiometry (modRatio) from mAFiA between a case and control dRNA-Seq sample — e.g. Arabidopsis thaliana vir1 mutant vs col0 wild-type — to identify transcriptome-wide down- or up-regulation of m6A at otherwise highly modified sites.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Site coverage is below the min_coverage 50 threshold — the site will not appear in mAFiA.sites.bed and modRatio comparison is unreliable You need Ψ or motifs beyond the m6A DRACH subset covered by mAFiA classifiers — use the superseding psi-co-mAFiA model set instead You have no per-read modification calls (e.g. only bulk chemical-assay stoichiometry) — this skill requires read-level MM/ML tags from mAFiA modBAMs

skills.description: Use when you have simulated IV–exposure (bx, bxse) and IV–outcome (by, byse) summary associations from simmrd's generate_summary() and want to benchmark MR estimator causal estimates against known true effects.
skills.name: causal-effect-benchmark-against-simulated-truth
skills.search_text: causal-effect-benchmark-against-simulated-truth Use when you have simulated IV–exposure (bx, bxse) and IV–outcome (by, byse) summary associations from simmrd's generate_summary() and want to benchmark MR estimator causal estimates against known true effects. Input is real, not simulated, GWAS summary data — there is no known truth (theta) to benchmark against You need multiple simulation replicates from a single call: simmrd's generate_summary() and generate_individual() each generate data for a single simulation replicate only You need individual-level genotype/phenotype simulation with direct confounding control — use generate_individual() workflow instead, which is slower but lets you set confounding directly http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Fit competing summary-data Mendelian randomization estimators (e.g. IVW, MR-Egger via the MendelianRandomization R package) on simmrd-generated GWAS summary replicates and compare each estimate against the true causal effects (theta) that simmrd returns, enabling benchmarking of estimator bias and validity. genomics/v1 10.1002/gepi.22544
skills.summary: Fit competing summary-data Mendelian randomization estimators (e.g. IVW, MR-Egger via the MendelianRandomization R package) on simmrd-generated GWAS summary replicates and compare each estimate against the true causal effects (theta) that simmrd returns, enabling benchmarking of estimator bias and validity.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is real, not simulated, GWAS summary data — there is no known truth (theta) to benchmark against You need multiple simulation replicates from a single call: simmrd's generate_summary() and generate_individual() each generate data for a single simulation replicate only You need individual-level genotype/phenotype simulation with direct confounding control — use generate_individual() workflow instead, which is slower but lets you set confounding directly

skills.description: Use when comparing phenotype-based gene prioritization tools on a patient-case benchmark and you need per-rank causal-gene counts, top-20 recall, or counts of causal genes uniquely detected in the top 20 by one tool.
skills.name: causal-gene-rank-recall-analysis
skills.search_text: causal-gene-rank-recall-analysis Use when comparing phenotype-based gene prioritization tools on a patient-case benchmark and you need per-rank causal-gene counts, top-20 recall, or counts of causal genes uniquely detected in the top 20 by one tool. You need tool-specific strengths near the bottom of the rank distribution — the paper notes VIBE lacks exceptionally well prioritized genes there and the benchmark does not demonstrate individual strengths of the tested tools. You want to benchmark PhenoTips — as of January 2020 it no longer offers a stand-alone downloadable solution, so that benchmark is deemed obsolete in the vibe-suppl README. Your aim is variant-level candidate filtering (allele frequency, inheritance mode, pathogenicity) rather than gene-level rank/recall evaluation of phenotype prioritizers. http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_0089 Reproduce the VIBE benchmark's causal-gene rank analysis: per-rank counts, cumulative top-20 recall (reaching 308 causal genes at rank 20), and unique top-20 hits (6 for VIBE), by stabilizing each case's causal-gene rank as the median of 25 permutations and counting unique detections across benchmarked tools. genomics/v1 10.1002/ggn2.10023
skills.summary: Reproduce the VIBE benchmark's causal-gene rank analysis: per-rank counts, cumulative top-20 recall (reaching 308 causal genes at rank 20), and unique top-20 hits (6 for VIBE), by stabilizing each case's causal-gene rank as the median of 25 permutations and counting unique detections across benchmarked tools.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You need tool-specific strengths near the bottom of the rank distribution — the paper notes VIBE lacks exceptionally well prioritized genes there and the benchmark does not demonstrate individual strengths of the tested tools. You want to benchmark PhenoTips — as of January 2020 it no longer offers a stand-alone downloadable solution, so that benchmark is deemed obsolete in the vibe-suppl README. Your aim is variant-level candidate filtering (allele frequency, inheritance mode, pathogenicity) rather than gene-level rank/recall evaluation of phenotype prioritizers.

skills.description: Use when you have per-case ranked gene lists from multiple phenotype-prioritization tools on a common benchmark and need to count causal genes uniquely detected by one tool within top-N cutoffs, e.g. N=1..20, to characterize stability and complementarity.
skills.name: causal-gene-rank-threshold-counting
skills.search_text: causal-gene-rank-threshold-counting Use when you have per-case ranked gene lists from multiple phenotype-prioritization tools on a common benchmark and need to count causal genes uniquely detected by one tool within top-N cutoffs, e.g. N=1..20, to characterize stability and complementarity. The input is a single tool's output without matched ranked lists for all eight tools, since unique-hit counting requires the full comparator set on the same cases You need raw prioritization performance (recall/rank distributions) rather than between-tool complementarity — Figure 1/2-style rank analyses cover that instead The benchmark relies on PhenoTips as a comparator and no local installation is possible, since PhenoTips no longer offers a stand-alone download and requires a paid cloud subscription (deemed obsolete in the benchmarking README) http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Skill for quantifying how many benchmark causal genes a phenotype-based gene prioritization tool (e.g. VIBE) uniquely detects within top-N ranked results, swept across thresholds N=1..20, as used to analyze VIBE's performance against Phenomizer, PhenoTips, hiPHIVE, PhenIX, PubCaseFinder, AMELIE and GADO on 305 patient cases. genomics/v1 10.1002/ggn2.10023
skills.summary: Skill for quantifying how many benchmark causal genes a phenotype-based gene prioritization tool (e.g. VIBE) uniquely detects within top-N ranked results, swept across thresholds N=1..20, as used to analyze VIBE's performance against Phenomizer, PhenoTips, hiPHIVE, PhenIX, PubCaseFinder, AMELIE and GADO on 305 patient cases.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is a single tool's output without matched ranked lists for all eight tools, since unique-hit counting requires the full comparator set on the same cases You need raw prioritization performance (recall/rank distributions) rather than between-tool complementarity — Figure 1/2-style rank analyses cover that instead The benchmark relies on PhenoTips as a comparator and no local installation is possible, since PhenoTips no longer offers a stand-alone download and requires a paid cloud subscription (deemed obsolete in the benchmarking README)

skills.description: Use when analyzing multisample VCFs from small related sample groups (parent-child trios or families) with pedigree and inheritance-mode metadata, to shortlist candidate causal variants for rare Mendelian disease diagnosis.
skills.name: causal-variant-prioritization
skills.search_text: causal-variant-prioritization Use when analyzing multisample VCFs from small related sample groups (parent-child trios or families) with pedigree and inheritance-mode metadata, to shortlist candidate causal variants for rare Mendelian disease diagnosis. The candidate variants are CNVs — CNV analysis is not yet integrated in eDiVA, which currently handles SNPs/indels only Samples are unrelated singletons without pedigree or inheritance-model information, so segregation-based filtering cannot be applied A prioritization ranking already exists (e.g. a precomputed ranked.csv) and the task is only annotation or downstream interpretation http://edamontology.org/topic_0625 http://edamontology.org/topic_0102 Rank causal coding variants in familial WES/WGS disease studies using eDiVA-Prioritize, which filters variants by inheritance-model segregation (dominant de novo, dominant inherited, recessive homozygous, compound heterozygous, X-linked), applies functional/population-genomic filters (AF ≤ 0.01), and prioritizes by the random-forest eDiVA-Score with optional HPO phenotype soft-filtering. genomics/v1 10.1002/humu.23772
skills.summary: Rank causal coding variants in familial WES/WGS disease studies using eDiVA-Prioritize, which filters variants by inheritance-model segregation (dominant de novo, dominant inherited, recessive homozygous, compound heterozygous, X-linked), applies functional/population-genomic filters (AF ≤ 0.01), and prioritizes by the random-forest eDiVA-Score with optional HPO phenotype soft-filtering.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The candidate variants are CNVs — CNV analysis is not yet integrated in eDiVA, which currently handles SNPs/indels only Samples are unrelated singletons without pedigree or inheritance-model information, so segregation-based filtering cannot be applied A prioritization ranking already exists (e.g. a precomputed ranked.csv) and the task is only annotation or downstream interpretation

skills.description: Use when processing PacBio PAIso-seq CCS BAMs where non-A residues within poly(A) tails must be called reliably and per-read subread pass counts need to gate which CCS reads enter tail-length and residue analysis.
skills.name: ccs-pass-count-filtering
skills.search_text: ccs-pass-count-filtering Use when processing PacBio PAIso-seq CCS BAMs where non-A residues within poly(A) tails must be called reliably and per-read subread pass counts need to gate which CCS reads enter tail-length and residue analysis. Input is short-read Illumina data (e.g. from the discontinued Genome Analyzer II used by PAL-seq), where no circular consensus pass counts exist to filter on. The analysis goal is isoform clustering or de novo transcript discovery with IsoSeq3/IsoSeq tools rather than per-read poly(A) tail residue analysis, which uses its own deduplication (UMI/barcode-based) logic. CCS reads were produced with polishing and rich QVs at very high pass depth such that a ≥10-pass floor is trivially satisfied and adds no accuracy benefit while discarding reads. http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_3169 Collects per-CCS-read subread pass counts from PacBio movie BAMs and restricts downstream PAIso-seq poly(A) tail analysis to circular consensus reads supported by ≥10 passes, ensuring the base-calling accuracy needed to trust non-adenosine (U/G/C) residues called inside poly(A) tail bodies. genomics/v1 10.1038/s41467-019-13228-9
skills.summary: Collects per-CCS-read subread pass counts from PacBio movie BAMs and restricts downstream PAIso-seq poly(A) tail analysis to circular consensus reads supported by ≥10 passes, ensuring the base-calling accuracy needed to trust non-adenosine (U/G/C) residues called inside poly(A) tail bodies.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is short-read Illumina data (e.g. from the discontinued Genome Analyzer II used by PAL-seq), where no circular consensus pass counts exist to filter on. The analysis goal is isoform clustering or de novo transcript discovery with IsoSeq3/IsoSeq tools rather than per-read poly(A) tail residue analysis, which uses its own deduplication (UMI/barcode-based) logic. CCS reads were produced with polishing and rich QVs at very high pass depth such that a ≥10-pass floor is trivially satisfied and adds no accuracy benefit while discarding reads.

skills.description: Use when you have PacBio CCS/HiFi reads (subreads.bam or hifi.bam) and need per-read 5mCpG methylation probabilities, or site-level CpG methylation frequencies validated against BS-seq/nanopore benchmarks.
skills.name: ccs-read-5mc-detection
skills.search_text: ccs-read-5mc-detection Use when you have PacBio CCS/HiFi reads (subreads.bam or hifi.bam) and need per-read 5mCpG methylation probabilities, or site-level CpG methylation frequencies validated against BS-seq/nanopore benchmarks. The input is Oxford Nanopore reads rather than PacBio CCS/HiFi reads — ccsmeth's models rely on PacBio-specific IPD/PW kinetics features, so nanopore-based callers (e.g., deepsignal2) are the appropriate choice. The goal is detecting hemimethylated CpGs, non-CpG 5mCs, or other modifications such as 6mA — the article states these methods only consider symmetric CpG methylation and cannot detect these states. Only very short CCS inserts are available — performance is reduced when CCS reads are shorter than ~10 Kb (the strand-specific model is significantly reduced due to limited subread depth). http://edamontology.org/topic_3173 http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Detect 5-methylcytosine at single-molecule (per-read per-CpG) resolution using ccsmeth deep-learning models on PacBio circular consensus sequencing (HiFi) reads, exploiting IPD and PW kinetics features, then aggregate calls to site-level methylation frequencies with ccsmethphase for benchmarking against BS-seq and nanopore methylation. genomics/v1 10.1038/s41467-023-39784-9
skills.summary: Detect 5-methylcytosine at single-molecule (per-read per-CpG) resolution using ccsmeth deep-learning models on PacBio circular consensus sequencing (HiFi) reads, exploiting IPD and PW kinetics features, then aggregate calls to site-level methylation frequencies with ccsmethphase for benchmarking against BS-seq and nanopore methylation.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is Oxford Nanopore reads rather than PacBio CCS/HiFi reads — ccsmeth's models rely on PacBio-specific IPD/PW kinetics features, so nanopore-based callers (e.g., deepsignal2) are the appropriate choice. The goal is detecting hemimethylated CpGs, non-CpG 5mCs, or other modifications such as 6mA — the article states these methods only consider symmetric CpG methylation and cannot detect these states. Only very short CCS inserts are available — performance is reduced when CCS reads are shorter than ~10 Kb (the strand-specific model is significantly reduced due to limited subread depth).

skills.description: Use when input is a PacBio CCS reads BAM (subreads.bam or hifi.bam) plus a reference genome and per-read 5mCpG methylation calls are needed, e.g. to build haplotype-tagged modbams for allele-specific methylation analysis.
skills.name: ccs-read-methylation-calling
skills.search_text: ccs-read-methylation-calling Use when input is a PacBio CCS reads BAM (subreads.bam or hifi.bam) plus a reference genome and per-read 5mCpG methylation calls are needed, e.g. to build haplotype-tagged modbams for allele-specific methylation analysis. Input reads are Oxford Nanopore rather than PacBio CCS — use nanopore-specific callers (nanopolish, Megalodon, deepsignal2) instead The target modification is not CpG 5mC — ccsmeth cannot detect non-CpG 5mCs or other modifications such as 6mA Hemimethylated CpGs are the biological question — the model only considers symmetric methylation and combines features from both strands, so hemimethylation is invisible http://edamontology.org/topic_3168 http://edamontology.org/topic_0654 Detect DNA 5mCpG methylation states from PacBio circular consensus sequencing (CCS/HiFi) reads at single-molecule (read-level) resolution using ccsmeth, a deep-learning model trained on kinetics features (IPDs and PWs) of treated DNA, producing modbam files that downstream haplotyping workflows consume. genomics/v1 10.1038/s41467-023-39784-9
skills.summary: Detect DNA 5mCpG methylation states from PacBio circular consensus sequencing (CCS/HiFi) reads at single-molecule (read-level) resolution using ccsmeth, a deep-learning model trained on kinetics features (IPDs and PWs) of treated DNA, producing modbam files that downstream haplotyping workflows consume.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input reads are Oxford Nanopore rather than PacBio CCS — use nanopore-specific callers (nanopolish, Megalodon, deepsignal2) instead The target modification is not CpG 5mC — ccsmeth cannot detect non-CpG 5mCs or other modifications such as 6mA Hemimethylated CpGs are the biological question — the model only considers symmetric methylation and combines features from both strands, so hemimethylation is invisible

skills.description: Use when raw dZ-DNA or native PacBio HiFi/CCS BAMs must be cleaned before kinetic-signal analysis (PW/IPD) or Z-Calling, i.e. when reads may lack fi/ri/fp/rp tags, have aberrant PW/IPD ratios, or too few polymerase passes.
skills.name: ccs-read-quality-filtering
skills.search_text: ccs-read-quality-filtering Use when raw dZ-DNA or native PacBio HiFi/CCS BAMs must be cleaned before kinetic-signal analysis (PW/IPD) or Z-Calling, i.e. when reads may lack fi/ri/fp/rp tags, have aberrant PW/IPD ratios, or too few polymerase passes. Input BAMs already carry kinetic tags and pass QC (e.g. the paper's own benchmark CCS outputs generated with '--keep-kinetics' that were pre-filtered) — re-filtering can bias pass-count distributions Analysis targets ONT ionic-current data or HPLC nucleotide-composition measurements rather than PacBio pulse kinetics — the PW/IPD thresholds do not apply Reads are intended for taxonomic identification only via sequence divergence (minimap2 dv tag) where kinetics are not required http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_3168 Pre-processes PacBio CCS BAM files by retaining only reads carrying kinetic tags (fi, ri, fp, rp), enforcing signal-quality (median PW / median IPD >= 0.3 and below the 99th percentile), and requiring >= 3 passes per strand (fn >= 3, rn >= 3), so downstream kinetic and Z-calling analyses operate on reliable pulse data. genomics/v1 10.1038/s42003-026-09849-8
skills.summary: Pre-processes PacBio CCS BAM files by retaining only reads carrying kinetic tags (fi, ri, fp, rp), enforcing signal-quality (median PW / median IPD >= 0.3 and below the 99th percentile), and requiring >= 3 passes per strand (fn >= 3, rn >= 3), so downstream kinetic and Z-calling analyses operate on reliable pulse data.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input BAMs already carry kinetic tags and pass QC (e.g. the paper's own benchmark CCS outputs generated with '--keep-kinetics' that were pre-filtered) — re-filtering can bias pass-count distributions Analysis targets ONT ionic-current data or HPLC nucleotide-composition measurements rather than PacBio pulse kinetics — the PW/IPD thresholds do not apply Reads are intended for taxonomic identification only via sequence divergence (minimap2 dv tag) where kinetics are not required

skills.description: Use when validating or benchmarking an RNA editing annotation method and you need plastid genomes whose editing sites are independently confirmed by cDNA data rather than predicted.
skills.name: cdna-confirmed-plastome-test-dataset-selection
skills.search_text: cdna-confirmed-plastome-test-dataset-selection Use when validating or benchmarking an RNA editing annotation method and you need plastid genomes whose editing sites are independently confirmed by cDNA data rather than predicted. The tool's purpose is to predict all RNA editing sites from RNA-Seq data — ReFernment is explicitly not intended for that, so this dataset cannot validate genome-wide editing site prediction Input annotation files were created in Sequin — ReFernment has a known error and does not produce annotations for Sequin-created files (files exported from Geneious still work) You need a substitute for manually checking gene annotations — ReFernment is not a fix for sloppy annotation and output quality depends on input annotation quality http://edamontology.org/topic_0085 http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Selects plastid genomes with cDNA-confirmed RNA editing sites (e.g., GenBank AB086179 and AY178864.1) as ground-truth test datasets for benchmarking automated RNA editing annotation tools such as ReFernment against manual curation. genomics/v1 10.1002/aps3.1216
skills.summary: Selects plastid genomes with cDNA-confirmed RNA editing sites (e.g., GenBank AB086179 and AY178864.1) as ground-truth test datasets for benchmarking automated RNA editing annotation tools such as ReFernment against manual curation.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The tool's purpose is to predict all RNA editing sites from RNA-Seq data — ReFernment is explicitly not intended for that, so this dataset cannot validate genome-wide editing site prediction Input annotation files were created in Sequin — ReFernment has a known error and does not produce annotations for Sequin-created files (files exported from Geneious still work) You need a substitute for manually checking gene annotations — ReFernment is not a fix for sloppy annotation and output quality depends on input annotation quality

skills.description: Use when long-read cDNA nanopore (SQK-PCS111) reads are aligned to a known plasmid/mRNA reference and you need a per-read error rate and per-nucleotide mismatch/insertion/deletion profile, e.g. characterising error in a poly(A) tail.
skills.name: cdna-sequencing-error-rate-analysis
skills.search_text: cdna-sequencing-error-rate-analysis Use when long-read cDNA nanopore (SQK-PCS111) reads are aligned to a known plasmid/mRNA reference and you need a per-read error rate and per-nucleotide mismatch/insertion/deletion profile, e.g. characterising error in a poly(A) tail. The goal is to call true sequence variants or build a consensus — this skill quantifies the sequencing error background, not biology; use variant calling/consensus generation (e.g. bcftools v1.15) instead. Input data is short-read Illumina — this pipeline's Minimap2 '-ax map-ont' preset and nanopore error modelling are specific to ONT cDNA reads. Reads have not passed the Q>9 quality filter — including low-quality nanopore reads will inflate the error profile beyond the reported baseline. http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_3569 Quantifies the per-read sequencing error rate and per-nucleotide mismatch/insertion/deletion profile of ONT cDNA nanopore reads (SQK-PCS111) aligned to a reference plasmid, including the elevated deletion rate within a template-encoded 3' poly(A) tail. It establishes the baseline error profile needed to distinguish sequencing error from true sequence variation in mRNA vaccine QC. genomics/v1 10.1038/s41467-023-41354-y
skills.summary: Quantifies the per-read sequencing error rate and per-nucleotide mismatch/insertion/deletion profile of ONT cDNA nanopore reads (SQK-PCS111) aligned to a reference plasmid, including the elevated deletion rate within a template-encoded 3' poly(A) tail. It establishes the baseline error profile needed to distinguish sequencing error from true sequence variation in mRNA vaccine QC.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is to call true sequence variants or build a consensus — this skill quantifies the sequencing error background, not biology; use variant calling/consensus generation (e.g. bcftools v1.15) instead. Input data is short-read Illumina — this pipeline's Minimap2 '-ax map-ont' preset and nanopore error modelling are specific to ONT cDNA reads. Reads have not passed the Q>9 quality filter — including low-quality nanopore reads will inflate the error profile beyond the reported baseline.

skills.description: Use when raw 10x-structured nanopore or PacBio long-read FASTQ reads need cell barcodes found, error-corrected against the 10x v3 whitelist, and assigned per read before alignment/quantification.
skills.name: cell-barcode-demultiplexing
skills.search_text: cell-barcode-demultiplexing Use when raw 10x-structured nanopore or PacBio long-read FASTQ reads need cell barcodes found, error-corrected against the 10x v3 whitelist, and assigned per read before alignment/quantification. Input reads are short-read (Illumina) data — scywalker is designed for Oxford nanopore long reads, with PacBio supported only via appropriate options Reads lack 10x v3 structure (no CTACACGACGCTCTTCCGATCT adapter with adjacent 16-bp barcode + 12-bp UMI), so whitelist scoring and UMI extraction would be invalid Data is already demultiplexed (barcode-corrected FASTQ/BAM available), making the droplet-discovery step redundant http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 scywalker's droplet barcoding module (Module 1) detects 10x droplet cell barcodes directly from raw nanopore (or PacBio) FASTQ reads — extracting the 16-bp barcode against the 10x v3 whitelist, absorbing single-mismatch barcodes, and emitting a corrected FASTQ with barcode/UMI prepended — without needing matched short-read data. genomics/v1 10.1093/bioinformatics/btae549
skills.summary: scywalker's droplet barcoding module (Module 1) detects 10x droplet cell barcodes directly from raw nanopore (or PacBio) FASTQ reads — extracting the 16-bp barcode against the 10x v3 whitelist, absorbing single-mismatch barcodes, and emitting a corrected FASTQ with barcode/UMI prepended — without needing matched short-read data.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input reads are short-read (Illumina) data — scywalker is designed for Oxford nanopore long reads, with PacBio supported only via appropriate options Reads lack 10x v3 structure (no CTACACGACGCTCTTCCGATCT adapter with adjacent 16-bp barcode + 12-bp UMI), so whitelist scoring and UMI extraction would be invalid Data is already demultiplexed (barcode-corrected FASTQ/BAM available), making the droplet-discovery step redundant

skills.description: Use when processing HIT-scISOseq CCS reads where primer-based FLNC classification must also yield per-read cellBC and UMI (isoseq_flnc.BarcodeUMI.fastq), or when corrected barcodes/UMIs are needed for isoform count matrices.
skills.name: cell-barcode-umi-extraction
skills.search_text: cell-barcode-umi-extraction Use when processing HIT-scISOseq CCS reads where primer-based FLNC classification must also yield per-read cellBC and UMI (isoseq_flnc.BarcodeUMI.fastq), or when corrected barcodes/UMIs are needed for isoform count matrices. Input reads are 10x ScISOr-Seq cell-barcode-free reads or TSO artifacts without both 5' and 3' primer hits in opposite orientation — classify_by_primer would reject them as non-FLNC. The library was not built with the 10x Genomics-compatible or HIT-scISOseq primer design; primer_F/primer_S names and sequences would not match the read structure. Data already consist of corrected, demultiplexed barcode/UMI tables (e.g. an existing cellBC-UMI matrix) rather than raw CCS reads. http://edamontology.org/topic_3168 http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Extracts 10x Genomics cell barcodes and UMIs embedded in HIT-scISOseq full-length non-concatemer (FLNC) reads during classify_by_primer, then corrects them with a CellRanger-like whitelist strategy so single-cell isoform matrices can be built from PacBio CCS data. genomics/v1 10.1038/s41467-023-38324-9
skills.summary: Extracts 10x Genomics cell barcodes and UMIs embedded in HIT-scISOseq full-length non-concatemer (FLNC) reads during classify_by_primer, then corrects them with a CellRanger-like whitelist strategy so single-cell isoform matrices can be built from PacBio CCS data.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input reads are 10x ScISOr-Seq cell-barcode-free reads or TSO artifacts without both 5' and 3' primer hits in opposite orientation — classify_by_primer would reject them as non-FLNC. The library was not built with the 10x Genomics-compatible or HIT-scISOseq primer design; primer_F/primer_S names and sequences would not match the read structure. Data already consist of corrected, demultiplexed barcode/UMI tables (e.g. an existing cellBC-UMI matrix) rather than raw CCS reads.

skills.search_text: centromeric-hor-monomer-decomposition Use when nanomonsv single breakend SVs are classified as 'High Repeat single breakend SVs' (mostly RepeatMasker 'Satellite/centr') and you need to test whether their contig sequences follow canonical, chromosome-specific centromeric HORs. skills.search_text: chain-score-feature-aggregation Use when you have a per-read feature table from RawHash2 signal mapping and need to decide mapped vs unmapped by thresholding a weighted combination of mapping-quality and chain-score ratios. You still need raw signal chaining or seed matching — produce the feature table with RawHash2 first; this skill only performs the decision step You need alignment-level scoring (e.g. DTW signal alignment via RawAlign) rather than a thresholded aggregate of mapping-quality and chain-score ratios The goal is reference-free all-vs-all overlapping (Rawsamble), which produces PAF overlaps rather than per-read mapped/unmapped decisions http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Reimplements RawHash2's weighted mapping-decision mechanism: per-read ratios (mapping-quality ratio, best and mean chain-score ratios) are aggregated into a weighted sum and compared against a configurable threshold, replacing RawHash's fixed conditional checks for real-time nanopore read mapping. genomics/v1 10.1093/bioinformatics/btae478
skills.summary: Reimplements RawHash2's weighted mapping-decision mechanism: per-read ratios (mapping-quality ratio, best and mean chain-score ratios) are aggregated into a weighted sum and compared against a configurable threshold, replacing RawHash's fixed conditional checks for real-time nanopore read mapping.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You still need raw signal chaining or seed matching — produce the feature table with RawHash2 first; this skill only performs the decision step You need alignment-level scoring (e.g. DTW signal alignment via RawAlign) rather than a thresholded aggregate of mapping-quality and chain-score ratios The goal is reference-free all-vs-all overlapping (Rawsamble), which produces PAF overlaps rather than per-read mapped/unmapped decisions

skills.description: Use when quality-controlled SAM/BAM alignments from nanopore-style reads have already been converted to 100x100 pixel deletion-region images and zero-padded encoded base sequences, and deletion/non-deletion classification per region is the goal.
skills.name: channel-attention-sequence-image-fusion
skills.search_text: channel-attention-sequence-image-fusion Use when quality-controlled SAM/BAM alignments from nanopore-style reads have already been converted to 100x100 pixel deletion-region images and zero-padded encoded base sequences, and deletion/non-deletion classification per region is the goal. The task requires insertion or base substitution detection — the article states 'This study currently focuses exclusively on experiments related to deletion variants calling' Input is raw, unaligned read data rather than quality-controlled SAM/BAM files (alignment quality <20 and FLAG 4/>256 fragments must already be removed) Only short-read Illumina data are available — the method is motivated by 'the long reads advantages of third-generation sequencing data' http://edamontology.org/topic_3673 http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 A dual-attention feature-fusion step from DASV that combines spatially attended 100x100 deletion-region images with GAP/GMP-downsampled genomic sequence features, feeding a ResNet multi-scale backbone for deletion structural variant calling in third-generation sequencing data. genomics/v1 10.1093/bib/bbae269
skills.summary: A dual-attention feature-fusion step from DASV that combines spatially attended 100x100 deletion-region images with GAP/GMP-downsampled genomic sequence features, feeding a ResNet multi-scale backbone for deletion structural variant calling in third-generation sequencing data.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The task requires insertion or base substitution detection — the article states 'This study currently focuses exclusively on experiments related to deletion variants calling' Input is raw, unaligned read data rather than quality-controlled SAM/BAM files (alignment quality <20 and FLAG 4/>256 fragments must already be removed) Only short-read Illumina data are available — the method is motivated by 'the long reads advantages of third-generation sequencing data'

skills.description: Use when filtering candidate transcripts from Iso-Seq/PacBio reads of highly similar gene copies, to test whether reads assigned to two candidates could have originated from the same transcript via a weighted-support hypothesis test.
skills.name: chernoff-bound-pvalue-computation
skills.search_text: chernoff-bound-pvalue-computation Use when filtering candidate transcripts from Iso-Seq/PacBio reads of highly similar gene copies, to test whether reads assigned to two candidates could have originated from the same transcript via a weighted-support hypothesis test. Candidate transcript pairs differ by more than the default threshold of 10 variant positions — they are not statistically evaluated Candidate c has X times (default 5, via --min_test_ratio) more support than t, in which case testing is omitted Input is raw un-corrected reads rather than IsoCon candidate transcripts; run the error-correction stage first http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 http://edamontology.org/topic_3168 Computes one-sided significance values P(T >= t) for a weighted-support statistic T (built from per-read Phred-derived error probabilities) in IsoCon's candidate filtering, using a closed-form Chernoff-type upper bound and defaulting the p-value to 0.5 when observed support falls below expectation (t' <= mu). genomics/v1 10.1038/s41467-018-06910-x
skills.summary: Computes one-sided significance values P(T >= t) for a weighted-support statistic T (built from per-read Phred-derived error probabilities) in IsoCon's candidate filtering, using a closed-form Chernoff-type upper bound and defaulting the p-value to 0.5 when observed support falls below expectation (t' <= mu).
skills.when_to_use_negative: Candidate transcript pairs differ by more than the default threshold of 10 variant positions — they are not statistically evaluated Candidate c has X times (default 5, via --min_test_ratio) more support than t, in which case testing is omitted Input is raw un-corrected reads rather than IsoCon candidate transcripts; run the error-correction stage first

skills.description: Use when computing per-context methylation-site coverage fractions in repetitive regions (centromeres, TEs) to compare nanopore methylation calls against BS-seq, e.g. reproducing Fig. 3b-style 88.0% vs 37.7% centromeric CHH coverage benchmarks.
skills.name: chh-methylation-coverage-quantification
skills.search_text: chh-methylation-coverage-quantification Use when computing per-context methylation-site coverage fractions in repetitive regions (centromeres, TEs) to compare nanopore methylation calls against BS-seq, e.g. reproducing Fig. 3b-style 88.0% vs 37.7% centromeric CHH coverage benchmarks. Data from ONT R9.4 FlowCells — Tombo, Megalodon, and DeepSignal-Plant were built for R9.4 and cannot be directly applied to R10.4, and this skill assumes R10.4 chemistry and the DeepPlant Bi-LSTM model. Non-plant or low-CHH-methylation organisms — DeepPlant was trained on plant species screened for abundant high-methylation CHH sites, so CHH generalization outside that training distribution is not supported by this paper. When the goal is per-molecule or per-site methylation-level accuracy (F1, correlation with BS-seq methylation frequency) rather than the fraction of sites meeting a coverage threshold. http://edamontology.org/topic_0160 http://edamontology.org/topic_3295 Quantifies the fraction of CHH cytosines profiled (i.e., meeting a minimum read-coverage threshold) in centromeric vs non-centromeric regions, comparing DeepPlant 5mC calls on ONT R10.4 data against whole-genome BS-seq on the O. sativa T2T-NIP40 reference. It demonstrates that nanopore-based CHH detection rescues coverage in repetitive centromeres where short-read BS-seq fails. genomics/v1 10.1038/s41467-025-58576-x
skills.summary: Quantifies the fraction of CHH cytosines profiled (i.e., meeting a minimum read-coverage threshold) in centromeric vs non-centromeric regions, comparing DeepPlant 5mC calls on ONT R10.4 data against whole-genome BS-seq on the O. sativa T2T-NIP40 reference. It demonstrates that nanopore-based CHH detection rescues coverage in repetitive centromeres where short-read BS-seq fails.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Data from ONT R9.4 FlowCells — Tombo, Megalodon, and DeepSignal-Plant were built for R9.4 and cannot be directly applied to R10.4, and this skill assumes R10.4 chemistry and the DeepPlant Bi-LSTM model. Non-plant or low-CHH-methylation organisms — DeepPlant was trained on plant species screened for abundant high-methylation CHH sites, so CHH generalization outside that training distribution is not supported by this paper. When the goal is per-molecule or per-site methylation-level accuracy (F1, correlation with BS-seq methylation frequency) rather than the fraction of sites meeting a coverage threshold.

skills.description: Use when building training data for plant 5mC methylation detection where CHH-positive samples are scarce and per-9-mer context balance between positive and negative classes is required.
skills.name: chh-methylation-training-data-balancing
skills.search_text: chh-methylation-training-data-balancing Use when building training data for plant 5mC methylation detection where CHH-positive samples are scarce and per-9-mer context balance between positive and negative classes is required. When processing CpG or CHG contexts, where the scarcity of methylation-positive samples and per-9-mer balancing criterion described for CHH does not apply When the positive and negative npz files are already balanced or the input is the final balanced_chh_training_samples.npz, not raw extract_hc_sites output http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 Balances CHH methylation-positive and negative training samples across 9-mer sequence contexts when constructing the DeepPlant dataset from S. miltiorrhiza, S. tuberosum, and R. communis, so every retained 9-mer motif contributes paired positive/negative examples. genomics/v1 10.1038/s41467-025-58576-x
skills.summary: Balances CHH methylation-positive and negative training samples across 9-mer sequence contexts when constructing the DeepPlant dataset from S. miltiorrhiza, S. tuberosum, and R. communis, so every retained 9-mer motif contributes paired positive/negative examples.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When processing CpG or CHG contexts, where the scarcity of methylation-positive samples and per-9-mer balancing criterion described for CHH does not apply When the positive and negative npz files are already balanced or the input is the final balanced_chh_training_samples.npz, not raw extract_hc_sites output

skills.description: Use when assembling or auditing a nanopore 5mC training corpus for CHH methylation detection and you need to measure motif diversity — e.g., computing the fraction of 36,864 possible 9-mer CHH contexts with sufficient positive/negative support across species datasets.
skills.name: chh-motif-kmer-enumeration
skills.search_text: chh-motif-kmer-enumeration Use when assembling or auditing a nanopore 5mC training corpus for CHH methylation detection and you need to measure motif diversity — e.g., computing the fraction of 36,864 possible 9-mer CHH contexts with sufficient positive/negative support across species datasets. The methylation context of interest is CpG or CHG, not CHH — the 36,864 enumeration space and >=50/50 support threshold were designed for CHH scarcity You only need per-site methylation calls from nanopore reads (use DeepPlant or Dorado inference directly, not motif-coverage auditing) Sites lack strand/context annotation or the flanking sequence around each cytosine cannot be extracted from the reference, making 9-mer context reconstruction impossible http://edamontology.org/topic_0654 http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Enumerates all possible 9-mer sequence contexts centered on a CHH motif (9 central trinucleotides x 4^6 flanking bases = 36,864) and quantifies how many are covered by high-confidence CHH methylation training samples, replicating the DeepPlant training-set coverage statistic of 97.2% at >=50 positive and >=50 negative samples per context. genomics/v1 10.1038/s41467-025-58576-x
skills.summary: Enumerates all possible 9-mer sequence contexts centered on a CHH motif (9 central trinucleotides x 4^6 flanking bases = 36,864) and quantifies how many are covered by high-confidence CHH methylation training samples, replicating the DeepPlant training-set coverage statistic of 97.2% at >=50 positive and >=50 negative samples per context.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The methylation context of interest is CpG or CHG, not CHH — the 36,864 enumeration space and >=50/50 support threshold were designed for CHH scarcity You only need per-site methylation calls from nanopore reads (use DeepPlant or Dorado inference directly, not motif-coverage auditing) Sites lack strand/context annotation or the flanking sequence around each cytosine cannot be extracted from the reference, making 9-mer context reconstruction impossible

skills.description: Use when a variant callset has been classified into true and false positives against a truth set (e.g., HGSVC 5,630-insertion set) and you must statistically justify using a sequence feature as a call filter.
skills.name: chi-squared-true-false-positive-comparison
skills.search_text: chi-squared-true-false-positive-comparison Use when a variant callset has been classified into true and false positives against a truth set (e.g., HGSVC 5,630-insertion set) and you must statistically justify using a sequence feature as a call filter. Calls have not been labeled against a truth set — there are no true/false positive classes to tabulate, so χ² comparison is meaningless The hallmark annotations themselves (polyA tails, TTTTT/AA motif) have not yet been extracted from reassembled sequences Evaluating a non-retrotransposition variant type (deletions, inversions) where polyA/L1-motif hallmarks do not apply http://edamontology.org/topic_2269 Applies a χ-squared test to compare the proportion of retrotransposition hallmarks (polyA tails, L1 endonuclease TTTTT/AA target motif) between true and false positives in a TE insertion callset, quantifying whether each hallmark discriminates real insertions from caller noise before adopting it as a filter. genomics/v1 10.1038/s41598-025-98847-7
skills.summary: Applies a χ-squared test to compare the proportion of retrotransposition hallmarks (polyA tails, L1 endonuclease TTTTT/AA target motif) between true and false positives in a TE insertion callset, quantifying whether each hallmark discriminates real insertions from caller noise before adopting it as a filter.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Calls have not been labeled against a truth set — there are no true/false positive classes to tabulate, so χ² comparison is meaningless The hallmark annotations themselves (polyA tails, TTTTT/AA motif) have not yet been extracted from reassembled sequences Evaluating a non-retrotransposition variant type (deletions, inversions) where polyA/L1-motif hallmarks do not apply

skills.description: Use when coding genes predicted from a genome-guided transcriptome assembly (e.g. StringTie GTF of chicken SCO PacBio+Illumina data) are absent from NCBI/Ensembl reference annotations and you need homolog names, functional descriptions, and single-copy vs paralog assignment.
skills.name: chicken-genome-coordinate-mapping
skills.search_text: chicken-genome-coordinate-mapping Use when coding genes predicted from a genome-guided transcriptome assembly (e.g. StringTie GTF of chicken SCO PacBio+Illumina data) are absent from NCBI/Ensembl reference annotations and you need homolog names, functional descriptions, and single-copy vs paralog assignment. The organism lacks an assembled genome and an NCBI-available annotation in GTF format, since the upstream pipeline requires both The goal is de novo gene prediction without a reference genome or homology evidence — use ab initio tools (BRAKER/AUGUSTUS) instead Transcripts are already present in the NCBI RefSeq or Ensembl reference annotations; reconciliation, not homology-based recovery, is the appropriate step http://edamontology.org/topic_0102 http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Recovers genes missing from chicken reference annotations by blasting novel predicted proteins from an assembled SCO transcriptome against the UniProt Gallus gallus proteome (taxid 9031) and mapping hits to genomic loci, classifying single-copy homologs versus paralogs based on homology percentage and locus proximity. genomics/v1 10.1093/gigascience/giac099
skills.summary: Recovers genes missing from chicken reference annotations by blasting novel predicted proteins from an assembled SCO transcriptome against the UniProt Gallus gallus proteome (taxid 9031) and mapping hits to genomic loci, classifying single-copy homologs versus paralogs based on homology percentage and locus proximity.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The organism lacks an assembled genome and an NCBI-available annotation in GTF format, since the upstream pipeline requires both The goal is de novo gene prediction without a reference genome or homology evidence — use ab initio tools (BRAKER/AUGUSTUS) instead Transcripts are already present in the NCBI RefSeq or Ensembl reference annotations; reconciliation, not homology-based recovery, is the appropriate step

skills.description: Use when evaluating whether an assembly or contig-merging step created or removed chimeras, and per-reference reference genomes are available for Nucmer contig alignment and chimera flagging.
skills.name: chimera-detection-in-metagenomic-assemblies
skills.search_text: chimera-detection-in-metagenomic-assemblies Use when evaluating whether an assembly or contig-merging step created or removed chimeras, and per-reference reference genomes are available for Nucmer contig alignment and chimera flagging. No reference genomes are available — chimera flagging here depends on Nucmer alignment to references and cannot be performed from reads alone The question is total assembly size or N50/N90, which the authors describe as 'not very useful for comparing metagenome assembly performance' and which are additionally affected by removal of small contigs Input contigs are <2 kb — the MeGAMerge workflow removes these before merging, so they would not be part of the merged contig set being evaluated http://edamontology.org/topic_0196 http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Identifies chimeric contigs in metagenomic assemblies by aligning contigs to reference genomes with Nucmer and flagging any contig that does not contiguously align to a single reference genome, enabling quantification of chimeras introduced or removed by post-assembly merging (e.g. MeGAMerge). genomics/v1 10.1038/srep06480
skills.summary: Identifies chimeric contigs in metagenomic assemblies by aligning contigs to reference genomes with Nucmer and flagging any contig that does not contiguously align to a single reference genome, enabling quantification of chimeras introduced or removed by post-assembly merging (e.g. MeGAMerge).
skills.when_to_use_negative: No reference genomes are available — chimera flagging here depends on Nucmer alignment to references and cannot be performed from reads alone The question is total assembly size or N50/N90, which the authors describe as 'not very useful for comparing metagenome assembly performance' and which are additionally affected by removal of small contigs Input contigs are <2 kb — the MeGAMerge workflow removes these before merging, so they would not be part of the merged contig set being evaluated

skills.description: Use when aligning Oxford Nanopore MinION reads against a target sequence and reads may map to multiple or disjoint target regions (rearrangements, fusions, chimeras), or when reporting per-chromosome mapping statistics is required.
skills.name: chimeric-and-split-read-mapping-for-rearrangement-detection
skills.search_text: chimeric-and-split-read-mapping-for-rearrangement-detection Use when aligning Oxford Nanopore MinION reads against a target sequence and reads may map to multiple or disjoint target regions (rearrangements, fusions, chimeras), or when reporting per-chromosome mapping statistics is required. The downstream goal is metagenomics analysis — NanoPipe does not yet support it (implementation is planned future work) The reads are not nanopore MinION reads — alignment parameters are specifically adjusted for MinION sequencing technology specifics http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Maps MinION nanopore query reads to a target genome with the LAST aligner (lastal) using last-train-derived parameters, then pipes the output through last-split so reads whose best-scoring alignment is split across target regions receive their most probable part-wise alignments, handling rearrangements, gene fusions, and chimeric sequences. genomics/v1 10.1093/gigascience/giy169
skills.summary: Maps MinION nanopore query reads to a target genome with the LAST aligner (lastal) using last-train-derived parameters, then pipes the output through last-split so reads whose best-scoring alignment is split across target regions receive their most probable part-wise alignments, handling rearrangements, gene fusions, and chimeric sequences.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The downstream goal is metagenomics analysis — NanoPipe does not yet support it (implementation is planned future work) The reads are not nanopore MinION reads — alignment parameters are specifically adjusted for MinION sequencing technology specifics

skills.description: Use when scRNA-seq libraries incompletely capture CAR transgenes and you need per-cell CAR vs wildtype classification from targeted long-read amplicon FASTQ (e.g. ONT reads of 10x 5' cDNA).
skills.name: chimeric-antigen-receptor-transcript-alignment
skills.search_text: chimeric-antigen-receptor-transcript-alignment Use when scRNA-seq libraries incompletely capture CAR transgenes and you need per-cell CAR vs wildtype classification from targeted long-read amplicon FASTQ (e.g. ONT reads of 10x 5' cDNA). When the question requires full-transcriptome gene expression rather than targeted detection of a specific transgene/isoform — nanoranger is a targeted, limited-primer approach When the target locus is far from the 5' end, lowly expressed, or longer than 4 kB — these are suboptimal nanoranger targets When input is bulk (non-single-cell) sequencing without 10x cell barcodes and UMIs, since per-cell classification depends on barcode/UMI extraction http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 http://edamontology.org/topic_0102 Targeted long-read detection and quantification of CD19 CAR transcripts from 10x Genomics 5'-anchored single-cell cDNA libraries using nanoranger, distinguishing the chimeric construct from wildtype CD28 transcripts via a CD28-specific primer and a combined CAR_CD28 reference. genomics/v1 10.1038/s41467-023-44137-7
skills.summary: Targeted long-read detection and quantification of CD19 CAR transcripts from 10x Genomics 5'-anchored single-cell cDNA libraries using nanoranger, distinguishing the chimeric construct from wildtype CD28 transcripts via a CD28-specific primer and a combined CAR_CD28 reference.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the question requires full-transcriptome gene expression rather than targeted detection of a specific transgene/isoform — nanoranger is a targeted, limited-primer approach When the target locus is far from the 5' end, lowly expressed, or longer than 4 kB — these are suboptimal nanoranger targets When input is bulk (non-single-cell) sequencing without 10x cell barcodes and UMIs, since per-cell classification depends on barcode/UMI extraction

skills.description: Use when a de novo draft assembly (e.g. Falcon/Canu contigs) may contain misjoins, and raw Illumina short reads plus PacBio/ONT long reads are available to detect CSE breakpoints before scaffolding with Hi-C or optical maps.
skills.name: chimeric-contig-breakpoint-splitting
skills.search_text: chimeric-contig-breakpoint-splitting Use when a de novo draft assembly (e.g. Falcon/Canu contigs) may contain misjoins, and raw Illumina short reads plus PacBio/ONT long reads are available to detect CSE breakpoints before scaffolding with Hi-C or optical maps. Candidate breakpoints fall in heterozygous loci (clipping ratio within h = 0.4-0.6) — these are haplotype differences, not misjoins, and must not be split The assembly is already reference quality (AQI > 90) with no optical-map or read-mapping conflict signal The genome is polyploid — the paper states CRAQ evaluation accuracy 'may not be as accurate as the benchmarked cases' for higher ploidy levels http://edamontology.org/topic_0102 Detects chimeric misjoined contigs by mapping NGS and SMS reads back to a draft assembly with CRAQ, then splits contigs at Clip-based Structural Error (CSE) breakpoints so downstream scaffolding (Bionano optical maps, Hi-C/3D-DNA) joins the correct pieces. Splitting before rescaffolding raised the A. oxysepala S-AQI from 39.0 to 58.1 and N50 from 20 Mb to 28 Mb. genomics/v1 10.1038/s41467-023-42336-w
skills.summary: Detects chimeric misjoined contigs by mapping NGS and SMS reads back to a draft assembly with CRAQ, then splits contigs at Clip-based Structural Error (CSE) breakpoints so downstream scaffolding (Bionano optical maps, Hi-C/3D-DNA) joins the correct pieces. Splitting before rescaffolding raised the A. oxysepala S-AQI from 39.0 to 58.1 and N50 from 20 Mb to 28 Mb.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Candidate breakpoints fall in heterozygous loci (clipping ratio within h = 0.4-0.6) — these are haplotype differences, not misjoins, and must not be split The assembly is already reference quality (AQI > 90) with no optical-map or read-mapping conflict signal The genome is polyploid — the paper states CRAQ evaluation accuracy 'may not be as accurate as the benchmarked cases' for higher ploidy levels

skills.description: Use when running DBG2OLC overlap/layout on long erroneous PacBio or Nanopore reads with >10x coverage, where chimeric reads and spurious contig identifiers would corrupt the backbone layout.
skills.name: chimeric-read-detection
skills.search_text: chimeric-read-detection Use when running DBG2OLC overlap/layout on long erroneous PacBio or Nanopore reads with >10x coverage, where chimeric reads and spurious contig identifiers would corrupt the backbone layout. Dataset coverage is <=10x long-read coverage, where the README only suggests RemoveChimera 1 for >10x coverage Input contigs come from short-read assemblies that used repeat-resolving heuristics such as gap closing or scaffolding, which the README warns introduces errors and gives poor final results The task is base-level consensus polishing (Sparc/BLASR step), not structural/chimeric read filtering http://edamontology.org/topic_0196 http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Chimera-cleaning step of DBG2OLC that detects chimeric long reads and false contig anchors via multiple sequence alignment of compressed reads during overlap-layout, controlled by the RemoveChimera flag and related thresholds. genomics/v1 10.1038/srep31900
skills.summary: Chimera-cleaning step of DBG2OLC that detects chimeric long reads and false contig anchors via multiple sequence alignment of compressed reads during overlap-layout, controlled by the RemoveChimera flag and related thresholds.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Dataset coverage is <=10x long-read coverage, where the README only suggests RemoveChimera 1 for >10x coverage Input contigs come from short-read assemblies that used repeat-resolving heuristics such as gap closing or scaffolding, which the README warns introduces errors and gives poor final results The task is base-level consensus polishing (Sparc/BLASR step), not structural/chimeric read filtering

skills.description: Use when a Nanopore BAM with BC, U8 and GE tags is about to be collapsed into per-UMI consensus sequences and you must drop chimeric (clipped) reads and MAPQ=0 alignments beforehand.
skills.name: chimeric-read-filtering
skills.search_text: chimeric-read-filtering Use when a Nanopore BAM with BC, U8 and GE tags is about to be collapsed into per-UMI consensus sequences and you must drop chimeric (clipped) reads and MAPQ=0 alignments beforehand. Input is raw Nanopore FASTQ before barcode/UMI assignment — chimeras are first split and reads stranded in Step 1 (NanoporeBC_UMI_finder.jar), not filtered via MAXCLIP on a BAM You only need short-read-free matrix generation (Step 4a) that skips consensus sequences per UMI and thus does not require the ComputeConsensus filtering chain Clipped reads are intentionally being exported for inspection (ExportClippedReads with MINCLIP) rather than discarded http://edamontology.org/topic_0080 http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Removes potentially chimeric cDNA reads (excessive terminal hard/soft clipping, MAXCLIP > 150 nt) and low-confidence alignments (minimap2 MAPQ = 0) from barcode-, UMI- and gene-tagged Nanopore SAM records so that downstream UMI-guided consensus generation in Sicelore's ComputeConsensus is not corrupted by chimeric or poorly mapped molecules. genomics/v1 10.1038/s41467-020-17800-6
skills.summary: Removes potentially chimeric cDNA reads (excessive terminal hard/soft clipping, MAXCLIP > 150 nt) and low-confidence alignments (minimap2 MAPQ = 0) from barcode-, UMI- and gene-tagged Nanopore SAM records so that downstream UMI-guided consensus generation in Sicelore's ComputeConsensus is not corrupted by chimeric or poorly mapped molecules.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw Nanopore FASTQ before barcode/UMI assignment — chimeras are first split and reads stranded in Step 1 (NanoporeBC_UMI_finder.jar), not filtered via MAXCLIP on a BAM You only need short-read-free matrix generation (Step 4a) that skips consensus sequences per UMI and thus does not require the ComputeConsensus filtering chain Clipped reads are intentionally being exported for inspection (ExportClippedReads with MINCLIP) rather than discarded

skills.description: Use when processing PacBio subread BAMs through the nf-core/isoseq pipeline and primer removal (LIMA) is done: CCS reads must be screened for chimeric sequences before FLNC reads are converted and polyA-trimmed.
skills.name: chimeric-read-filtering-long-reads
skills.search_text: chimeric-read-filtering-long-reads Use when processing PacBio subread BAMs through the nf-core/isoseq pipeline and primer removal (LIMA) is done: CCS reads must be screened for chimeric sequences before FLNC reads are converted and polyA-trimmed. Input reads are raw subreads that have not yet been converted to CCS or primer-trimmed by LIMA — run ccs and LIMA first The analysis goal is splice-aware genome alignment (minimap2/uLTRA) or transcriptome collapsing rather than FLNC read cleaning Reads are short-read or non-PacBio transcriptomic data outside the Iso-Seq subread-to-FLNC preprocessing context http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Detection and removal of chimeric PacBio Iso-Seq reads using isoseq3 refine, the ISOSEQ REFINE step of the nf-core/isoseq pipeline, applied to primer-trimmed CCS reads to yield FLNC BAM output. genomics/v1 10.1093/bioinformatics/btad150
skills.summary: Detection and removal of chimeric PacBio Iso-Seq reads using isoseq3 refine, the ISOSEQ REFINE step of the nf-core/isoseq pipeline, applied to primer-trimmed CCS reads to yield FLNC BAM output.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input reads are raw subreads that have not yet been converted to CCS or primer-trimmed by LIMA — run ccs and LIMA first The analysis goal is splice-aware genome alignment (minimap2/uLTRA) or transcriptome collapsing rather than FLNC read cleaning Reads are short-read or non-PacBio transcriptomic data outside the Iso-Seq subread-to-FLNC preprocessing context

skills.description: Use when running DBG2OLC overlap/layout on raw long (PacBio/3GS) reads for hybrid assembly and the long-read set may contain chimeric molecules, especially with >10x long-read coverage.
skills.name: chimeric-read-removal
skills.search_text: chimeric-read-removal Use when running DBG2OLC overlap/layout on raw long (PacBio/3GS) reads for hybrid assembly and the long-read set may contain chimeric molecules, especially with >10x long-read coverage. skills.name: classification-difficulty-index-computation
skills.search_text: classification-difficulty-index-computation Use when benchmarking single-cell annotation methods across multiple reference/query test pairs and you need a principled ranking of test difficulty to show which methods remain stable as batch effects grow and fewer query cell types are covered by the reference. The analysis goal is a single reference/query pair rather than a panel of benchmark tests — CDI ranking is meaningless with one test. You need an absolute difficulty score for one method in isolation; the CDI regression comparison requires per-test accuracies from multiple methods on identical test sets. Reference and query share cell types and platform with no batch effects — F1-ASW batch-effect scoring and classifiability proportions will be uninformative. http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Computes a classification difficulty index (CDI) that ranks reference-based classification (RBC) benchmark tests by difficulty, combining an F1-ASW batch-effect score with the proportion of classifiable query cells, and then quantifies how each method's accuracy degrades with CDI rank via OLS slope Z-scores. genomics/v1 10.1093/nar/gkab1275

skills.search_text: classification-metrics-computation Use when you have per-read prediction outputs (.tsv) from a signal-based RNA classifier (e.g., RISER run over HeLa fast5-derived signals) and need accuracy/precision/TPR/FPR to check reproduction of published accuracy (mRNA ~94%, mtRNA ~99%). skills.search_text: clinical-hla-type-comparison Use when you have HLAminer prediction CSVs (HLAminer_HPRA.csv/HLAminer_HPTASR.csv) for individuals with clinically derived HLA types (e.g. NA12878, NA19240 from Tables 4/5) and need to quantify 2-digit group-level concordance. The individual/sample has no clinically derived HLA types available, so there is no ground truth to compare against. You need allele-level (4-digit) concordance assessment — the article's benchmark is group-level (2-digit) resolution only. The goal is to generate the predictions themselves (alignment and streaming into HLAminer.pl) rather than to score already-produced HLAminer_HPRA.csv files. Benchmarks HLAminer group-level (2-digit) HLA-I and HLA-II predictions from long-read WGS datasets against clinically confirmed HLA types, computing per-gene and per-class concordance (reported as 94% HLA-I and 88% HLA-II accuracy). This is the validation step that turns HLAminer_HPRA.csv prediction files into a quantified accuracy report. genomics/v1 10.1002/cpz1.70124
skills.summary: Benchmarks HLAminer group-level (2-digit) HLA-I and HLA-II predictions from long-read WGS datasets against clinically confirmed HLA types, computing per-gene and per-class concordance (reported as 94% HLA-I and 88% HLA-II accuracy). This is the validation step that turns HLAminer_HPRA.csv prediction files into a quantified accuracy report.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The individual/sample has no clinically derived HLA types available, so there is no ground truth to compare against. You need allele-level (4-digit) concordance assessment — the article's benchmark is group-level (2-digit) resolution only. The goal is to generate the predictions themselves (alignment and streaming into HLAminer.pl) rather than to score already-produced HLAminer_HPRA.csv files.

skills.description: Use when a germline SNV/InDel VCF (PASS-filtered, multi-allelic sites decomposed, chrM removed) must be enriched with clinical significance, biomarker, population allele frequency and in-silico deleteriousness annotations before ACMG/AMP classification.
skills.name: clinical-variant-database-matching
skills.search_text: clinical-variant-database-matching Use when a germline SNV/InDel VCF (PASS-filtered, multi-allelic sites decomposed, chrM removed) must be enriched with clinical significance, biomarker, population allele frequency and in-silico deleteriousness annotations before ACMG/AMP classification. Input is somatic tumor variant data — CPSR targets germline variant interpretation, and the accompanying PCGR tool is the intended choice for somatic SNVs/InDels, CNAs and RNA fusions. Variants are not in VCF format or are multi-allelic without prior decomposition, since the annotation step expects decomposed PASS records with one picked consequence block each. The goal is de novo variant discovery or calling rather than annotation of existing germline calls against clinical databases. http://edamontology.org/topic_0199 http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Annotate germline variant calls against public clinical and population databases — ClinVar, CIViC, gnomAD, dbNSFP, cancerhotspots.org and the GWAS Catalog — as CPSR does in its functional variant annotation step using VEP and vcfanno. genomics/v1 10.1002/ijc.33749
skills.summary: Annotate germline variant calls against public clinical and population databases — ClinVar, CIViC, gnomAD, dbNSFP, cancerhotspots.org and the GWAS Catalog — as CPSR does in its functional variant annotation step using VEP and vcfanno.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is somatic tumor variant data — CPSR targets germline variant interpretation, and the accompanying PCGR tool is the intended choice for somatic SNVs/InDels, CNAs and RNA fusions. Variants are not in VCF format or are multi-allelic without prior decomposition, since the annotation step expects decomposed PASS records with one picked consequence block each. The goal is de novo variant discovery or calling rather than annotation of existing germline calls against clinical databases.

skills.description: Use when a variant list must be periodically re-annotated and changes such as a ClinVar classification update, a ≥1-order-of-magnitude gnomAD allele-frequency shift, or newly reported COSMIC presence must be flagged.
skills.name: clinvar-classification-diff-tracking
skills.search_text: clinvar-classification-diff-tracking Use when a variant list must be periodically re-annotated and changes such as a ClinVar classification update, a ≥1-order-of-magnitude gnomAD allele-frequency shift, or newly reported COSMIC presence must be flagged. Allele frequencies differing by less than one order of magnitude (e.g., 3.830e-06 vs 3.979e-06) — by design this must not produce an alert Re-execution of the sequence analysis pipeline (alignment/variant calling) or reference genome updates — this skill only tracks annotation/knowledge-base updates Untrusted data destined for a public platform where privacy policies prevent uploading genetic data — prefer a local deployment of the tool instead http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Detects changes in a variant's annotations (ClinVar CLNSIG classification, gnomAD allele frequency, COSMIC presence) between an older and a newer annotation snapshot and emits an email/JSON change report per variant, as implemented by VariantAlert. genomics/v1 10.1002/humu.24495
skills.summary: Detects changes in a variant's annotations (ClinVar CLNSIG classification, gnomAD allele frequency, COSMIC presence) between an older and a newer annotation snapshot and emits an email/JSON change report per variant, as implemented by VariantAlert.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Allele frequencies differing by less than one order of magnitude (e.g., 3.830e-06 vs 3.979e-06) — by design this must not produce an alert Re-execution of the sequence analysis pipeline (alignment/variant calling) or reference genome updates — this skill only tracks annotation/knowledge-base updates Untrusted data destined for a public platform where privacy policies prevent uploading genetic data — prefer a local deployment of the tool instead

skills.description: Use when you need to calibrate or validate automated germline variant pathogenicity score thresholds against ClinVar expert-reviewed assertions and report per-class concordance.
skills.name: clinvar-concordance-evaluation
skills.search_text: clinvar-concordance-evaluation Use when you need to calibrate or validate automated germline variant pathogenicity score thresholds against ClinVar expert-reviewed assertions and report per-class concordance. The variants of interest are somatic/tumor variants interpreted for oncogenicity and actionability (PCGR's VICC/CGC/ClinGen and AMP/ASCO/CAP scope), not germline cancer predisposition classification. ClinVar assertions lack review status (fewer than two stars) — unreviewed assertions are too noisy to serve as a calibration ground truth. You only need to run CPSR's classification on a sample VCF without evaluating or recalibrating the score thresholds themselves. http://edamontology.org/topic_3053 Calibrates and validates a variant classification scheme (e.g. CPSR's point-based ACMG/AMP implementation) against high-confidence ClinVar assertions, measuring per-class concordance for P/LP, VUS, and B/LB calls across five score-to-classification cut-offs. genomics/v1 10.1002/ijc.33749
skills.summary: Calibrates and validates a variant classification scheme (e.g. CPSR's point-based ACMG/AMP implementation) against high-confidence ClinVar assertions, measuring per-class concordance for P/LP, VUS, and B/LB calls across five score-to-classification cut-offs.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The variants of interest are somatic/tumor variants interpreted for oncogenicity and actionability (PCGR's VICC/CGC/ClinGen and AMP/ASCO/CAP scope), not germline cancer predisposition classification. ClinVar assertions lack review status (fewer than two stars) — unreviewed assertions are too noisy to serve as a calibration ground truth. You only need to run CPSR's classification on a sample VCF without evaluating or recalibrating the score thresholds themselves.

skills.description: Use when you need to verify which of the 11 eDiVA-Score annotation features drive pathogenicity predictions, or when interpreting how ClinVar-derived pathogenicity classifiers weight allele frequency, functional impact, and conservation signals.
skills.name: clinvar-gnomad-training-set-interpretation
skills.search_text: clinvar-gnomad-training-set-interpretation Use when you need to verify which of the 11 eDiVA-Score annotation features drive pathogenicity predictions, or when interpreting how ClinVar-derived pathogenicity classifiers weight allele frequency, functional impact, and conservation signals. Input is already a ranked feature-importance table or only a variant list without the trained model object The goal is variant filtering or prioritization for a pedigree (use eDiVA-Prioritize skills instead of model-interpretation) The classifier was not trained on ClinVar pathogenic variants with the paper's 11 genomic and evolutionary features, making importance ranks incomparable to the reported ordering http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_0102 Reproduce and interpret the feature-importance ranking of the eDiVA-Score random forest, which was trained on ~15,000 ClinVar pathogenic variants using population allele frequencies (1000 Genomes, GnomAD), functional impact scores (Condel, CADD, Eigen, Mutation Assessor), and PhastCons/PhyloP conservation signatures. genomics/v1 10.1002/humu.23772
skills.summary: Reproduce and interpret the feature-importance ranking of the eDiVA-Score random forest, which was trained on ~15,000 ClinVar pathogenic variants using population allele frequencies (1000 Genomes, GnomAD), functional impact scores (Condel, CADD, Eigen, Mutation Assessor), and PhastCons/PhyloP conservation signatures.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a ranked feature-importance table or only a variant list without the trained model object The goal is variant filtering or prioritization for a pedigree (use eDiVA-Prioritize skills instead of model-interpretation) The classifier was not trained on ClinVar pathogenic variants with the paper's 11 genomic and evolutionary features, making importance ranks incomparable to the reported ordering
