skills.summary: A benchmarking skill for computing normalized speedup ratios of raw nanopore signal mappers: it runs RawHash2 against RawHash, UNCALLED, and Sigmap on identical R9.4.1 FAST5 datasets, parses each tool's PAF output, and derives mapped-bases-per-second-per-thread throughput ratios plus early-termination sequencing-length reduction.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is accuracy (F1) benchmarking rather than speed — that requires a separate accuracy evaluation protocol, not throughput ratio computation Input data is R10.4 or POD5/SLOW5/BLOW5 — the reported speedup ratios (26.5x/19.2x/4.0x) were established for R9.4.1 FAST5 data with default parameters, and UNCALLED can only be applied to legacy R9.4.1 data The task is all-vs-all overlap generation with Rawsamble (no reference genome) rather than reference-guided mapping throughput

skills.description: Use when IsoTools (long-read LRTS) differential splicing results need independent validation against a short-read tool such as rMATS, and a quantitative agreement metric (Spearman correlation) is required.
skills.name: cross-tool-splicing-statistics-comparison
skills.search_text: cross-tool-splicing-statistics-comparison Use when IsoTools (long-read LRTS) differential splicing results need independent validation against a short-read tool such as rMATS, and a quantitative agreement metric (Spearman correlation) is required. The transcriptome has not been reconstructed and quality-controlled in IsoTools yet (no saved pickle from bam import) — run the import/QC workflow first The goal is de novo event discovery, not cross-tool statistical agreement — use IsoTools' segment-graph event extraction alone Only short-read RNA-seq data is available and no LRTS bam files exist — IsoTools' differential event framework and this comparison are designed for long-read transcriptome sequencing data http://edamontology.org/topic_0102 http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Validates long-read differential splicing results by exporting IsoTools alternative splicing events for rMATS and comparing the two tools' statistics with a Spearman rank correlation, as demonstrated on PacBio LRTS data of valproic-acid-treated vs control human hepatocytes. genomics/v1 10.1093/bioinformatics/btad364
skills.summary: Validates long-read differential splicing results by exporting IsoTools alternative splicing events for rMATS and comparing the two tools' statistics with a Spearman rank correlation, as demonstrated on PacBio LRTS data of valproic-acid-treated vs control human hepatocytes.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The transcriptome has not been reconstructed and quality-controlled in IsoTools yet (no saved pickle from bam import) — run the import/QC workflow first The goal is de novo event discovery, not cross-tool statistical agreement — use IsoTools' segment-graph event extraction alone Only short-read RNA-seq data is available and no LRTS bam files exist — IsoTools' differential event framework and this comparison are designed for long-read transcriptome sequencing data

skills.description: Use when you need to score a ΔΨ regression model on the CAGI-5 vex-seq data by 10-fold cross-validation on TR957 plus a blind test on TS1098, comparing predicted vs. measured delta-PSI via PCC.
skills.name: cross-validation-pcc-evaluation
skills.search_text: cross-validation-pcc-evaluation Use when you need to score a ΔΨ regression model on the CAGI-5 vex-seq data by 10-fold cross-validation on TR957 plus a blind test on TS1098, comparing predicted vs. measured delta-PSI via PCC. There are no measured/observed ΔΨ values for the variants, so a Pearson correlation against ground truth cannot be computed. The task is variant classification or harmfulness ranking (e.g. the SilVA-style synonymous-variant task) rather than regression on continuous ΔΨ values. The variant set is the heavily filtered 53-mutation subset used only for the 2-standard-deviation sensitivity analysis, where PCC estimates are unstable. http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 http://edamontology.org/topic_3512 http://edamontology.org/topic_2269 Evaluates ΔΨ-prediction regression models (e.g. PredPSI-SVR trained with libsvm) by 10-fold cross-validation on the vex-seq training set (TR957) and on an independent blind test set (TS1098), reporting the Pearson correlation coefficient (PCC) between predicted and measured ΔΨ. genomics/v1 10.1002/humu.23785
skills.summary: Evaluates ΔΨ-prediction regression models (e.g. PredPSI-SVR trained with libsvm) by 10-fold cross-validation on the vex-seq training set (TR957) and on an independent blind test set (TS1098), reporting the Pearson correlation coefficient (PCC) between predicted and measured ΔΨ.
skills.when_to_use_negative: There are no measured/observed ΔΨ values for the variants, so a Pearson correlation against ground truth cannot be computed. The task is variant classification or harmfulness ranking (e.g. the SilVA-style synonymous-variant task) rather than regression on continuous ΔΨ values. The variant set is the heavily filtered 53-mutation subset used only for the 2-standard-deviation sensitivity analysis, where PCC estimates are unstable.

skills.description: Use when a newly trained Chiron checkpoint (e.g., 3 epochs on ~4,000 E. coli/Lambda reads on a K80) must be judged fit for use by held-out read-level accuracy rather than training loss alone.
skills.name: cross-validation-read-level-accuracy-evaluation
skills.search_text: cross-validation-read-level-accuracy-evaluation Use when a newly trained Chiron checkpoint (e.g., 3 epochs on ~4,000 E. coli/Lambda reads on a K80) must be judged fit for use by held-out read-level accuracy rather than training loss alone. All reads were included in training (no cross-validation remainder exists), so held-out read-level accuracy cannot be computed without re-partitioning. Evaluating a pre-shipped DNA_default/RNA_default model on the README sample fast5 files rather than validating a user-trained checkpoint. Human DNA data, where the paper reports a larger ~2% accuracy gap to Albacore — read-level parity conclusions from 4,000 bacterial/viral reads do not transfer. http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_0102 Validates a freshly trained Chiron CNN+RNN+CTC basecalling checkpoint by measuring read-level accuracy on the cross-validation remainder (reads excluded from the small ~4,000-read training set), benchmarked against ONT Albacore accuracy expectations. genomics/v1 10.1093/gigascience/giy037
skills.summary: Validates a freshly trained Chiron CNN+RNN+CTC basecalling checkpoint by measuring read-level accuracy on the cross-validation remainder (reads excluded from the small ~4,000-read training set), benchmarked against ONT Albacore accuracy expectations.
skills.when_to_use_negative: All reads were included in training (no cross-validation remainder exists), so held-out read-level accuracy cannot be computed without re-partitioning. Evaluating a pre-shipped DNA_default/RNA_default model on the README sample fast5 files rather than validating a user-trained checkpoint. Human DNA data, where the paper reports a larger ~2% accuracy gap to Albacore — read-level parity conclusions from 4,000 bacterial/viral reads do not transfer.

skills.description: Use when the fusion-driver exon of a known gene (e.g., BRAF Exon 10, EWSR1 Exon 7, SS18 Exon 9) is known but the fusion partner gene and breakpoint are unknown and Cas9-enriched nanopore sequencing is planned.
skills.name: crrna-guide-sequence-design
skills.search_text: crrna-guide-sequence-design Use when the fusion-driver exon of a known gene (e.g., BRAF Exon 10, EWSR1 Exon 7, SS18 Exon 9) is known but the fusion partner gene and breakpoint are unknown and Cas9-enriched nanopore sequencing is planned. Both fusion partners and the breakpoint are already known — then targeted breakpoint PCR or a two-partner design is sufficient, and the article notes WGA on low-input DNA only works with prior knowledge of both partners Input DNA is fragmented, e.g. FFPE material — the FUDGE crRNA protocol is reported to most likely fail on such degraded DNA No NGG PAM exists on the strand that would orient Cas9 cutting toward the unknown fusion partner at the driver exon — a strand-directed guide cannot be designed and the enrichment directionality requirement fails Design strand-directed CRISPR-Cas9 crRNAs against known fusion-driver exon loci so that nanopore sequencing reads extend from the cut site into the unknown fusion partner, as implemented in FUDGE (FUsion Detection from Gene Enrichment). genomics/v1 10.1038/s41467-020-16641-7
skills.summary: Design strand-directed CRISPR-Cas9 crRNAs against known fusion-driver exon loci so that nanopore sequencing reads extend from the cut site into the unknown fusion partner, as implemented in FUDGE (FUsion Detection from Gene Enrichment).
skills.when_to_use_negative: Both fusion partners and the breakpoint are already known — then targeted breakpoint PCR or a two-partner design is sufficient, and the article notes WGA on low-input DNA only works with prior knowledge of both partners Input DNA is fragmented, e.g. FFPE material — the FUDGE crRNA protocol is reported to most likely fail on such degraded DNA No NGG PAM exists on the strand that would orient Cas9 cutting toward the unknown fusion partner at the driver exon — a strand-directed guide cannot be designed and the enrichment directionality requirement fails

skills.description: Use when analysing ONT cDNA (or Illumina TruSeq) alignments of an IVT mRNA product and you need to split reads into on-target mRNA versus off-target RNA classes, including reads derived from cryptic transcription start sites.
skills.name: cryptic-transcription-start-site-detection
skills.search_text: cryptic-transcription-start-site-detection Use when analysing ONT cDNA (or Illumina TruSeq) alignments of an IVT mRNA product and you need to split reads into on-target mRNA versus off-target RNA classes, including reads derived from cryptic transcription start sites. Input is raw FASTQ that has not yet been barcode-trimmed (Porechop) and aligned to a reference to produce a sorted, indexed BAM The question is poly(A) tail length, sequence identity, or nucleoside-modification chemistry rather than off-target RNA classification No reference mRNA feature boundaries exist to define the on-target interval for strand-aware intersect http://edamontology.org/topic_0102 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 A VAX-seq analysis skill that classifies reads in sorted, indexed BAM alignments of in-vitro-transcribed mRNA into on-target versus off-target classes — upstream, downstream, antisense, cryptic transcription start site (TSS)-derived, and contaminant reads such as E. coli — to quantify mRNA product purity. genomics/v1 10.1038/s41467-023-41354-y
skills.summary: A VAX-seq analysis skill that classifies reads in sorted, indexed BAM alignments of in-vitro-transcribed mRNA into on-target versus off-target classes — upstream, downstream, antisense, cryptic transcription start site (TSS)-derived, and contaminant reads such as E. coli — to quantify mRNA product purity.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw FASTQ that has not yet been barcode-trimmed (Porechop) and aligned to a reference to produce a sorted, indexed BAM The question is poly(A) tail length, sequence identity, or nucleoside-modification chemistry rather than off-target RNA classification No reference mRNA feature boundaries exist to define the on-target interval for strand-aware intersect

skills.description: Use when basecalling raw fast5 nanopore signal with Chiron and you must choose between greedy CTC decoding for throughput and beam-search decoding for maximum read-level accuracy.
skills.name: ctc-beam-search-decoding
skills.search_text: ctc-beam-search-decoding Use when basecalling raw fast5 nanopore signal with Chiron and you must choose between greedy CTC decoding for throughput and beam-search decoding for maximum read-level accuracy. Input is already basecalled FASTQ/FASTA — decoding is only applied to raw signal fast5 files. Direct-RNA data without prior preprocessing — use BoostNano to trim adapter and polyA tails before RNA basecalling. Throughput-constrained production runs where the ~2% accuracy gain of beam search over greedy does not justify the slower decoding speed. http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_3168 Decodes Chiron's CTC output layer from raw nanopore signal into nucleotide sequence, choosing between a greedy decoder (--beam 0) and a beam-search decoder (--beam <width>) that trades decoding speed for higher basecalling accuracy. genomics/v1 10.1093/gigascience/giy037
skills.summary: Decodes Chiron's CTC output layer from raw nanopore signal into nucleotide sequence, choosing between a greedy decoder (--beam 0) and a beam-search decoder (--beam <width>) that trades decoding speed for higher basecalling accuracy.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already basecalled FASTQ/FASTA — decoding is only applied to raw signal fast5 files. Direct-RNA data without prior preprocessing — use BoostNano to trim adapter and polyA tails before RNA basecalling. Throughput-constrained production runs where the ~2% accuracy gain of beam search over greedy does not justify the slower decoding speed.

The basecalling pipeline still relies on event segmentation into k-mer signal segments — CTC is specifically for segmentation-free end-to-end basecalling You need the fastest possible decoding and accuracy loss from greedy decoding is unacceptable for your application http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 Implement and configure the CTC loss and decoding layer of a segmentation-free basecaller like Chiron, offering a greedy decoder (beam 0) and a beam search decoder (default width 30 in the dna-pre preset) over per-timestep nucleotide logits. genomics/v1 10.1093/gigascience/giy037
skills.summary: Implement and configure the CTC loss and decoding layer of a segmentation-free basecaller like Chiron, offering a greedy decoder (beam 0) and a beam search decoder (default width 30 in the dna-pre preset) over per-timestep nucleotide logits.

skills.description: Use when training a nanopore signal simulator (e.g. NanoSimFormer) and you need the generated signals to be decode-accurate under a fixed production basecaller, via a differentiable CTC objective.
skills.name: ctc-loss-computation
skills.search_text: ctc-loss-computation Use when training a nanopore signal simulator (e.g. NanoSimFormer) and you need the generated signals to be decode-accurate under a fixed production basecaller, via a differentiable CTC objective. You only need to basecall existing reads into FASTQ/BAM — use Dorado directly via the simulate --basecall option instead of a training loss. You are preparing the training data rather than training: dataset creation uses remora signal-to-sequence alignment, not the CTC objective. The simulator output is not intended to be decoded by an ONT basecaller (e.g. purely statistical k-mer-level simulation), where basecaller guidance is unnecessary. http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Computes a basecaller-guided CTC negative log-likelihood loss by running simulated nanopore signals through a frozen, pre-trained ONT basecaller (Dorado v5 super-accuracy model loaded via bonito), so the Transformer simulator is trained to produce signals the basecaller decodes correctly. genomics/v1 10.1093/bioinformatics/btag402
skills.summary: Computes a basecaller-guided CTC negative log-likelihood loss by running simulated nanopore signals through a frozen, pre-trained ONT basecaller (Dorado v5 super-accuracy model loaded via bonito), so the Transformer simulator is trained to produce signals the basecaller decodes correctly.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You only need to basecall existing reads into FASTQ/BAM — use Dorado directly via the simulate --basecall option instead of a training loss. You are preparing the training data rather than training: dataset creation uses remora signal-to-sequence alignment, not the CTC objective. The simulator output is not intended to be decoded by an ONT basecaller (e.g. purely statistical k-mer-level simulation), where basecaller guidance is unnecessary.

skills.description: Use when raw nanopore fast5 signals and reference-derived labels are available and a custom basecalling model must be trained or fine-tuned (e.g. new species, modified bases) instead of using a pretrained basecaller.
skills.name: ctc-neural-network-training
skills.search_text: ctc-neural-network-training Use when raw nanopore fast5 signals and reference-derived labels are available and a custom basecalling model must be trained or fine-tuned (e.g. new species, modified bases) instead of using a pretrained basecaller. skills.search_text: de-bruijn-graph-construction Use when assembling de novo transcriptome data and the goal is an isoform-preserving assembly graph from Illumina FASTQ reads, rather than a genome-oriented contig set that collapses alternative splicing paths. When the input is genomic (single-cell or bacterial) DNA rather than transcriptomic RNA-Seq — the standard SPAdes genome pipeline and its graph handling are appropriate there When the goal is to collapse alternative isoforms into gene-level contigs; this graph deliberately preserves branching vertices and multiple distinct paths through shared k-mer junctions When using k-mer sizes below 29 for transcriptome assembly — small k-values dramatically increase erroneous contigs from transcripts sharing k-mers http://edamontology.org/topic_0196 http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 Builds a condensed de Bruijn assembly graph from RNA-Seq reads at rnaSPAdes-style k-mer sizes, compressing non-branching paths into edges while preserving every branching vertex so that alternatively spliced isoform paths are retained rather than collapsed. genomics/v1 10.1093/gigascience/giz100
skills.summary: Builds a condensed de Bruijn assembly graph from RNA-Seq reads at rnaSPAdes-style k-mer sizes, compressing non-branching paths into edges while preserving every branching vertex so that alternatively spliced isoform paths are retained rather than collapsed.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the input is genomic (single-cell or bacterial) DNA rather than transcriptomic RNA-Seq — the standard SPAdes genome pipeline and its graph handling are appropriate there When the goal is to collapse alternative isoforms into gene-level contigs; this graph deliberately preserves branching vertices and multiple distinct paths through shared k-mer junctions When using k-mer sizes below 29 for transcriptome assembly — small k-values dramatically increase erroneous contigs from transcripts sharing k-mers

skills.description: Use when polishing MSA-derived consensus sequences (or contigs) that still contain errors, and a local de Bruijn graph over a single window's sequences can recover low-quality regions via solid k-mer anchoring.
skills.name: de-bruijn-graph-construction-from-window-sequences
skills.search_text: de-bruijn-graph-construction-from-window-sequences Use when polishing MSA-derived consensus sequences (or contigs) that still contain errors, and a local de Bruijn graph over a single window's sequences can recover low-quality regions via solid k-mer anchoring. The input is raw long reads requiring the first correction phase (overlap computation and MSA consensus) rather than polishing of already-computed consensuses. A weak region has no connecting path between its flanking solid anchors — the region is left unpolished, so the graph search cannot help. Window contains fewer than the required number of solid anchors (--minAnchors, default 2), so consensus/polishing cannot proceed meaningfully. http://edamontology.org/topic_0196 http://edamontology.org/topic_3673 Builds a small-k local de Bruijn graph from the sequences of a single MSA window and polishes the consensus by replacing weak-k-mer regions with paths anchored on solid k-mers, as done in CONSENT's second correction phase. genomics/v1 10.1038/s41598-020-80757-5
skills.summary: Builds a small-k local de Bruijn graph from the sequences of a single MSA window and polishes the consensus by replacing weak-k-mer regions with paths anchored on solid k-mers, as done in CONSENT's second correction phase.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is raw long reads requiring the first correction phase (overlap computation and MSA consensus) rather than polishing of already-computed consensuses. A weak region has no connecting path between its flanking solid anchors — the region is left unpolished, so the graph search cannot help. Window contains fewer than the required number of solid anchors (--minAnchors, default 2), so consensus/polishing cannot proceed meaningfully.

skills.description: Use when running rnaSPAdes (or SPAdes-family assemblers) on Illumina RNA-Seq reads and you must decide the multi-k schedule: lower k ≈ read_length/3 (min 29) and upper k ≈ largest odd number ≤ read_length/2 − 1.
skills.name: de-bruijn-graph-k-mer-parameter-selection
skills.search_text: de-bruijn-graph-k-mer-parameter-selection Use when running rnaSPAdes (or SPAdes-family assemblers) on Illumina RNA-Seq reads and you must decide the multi-k schedule: lower k ≈ read_length/3 (min 29) and upper k ≈ largest odd number ≤ read_length/2 − 1. Input is long reads (Oxford Nanopore/PacBio) rather than short Illumina reads — the k-mer de Bruijn schedule is designed for short-read RNA-Seq Data is metatranscriptomic; the k selection logic was designed for single-organism RNA-Seq and the authors note the approach 'was not designed or evaluated for metatranscriptome assembly' Assembly quality is limited by transcript filtration thresholds rather than k coverage — tune filtration (Supplementary Table S14) instead of re-deriving the k schedule http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 Selects the set of de Bruijn graph k-mer sizes (and the 200 bp contig cutoff) used when assembling transcriptomic reads with rnaSPAdes, since k choice directly governs recovery of low-coverage genes versus erroneous edges in RNA-Seq assemblies. genomics/v1 10.1093/gigascience/giz100
skills.summary: Selects the set of de Bruijn graph k-mer sizes (and the 200 bp contig cutoff) used when assembling transcriptomic reads with rnaSPAdes, since k choice directly governs recovery of low-coverage genes versus erroneous edges in RNA-Seq assemblies.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is long reads (Oxford Nanopore/PacBio) rather than short Illumina reads — the k-mer de Bruijn schedule is designed for short-read RNA-Seq Data is metatranscriptomic; the k selection logic was designed for single-organism RNA-Seq and the authors note the approach 'was not designed or evaluated for metatranscriptome assembly' Assembly quality is limited by transcript filtration thresholds rather than k coverage — tune filtration (Supplementary Table S14) instead of re-deriving the k schedule

skills.description: Use when starting a DBG2OLC hybrid assembly and you have ~50x Illumina FASTQ/FASTQ.gz short reads that must first be converted into raw DBG contigs (Contigs.txt) before overlap/layout with long reads.
skills.name: de-bruijn-graph-short-read-preassembly
skills.search_text: de-bruijn-graph-short-read-preassembly Use when starting a DBG2OLC hybrid assembly and you have ~50x Illumina FASTQ/FASTQ.gz short reads that must first be converted into raw DBG contigs (Contigs.txt) before overlap/layout with long reads. The long-read dataset alone is sufficient and a pure long-read assembler (HGAP, Falcon, MHAP-based CA) is intended instead of the hybrid route You need finished, scaffolded short-read contigs — scaffolding/gap closing introduces errors that the DBG2OLC README warns will produce poor final results Coverage is far below ~50x Illumina, where NodeCovTh 1 / EdgeCovTh 0 defaults were validated http://edamontology.org/topic_0196 http://edamontology.org/topic_3697 Preassemble highly accurate NGS short reads (e.g., 50x Illumina) into raw, unscaffolded de Bruijn graph contigs with SparseAssembler; these contigs become the 'Contigs' input that DBG2OLC compresses long erroneous 3GS reads against in hybrid assembly. genomics/v1 10.1038/srep31900
skills.summary: Preassemble highly accurate NGS short reads (e.g., 50x Illumina) into raw, unscaffolded de Bruijn graph contigs with SparseAssembler; these contigs become the 'Contigs' input that DBG2OLC compresses long erroneous 3GS reads against in hybrid assembly.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The long-read dataset alone is sufficient and a pure long-read assembler (HGAP, Falcon, MHAP-based CA) is intended instead of the hybrid route You need finished, scaffolded short-read contigs — scaffolding/gap closing introduces errors that the DBG2OLC README warns will produce poor final results Coverage is far below ~50x Illumina, where NodeCovTh 1 / EdgeCovTh 0 defaults were validated

skills.description: Use when benchmarking or verifying untargeted nanopore viral pipelines on known-virus samples, especially at high mutation levels or with partial genomes (<50% completeness) where reference-tethered pipelines fail.
skills.name: de-novo-contig-to-consensus-evaluation
skills.search_text: de-novo-contig-to-consensus-evaluation Use when benchmarking or verifying untargeted nanopore viral pipelines on known-virus samples, especially at high mutation levels or with partial genomes (<50% completeness) where reference-tethered pipelines fail. When the goal is de novo discovery of novel, unknown viruses — ViMOP matches contigs to known references in its database and is intended for known virus species in untargeted data When working with large DNA viruses with extensive repetitive regions (e.g. mpox), where the pipeline itself warns assemblies may be inaccurate draft genomes When the input is not nanopore FASTQ data from untargeted/metagenomic sequencing http://edamontology.org/topic_0196 http://edamontology.org/topic_0102 Evaluates ViMOP's de novo assembly-to-consensus strategy: contigs assembled from untargeted nanopore reads are BLASTed against a virus reference database to select reference genomes, which then guide reference-based consensus reconstruction; benchmarked against INSaFLU-TELEVIR and VirDetector on simulated high-mutation read sets. genomics/v1 10.1093/bioinformatics/btaf687
skills.summary: Evaluates ViMOP's de novo assembly-to-consensus strategy: contigs assembled from untargeted nanopore reads are BLASTed against a virus reference database to select reference genomes, which then guide reference-based consensus reconstruction; benchmarked against INSaFLU-TELEVIR and VirDetector on simulated high-mutation read sets.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the goal is de novo discovery of novel, unknown viruses — ViMOP matches contigs to known references in its database and is intended for known virus species in untargeted data When working with large DNA viruses with extensive repetitive regions (e.g. mpox), where the pipeline itself warns assemblies may be inaccurate draft genomes When the input is not nanopore FASTQ data from untargeted/metagenomic sequencing

skills.search_text: de-novo-motif-enrichment-with-meme Use when reproducing the Tombo+MEME motif-enrichment baseline on ONT native/WGA sample pairs, or when a sensitivity benchmark for methylation motif discovery on H. pylori J99-like methylomes is needed. When high sensitivity or deterministic de novo motif discovery is required — the article states MEME-based approaches do not extract all H. pylori methylation sites de novo and return non-deterministic results When the goal is to run Snapper's greedy enrichment itself; this skill is only the MEME/Tombo baseline, not the Snapper workflow When no matched WGA control sample exists, since Tombo model_sample_compare between native and control is a prerequisite for defining modified sites http://edamontology.org/topic_3168 Baseline de novo methylation-motif discovery that runs MEME with Tombo-documented parameters on sequence contexts extracted around significantly modified ONT bases; it serves as the low-sensitivity reference point against which Snapper's greedy enrichment is compared. genomics/v1 10.1093/bioinformatics/btad702

skills.when_to_use_negative: When high sensitivity or deterministic de novo motif discovery is required — the article states MEME-based approaches do not extract all H. pylori methylation sites de novo and return non-deterministic results When the goal is to run Snapper's greedy enrichment itself; this skill is only the MEME/Tombo baseline, not the Snapper workflow When no matched WGA control sample exists, since Tombo model_sample_compare between native and control is a prerequisite for defining modified sites

skills.description: Use when raw nanopore (ONT MinION 2D/1D2 or R7 INC-Seq) 16S rRNA amplicon reads must be partitioned into organism-level OTUs and high-accuracy full-length consensus sequences built entirely de novo, without reference-based mapping.
skills.name: de-novo-read-clustering-consensus-calling
skills.search_text: de-novo-read-clustering-consensus-calling Use when raw nanopore (ONT MinION 2D/1D2 or R7 INC-Seq) 16S rRNA amplicon reads must be partitioned into organism-level OTUs and high-accuracy full-length consensus sequences built entirely de novo, without reference-based mapping. skills.summary: A de novo strategy for noisy nanopore amplicon reads that partitions reads into OTU clusters (nanoClust) and calls within-cluster consensus full-length 16S rRNA gene sequences without any reference database, achieving ~99.5% average accuracy on 2D and 1D2 ONT MinION mock community data.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When a reference-based clustering approach is acceptable and the target organisms are all present in the reference database — but note the article warns that incorrect reference mapping due to high raw nanopore error rates and absent organisms motivates the de novo route When only short-read data (Illumina MiSeq, Ion Torrent PGM) is available — the workflow targets long nanopore amplicon reads When the goal is classification-only assignment rather than consensus sequence generation — the article notes classification-only analysis is limited in differentiating closely related sequences

skills.description: Use when MinION amplicon reads (e.g. INC-Seq consensus 16S rRNA reads from a mock community or mixed microbial sample) must be grouped into OTUs and turned into consensus sequences without a reference database.
skills.name: de-novo-read-partition-clustering
skills.search_text: de-novo-read-partition-clustering Use when MinION amplicon reads (e.g. INC-Seq consensus 16S rRNA reads from a mock community or mixed microbial sample) must be grouped into OTUs and turned into consensus sequences without a reference database. Input is raw noisy MinION reads that have not been through INC-Seq (>=3 concatemers) and chopSeq fragmentation/orientation correction The goal is reference-based OTU assignment against SILVA or another curated 16S database rather than de novo clustering Short-read amplicon data (e.g. Illumina MiSeq) where read length does not support partitioning-based clustering http://edamontology.org/topic_0196 nanoClust-style de novo clustering of nanopore amplicon reads: reads are partitioned along the read length, clustered without any reference database, and a within-cluster consensus full-length 16S rRNA gene sequence is called per OTU. genomics/v1 10.1093/gigascience/giy140
skills.summary: nanoClust-style de novo clustering of nanopore amplicon reads: reads are partitioned along the read length, clustered without any reference database, and a within-cluster consensus full-length 16S rRNA gene sequence is called per OTU.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw noisy MinION reads that have not been through INC-Seq (>=3 concatemers) and chopSeq fragmentation/orientation correction The goal is reference-based OTU assignment against SILVA or another curated 16S database rather than de novo clustering Short-read amplicon data (e.g. Illumina MiSeq) where read length does not support partitioning-based clustering

skills.description: Use when you have trio variant calls (child + two parents) as joint-genotyped VCFs and need to extract DNVs present in the child but absent from both parents, with allele-level intersection and sex/PAR-aware logic.
skills.name: de-novo-variant-filtering
skills.search_text: de-novo-variant-filtering Use when you have trio variant calls (child + two parents) as joint-genotyped VCFs and need to extract DNVs present in the child but absent from both parents, with allele-level intersection and sex/PAR-aware logic. Input is still aligned reads (BAM/CRAM) with no variant calls — run the full Hare/Tortoise workflow including variant calling and GLnexus joint genotyping first, rather than filtering alone. You want to process single-sample VCFs or cohorts without trio structure — DNV detection requires child and both parents; HAT-FLEX operates on trio-level and multi-sample VCFs assuming trio relationships. You have PacBio HiFi long-read data — use the Tortoise branch (effective for WGS, WES and PacBio data), since Hare v1.2 is effective for WGS and WES data only. http://edamontology.org/topic_0199 http://edamontology.org/topic_0625 Extract candidate de novo variants (DNVs) by running family-level joint-genotyped VCFs (produced with GLnexus from Hare/Tortoise variant calls) through HAT's custom de novo variant filter, or apply HAT-FLEX directly to existing VCFs when BAM/CRAM files are not available. genomics/v1 10.1093/bioinformatics/btad775
skills.summary: Extract candidate de novo variants (DNVs) by running family-level joint-genotyped VCFs (produced with GLnexus from Hare/Tortoise variant calls) through HAT's custom de novo variant filter, or apply HAT-FLEX directly to existing VCFs when BAM/CRAM files are not available.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is still aligned reads (BAM/CRAM) with no variant calls — run the full Hare/Tortoise workflow including variant calling and GLnexus joint genotyping first, rather than filtering alone. You want to process single-sample VCFs or cohorts without trio structure — DNV detection requires child and both parents; HAT-FLEX operates on trio-level and multi-sample VCFs assuming trio relationships. You have PacBio HiFi long-read data — use the Tortoise branch (effective for WGS, WES and PacBio data), since Hare v1.2 is effective for WGS and WES data only.

skills.description: Use when no reference FASTA is available for a nanopore sample but the approximate genome size is known (e.g. ~11000 bases for West Nile virus), and a consensus genome is needed within the VirDetector pipeline.
skills.name: de-novo-viral-genome-assembly
skills.search_text: de-novo-viral-genome-assembly Use when no reference FASTA is available for a nanopore sample but the approximate genome size is known (e.g. ~11000 bases for West Nile virus), and a consensus genome is needed within the VirDetector pipeline. A user-supplied reference sequence is already configured via params.ref, in which case the plain reference-based assembly branch should be used instead of the hybrid approach. The expected genome size of the target organism is unknown, since Canu requires params.canu_genome_size to be set for the hybrid assembly. Input is already assembled contigs or FASTA sequences, which VirDetector passes to the alignment step onwards rather than through the assembly layer. http://edamontology.org/topic_0196 http://edamontology.org/topic_3673 Reconstruct a viral consensus genome without a pre-specified reference by first assembling nanopore reads de novo with Canu, then selecting a reference sequence from the VirDetector database via BLAST bit-score, after which the standard reference-based consensus branch proceeds. genomics/v1 10.1093/bioinformatics/btaf029
skills.summary: Reconstruct a viral consensus genome without a pre-specified reference by first assembling nanopore reads de novo with Canu, then selecting a reference sequence from the VirDetector database via BLAST bit-score, after which the standard reference-based consensus branch proceeds.
skills.when_to_use_negative: A user-supplied reference sequence is already configured via params.ref, in which case the plain reference-based assembly branch should be used instead of the hybrid approach. The expected genome size of the target organism is unknown, since Canu requires params.canu_genome_size to be set for the hybrid assembly. Input is already assembled contigs or FASTA sequences, which VirDetector passes to the alignment step onwards rather than through the assembly layer.

skills.description: Use when benchmarking a targeted NRS-insertion caller against the whole-genome-assembly paradigm: 10x linked-read BAM/FASTQ data are available for a diploid genome and insertion calls must be derived from a full assembly rather than a local-assembly caller.
skills.name: de-novo-whole-genome-assembly-pipeline-execution
skills.search_text: de-novo-whole-genome-assembly-pipeline-execution Use when benchmarking a targeted NRS-insertion caller against the whole-genome-assembly paradigm: 10x linked-read BAM/FASTQ data are available for a diploid genome and insertion calls must be derived from a full assembly rather than a local-assembly caller. The goal is efficient NRS insertion detection itself — the article shows a targeted local-assembly approach (Novel-X) is substantially more accurate and computationally cheaper than whole-genome de novo assembly Input reads are standard short reads without barcode/linked-read information, so a synthetic-long-read assembler like SuperNova cannot be applied The sample is haploid (CHM1/CHM13) or the goal is small insertions — SuperNova defaults are tuned for whole human genome diploid assembly and small insertions lack sufficient barcodes for anchor assembly http://edamontology.org/topic_0196 Runs a whole-genome diploid de novo assembler (SuperNova) on synthetic long-read (10x Genomics linked-read) data and extracts novel insertion sequences from the assembly-to-reference alignment, serving as the computationally expensive whole-genome-assembly baseline that Novel-X avoids. genomics/v1 10.1093/nar/gkac653
skills.summary: Runs a whole-genome diploid de novo assembler (SuperNova) on synthetic long-read (10x Genomics linked-read) data and extracts novel insertion sequences from the assembly-to-reference alignment, serving as the computationally expensive whole-genome-assembly baseline that Novel-X avoids.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is efficient NRS insertion detection itself — the article shows a targeted local-assembly approach (Novel-X) is substantially more accurate and computationally cheaper than whole-genome de novo assembly Input reads are standard short reads without barcode/linked-read information, so a synthetic-long-read assembler like SuperNova cannot be applied The sample is haploid (CHM1/CHM13) or the goal is small insertions — SuperNova defaults are tuned for whole human genome diploid assembly and small insertions lack sufficient barcodes for anchor assembly

skills.description: Use when you need to quantify how fast Chiron (or a comparable CTC-decoder basecaller) processes nanopore fast5 raw signal, and to compare greedy vs beam-search decoding throughput across CPU and GPU devices.
skills.name: decoding-rate-measurement-and-tabulation
skills.search_text: decoding-rate-measurement-and-tabulation Use when you need to quantify how fast Chiron (or a comparable CTC-decoder basecaller) processes nanopore fast5 raw signal, and to compare greedy vs beam-search decoding throughput across CPU and GPU devices. The goal is basecalling accuracy evaluation (read-level identity vs a reference) rather than throughput/speed measurement — this skill times decoding only. The basecaller lacks a CTC decoder option and cannot be run in both greedy and beam-search modes, so the decoder-speed comparison is not meaningful. Only a very small input (a single short read) is available, where timing noise will swamp the measured rate. http://edamontology.org/topic_3168 http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Benchmark the basecalling throughput (bp/s) of Chiron's greedy vs beam-search CTC decoders on CPU and GPU hardware, then compile the device × decoder rates into a table mirroring the paper's reported speeds. genomics/v1 10.1093/gigascience/giy037
skills.summary: Benchmark the basecalling throughput (bp/s) of Chiron's greedy vs beam-search CTC decoders on CPU and GPU hardware, then compile the device × decoder rates into a table mirroring the paper's reported speeds.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is basecalling accuracy evaluation (read-level identity vs a reference) rather than throughput/speed measurement — this skill times decoding only. The basecaller lacks a CTC decoder option and cannot be run in both greedy and beam-search modes, so the decoder-speed comparison is not meaningful. Only a very small input (a single short read) is available, where timing noise will swamp the measured rate.

skills.description: Use when you have binary segmented cell masks from multiplexed imaging (e.g., MIBI or multiplexed immunofluorescence) and need a learned, fixed-length shape representation per cell rather than hand-crafted morphological features.
skills.name: deep-learning-model-training
skills.search_text: deep-learning-model-training Use when you have binary segmented cell masks from multiplexed imaging (e.g., MIBI or multiplexed immunofluorescence) and need a learned, fixed-length shape representation per cell rather than hand-crafted morphological features. Input is a per-cell marker-intensity feature table rather than segmented cell masks — shape encoding is not applicable. Goal is per-compartment marker quantification (nucleus, membrane, cytoplasm) — that is MIRIAM's quantification stage, not the shape-descriptor stage. Latent vectors have already been computed and the goal is downstream analysis such as t-SNE on the encodings. Trains an autoencoder neural network to produce a compact latent-vector descriptor of cell shape from segmented multiplexed tissue images, as implemented in the MIRIAM pipeline (Matlab Deep Learning Toolbox or Python Keras) for downstream shape-based analyses such as t-SNE. genomics/v1 10.1002/cyto.a.24541
skills.summary: Trains an autoencoder neural network to produce a compact latent-vector descriptor of cell shape from segmented multiplexed tissue images, as implemented in the MIRIAM pipeline (Matlab Deep Learning Toolbox or Python Keras) for downstream shape-based analyses such as t-SNE.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is a per-cell marker-intensity feature table rather than segmented cell masks — shape encoding is not applicable. Goal is per-compartment marker quantification (nucleus, membrane, cytoplasm) — that is MIRIAM's quantification stage, not the shape-descriptor stage. Latent vectors have already been computed and the goal is downstream analysis such as t-SNE on the encodings.

skills.name: deep-learning-model-training-kinetics-features
skills.search_text: deep-learning-model-training-kinetics-features Use when PacBio CCS subreads.bam/hifi.bam reads plus a reference genome are available, M.SssI-treated and PCR-treated control reads exist as ground truth, and the goal is to train a deep-learning model on IPD/PW kinetics features for 5mCpG detection at read level. The target modification is not symmetric CpG methylation — the methods cannot detect hemimethylated CpGs or 5mC in non-CpG contexts, or other modifications such as 6mA Input is short-read sequencing (e.g., BS-seq, TAPS, EM-seq) or Oxford Nanopore reads — ccsmeth's kinetics features (IPDs and PWs) are specific to PacBio CCS data Only site-level aggregate methylation frequencies are needed and no per-read ground truth or model training is intended Train and evaluate ccsmeth, a deep-learning model that detects DNA 5mCpGs at read level using kinetics features (IPDs and PWs) extracted from PacBio CCS reads, on controlled M.SssI-methyltransferase-treated versus PCR-treated DNA datasets. genomics/v1 10.1038/s41467-023-39784-9
skills.summary: Train and evaluate ccsmeth, a deep-learning model that detects DNA 5mCpGs at read level using kinetics features (IPDs and PWs) extracted from PacBio CCS reads, on controlled M.SssI-methyltransferase-treated versus PCR-treated DNA datasets.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The target modification is not symmetric CpG methylation — the methods cannot detect hemimethylated CpGs or 5mC in non-CpG contexts, or other modifications such as 6mA Input is short-read sequencing (e.g., BS-seq, TAPS, EM-seq) or Oxford Nanopore reads — ccsmeth's kinetics features (IPDs and PWs) are specific to PacBio CCS data Only site-level aggregate methylation frequencies are needed and no per-read ground truth or model training is intended

skills.description: Use when a deep-learning model predicts both a methylation type and a methylated base position per motif, and the nucleotide at the predicted position is inconsistent with the predicted type (e.g. 6mA predicted at a non-adenine).
skills.name: deep-learning-prediction-postprocessing
skills.search_text: deep-learning-prediction-postprocessing Use when a deep-learning model predicts both a methylation type and a methylated base position per motif, and the nucleotide at the predicted position is inconsistent with the predicted type (e.g. 6mA predicted at a non-adenine). Predictions whose nucleotide at the predicted position already matches the predicted methylation type need no correction Data lacking basecall base features at candidate motif positions, since the correction requires checking the nucleotide at each candidate position Tasks focused on initial motif discovery/enrichment rather than refining model position predictions http://edamontology.org/topic_3673 http://edamontology.org/topic_0654 Post-processing module for Nanoident that corrects inconsistent methylation predictions by iteratively reassigning the methylated base to the candidate position with the next-highest predicted probability until the base matches the predicted methylation type (4mC/5mC/6mA). genomics/v1 10.1093/bioinformatics/btaf397
skills.summary: Post-processing module for Nanoident that corrects inconsistent methylation predictions by iteratively reassigning the methylated base to the candidate position with the next-highest predicted probability until the base matches the predicted methylation type (4mC/5mC/6mA).
skills.when_to_use_negative: Predictions whose nucleotide at the predicted position already matches the predicted methylation type need no correction Data lacking basecall base features at candidate motif positions, since the correction requires checking the nucleotide at each candidate position Tasks focused on initial motif discovery/enrichment rather than refining model position predictions

skills.description: Use when calling SNVs and small indels from single-molecule sequencing alignments (especially high-error ONT/PacBio BAMs) where traditional variant callers fail due to indel-enriched sequencing error, or when benchmarking caller accuracy against a GIAB truth set.
skills.name: deep-neural-network-variant-calling
skills.search_text: deep-neural-network-variant-calling Use when calling SNVs and small indels from single-molecule sequencing alignments (especially high-error ONT/PacBio BAMs) where traditional variant callers fail due to indel-enriched sequencing error, or when benchmarking caller accuracy against a GIAB truth set. Calling somatic variants, trio-based variants, or variants with two or more alternative alleles — the current Clairvoyante design does not support these and network version 3 outputs only one alternative allele per position Variant calling on completely novel sequencing technologies/chemistries lacking a high-quality GIAB-style training dataset Precise genotyping of long indels — exact alternative alleles are only provided for indels <= 4 bp and ONT indel F1 remains around 50% http://edamontology.org/topic_3673 http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 Applies Clairvoyante, a multi-task five-layer convolutional neural network built on TensorFlow, to call SNPs and small indels from single-molecule sequencing (Illumina, PacBio, Oxford Nanopore) read alignments by predicting variant type, zygosity, alternative allele and indel length from four-channel pileup tensors. genomics/v1 10.1038/s41467-019-09025-z
skills.summary: Applies Clairvoyante, a multi-task five-layer convolutional neural network built on TensorFlow, to call SNPs and small indels from single-molecule sequencing (Illumina, PacBio, Oxford Nanopore) read alignments by predicting variant type, zygosity, alternative allele and indel length from four-channel pileup tensors.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Calling somatic variants, trio-based variants, or variants with two or more alternative alleles — the current Clairvoyante design does not support these and network version 3 outputs only one alternative allele per position Variant calling on completely novel sequencing technologies/chemistries lacking a high-quality GIAB-style training dataset Precise genotyping of long indels — exact alternative alleles are only provided for indels <= 4 bp and ONT indel F1 remains around 50%

skills.description: Use when interpreting or reproducing Nanodisco automated-mode output on ONT methylation data where distinct detected motifs (e.g. CATG and GCGC on H.pylori J99) are merged into one degenerate IUPAC motif such as GCRYG.
skills.name: degenerate-iupac-motif-merging
skills.search_text: degenerate-iupac-motif-merging Use when interpreting or reproducing Nanodisco automated-mode output on ONT methylation data where distinct detected motifs (e.g. CATG and GCGC on H.pylori J99) are merged into one degenerate IUPAC motif such as GCRYG. When motifs are distinct and should be reported separately — the merge is an automated-mode artifact of motif collisions, and PacBio data for J99 confirms CATG and GCGC as independent methylated motifs When a deterministic tool without manual curation is required — Snapper does not require manual control during enrichment and was designed to avoid this failure mode When the goal is the true J99 methylome composition rather than reproducing Nanodisco's automated behavior http://edamontology.org/topic_0157 Reproduces and interprets Nanodisco's fully automated (non-iterative) methylation motif calling, in which its consensus step collapses the most-represented H.pylori J99 motifs CATG and GCGC into the single degenerate IUPAC motif GCRYG due to excessive motif collisions — a documented failure mode of automated motif discovery. genomics/v1 10.1093/bioinformatics/btad702
skills.summary: Reproduces and interprets Nanodisco's fully automated (non-iterative) methylation motif calling, in which its consensus step collapses the most-represented H.pylori J99 motifs CATG and GCGC into the single degenerate IUPAC motif GCRYG due to excessive motif collisions — a documented failure mode of automated motif discovery.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When motifs are distinct and should be reported separately — the merge is an automated-mode artifact of motif collisions, and PacBio data for J99 confirms CATG and GCGC as independent methylated motifs When a deterministic tool without manual curation is required — Snapper does not require manual control during enrichment and was designed to avoid this failure mode When the goal is the true J99 methylome composition rather than reproducing Nanodisco's automated behavior

skills.name: degenerate-motif-disambiguation
skills.search_text: degenerate-motif-disambiguation Use when Snapper's final_motifs_[strand]_[contig_name].fasta outputs contain degenerate-base motifs that must be reconciled with REBASE reference motifs or resolved to concrete k-mers before declaring a run validated. Motifs are already concrete (no IUPAC ambiguity codes) and match REBASE references exactly — direct table comparison suffices The goal is de novo motif discovery itself rather than post-hoc reconciliation of Snapper output against reference specificities http://edamontology.org/topic_3295 http://edamontology.org/topic_0080 Resolves degenerate IUPAC-coded methylation motifs reported by Snapper (e.g., the REBASE reference CACNNNNNRTAAA) into the concrete sequence instances actually detected in a strain (e.g., CACNNNNNATAAA), so Snapper output can be judged against REBASE methyltransferase specificities. genomics/v1 10.1093/bioinformatics/btad702
skills.summary: Resolves degenerate IUPAC-coded methylation motifs reported by Snapper (e.g., the REBASE reference CACNNNNNRTAAA) into the concrete sequence instances actually detected in a strain (e.g., CACNNNNNATAAA), so Snapper output can be judged against REBASE methyltransferase specificities.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Motifs are already concrete (no IUPAC ambiguity codes) and match REBASE references exactly — direct table comparison suffices The goal is de novo motif discovery itself rather than post-hoc reconciliation of Snapper output against reference specificities

skills.description: Use when polishing variant-caller output (Sniffles, CuteSV, SVIM, NanoVar) on nanopore WGS data where DEL/DUP calls must be kept or discarded based on coverage evidence, especially large (>50 kb) CNVs prone to false positives.
skills.name: deletion-duplication-coverage-filtering
skills.search_text: deletion-duplication-coverage-filtering Use when polishing variant-caller output (Sniffles, CuteSV, SVIM, NanoVar) on nanopore WGS data where DEL/DUP calls must be kept or discarded based on coverage evidence, especially large (>50 kb) CNVs prone to false positives. The input SVs are not deletions or duplications (e.g. insertions, translocations, inversions), since coverage analysis can only check DEL/DUP types You need a standalone variant caller: disCoverage is not a variant caller and requires putative SV positions from another technique or multi-sample analysis Coverage in the target region is confounded by local peaks/valleys or unresolved regions, making the coverage-difference test unreliable http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Refines nanopore WGS structural variant calls for deletions and duplications by testing whether per-region read coverage (computed with Mosdepth) statistically supports the called SV type, using disCoverage with a two-tailed Welch t-test p-value threshold of < 0.05. genomics/v1 10.1016/j.jare.2022.10.012
skills.summary: Refines nanopore WGS structural variant calls for deletions and duplications by testing whether per-region read coverage (computed with Mosdepth) statistically supports the called SV type, using disCoverage with a two-tailed Welch t-test p-value threshold of < 0.05.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input SVs are not deletions or duplications (e.g. insertions, translocations, inversions), since coverage analysis can only check DEL/DUP types You need a standalone variant caller: disCoverage is not a variant caller and requires putative SV positions from another technique or multi-sample analysis Coverage in the target region is confounded by local peaks/valleys or unresolved regions, making the coverage-difference test unreliable

skills.description: Use when a trained ΔΨ prediction model (e.g. ε-SVR on vex-seq variants) must be assessed via 10-fold cross-validation PCC, or when benchmarking against PredPSI-SVR's reported 0.570 CV / 0.566 blind-test performance.
skills.name: delta-psi-prediction-performance-evaluation
skills.search_text: delta-psi-prediction-performance-evaluation Use when a trained ΔΨ prediction model (e.g. ε-SVR on vex-seq variants) must be assessed via 10-fold cross-validation PCC, or when benchmarking against PredPSI-SVR's reported 0.570 CV / 0.566 blind-test performance. Input is already an annotated, model-ready feature matrix and only a delta-PSI prediction is needed (use the PredPSI-SVR prediction workflow, not evaluation). The dataset has too few samples with extreme ΔΨ values removed (fewer than the 53 mutations retained after removing ΔΨ with absolute values less than two times the standard deviation), making CV PCC unstable. The goal is splice-site or branch-point feature prediction for a single exon, not variant-level ΔΨ regression evaluation — PredPSI-SVR does not include branch point sequence features. http://edamontology.org/topic_3320 http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Evaluates support-vector-regression models predicting variant-induced ΔΨ (change of percent spliced in) by computing Pearson correlation coefficient (PCC) under 10-fold cross-validation on the CAGI 5 vex-seq TR957 training set and comparing against the reported PredPSI-SVR benchmark of PCC 0.570 (CV) and 0.566 (blind test). genomics/v1 10.1002/humu.23785
skills.summary: Evaluates support-vector-regression models predicting variant-induced ΔΨ (change of percent spliced in) by computing Pearson correlation coefficient (PCC) under 10-fold cross-validation on the CAGI 5 vex-seq TR957 training set and comparing against the reported PredPSI-SVR benchmark of PCC 0.570 (CV) and 0.566 (blind test).
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already an annotated, model-ready feature matrix and only a delta-PSI prediction is needed (use the PredPSI-SVR prediction workflow, not evaluation). The dataset has too few samples with extreme ΔΨ values removed (fewer than the 53 mutations retained after removing ΔΨ with absolute values less than two times the standard deviation), making CV PCC unstable. The goal is splice-site or branch-point feature prediction for a single exon, not variant-level ΔΨ regression evaluation — PredPSI-SVR does not include branch point sequence features.

skills.description: Use when Nanopore FASTQ reads need demultiplexing/trimming under ONT kit presets (e.g. SQK-RBK114-96, SQK-NBD114-96), or when many reads deviate from the expected single-barcode configuration (contamination, partial trims, fused double barcodes).
skills.name: demultiplex-pattern-filtering
skills.search_text: demultiplex-pattern-filtering Use when Nanopore FASTQ reads need demultiplexing/trimming under ONT kit presets (e.g. SQK-RBK114-96, SQK-NBD114-96), or when many reads deviate from the expected single-barcode configuration (contamination, partial trims, fused double barcodes). Reads are not Nanopore kit-barcoded data, or the kit is not in Barbell's supported_kits.txt (only rapid/native DNA kits were thoroughly tested; RNA and Twist kits are exceptions) You need ultra-strict single-barcode configurations and cannot tolerate the ~3x slowdown of --use-extended when fusion-point searching is unnecessary The analysis goal is adapter trimming alone with no barcode assignment; a simple trimmer may suffice rather than pattern-aware demux http://edamontology.org/topic_3168 Pattern-aware demultiplexing and pattern-group filtering of Nanopore reads using Barbell, which detects complex barcode configurations (flank-only, fused double barcodes via --use-extended) that flat-matchers like Dorado miss, and trims reads based on inspected pattern groups. genomics/v1 10.1093/bioinformatics/btag349
skills.summary: Pattern-aware demultiplexing and pattern-group filtering of Nanopore reads using Barbell, which detects complex barcode configurations (flank-only, fused double barcodes via --use-extended) that flat-matchers like Dorado miss, and trims reads based on inspected pattern groups.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Reads are not Nanopore kit-barcoded data, or the kit is not in Barbell's supported_kits.txt (only rapid/native DNA kits were thoroughly tested; RNA and Twist kits are exceptions) You need ultra-strict single-barcode configurations and cannot tolerate the ~3x slowdown of --use-extended when fusion-point searching is unnecessary The analysis goal is adapter trimming alone with no barcode assignment; a simple trimmer may suffice rather than pattern-aware demux

skills.description: Use when validating a barcode demultiplexing tool against spiked-in SIRV FLNC reads with known isoform ground truth, to compute accuracy, specificity, and a confusion matrix of assignment errors.
skills.name: demultiplexing-confusion-matrix-evaluation
skills.search_text: demultiplexing-confusion-matrix-evaluation Use when validating a barcode demultiplexing tool against spiked-in SIRV FLNC reads with known isoform ground truth, to compute accuracy, specificity, and a confusion matrix of assignment errors. Input reads lack a ground-truth identity (e.g., ordinary cellular transcriptomes without spike-ins), so a confusion matrix against expected isoforms cannot be built The goal is isoform quantification per cell (use scIsoform_matrix) rather than evaluating demultiplexing accuracy itself Reads are raw CCS reads not yet classified to FLNC with cell barcode and UMI extracted http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Benchmarks single-cell barcode demultiplexing accuracy by assigning demultiplexed reads to a ground-truth spike-in identity (SIRV-Set 4 isoforms), building an isoform assignment confusion matrix, and computing accuracy and specificity metrics. This reproduces the scISA-Tools evaluation showing >99.99% accuracy/specificity on HIT-scISOseq data. genomics/v1 10.1038/s41467-023-38324-9
skills.summary: Benchmarks single-cell barcode demultiplexing accuracy by assigning demultiplexed reads to a ground-truth spike-in identity (SIRV-Set 4 isoforms), building an isoform assignment confusion matrix, and computing accuracy and specificity metrics. This reproduces the scISA-Tools evaluation showing >99.99% accuracy/specificity on HIT-scISOseq data.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input reads lack a ground-truth identity (e.g., ordinary cellular transcriptomes without spike-ins), so a confusion matrix against expected isoforms cannot be built The goal is isoform quantification per cell (use scIsoform_matrix) rather than evaluating demultiplexing accuracy itself Reads are raw CCS reads not yet classified to FLNC with cell barcode and UMI extracted

skills.name: density-scatter-plot-visualization
skills.search_text: density-scatter-plot-visualization Use when you need to assess quantitative agreement between site-level modification stoichiometry measurements and a reference (e.g., mAFiA modRatio vs GLORI) across a titration or dilution series, by visualizing the joint distribution and regressing one against the other. The downstream tool does not accept Bloom filter sizing in suffix notation (e.g. ABySS-Bloom b=200M), or the analysis uses alignment-based polishing tools like Pilon or Racon that do not use Bloom filters. K-mer sizes other than the protocol's descending set are used without re-histogramming, since n must be recomputed per k. http://edamontology.org/topic_0102 http://edamontology.org/topic_0080 Estimates the number of distinct (non-erroneous) k-mers in short-read data from ntCard k-mer frequency histograms, by subtracting singleton counts from the estimated total F0 per k-mer size, and uses the largest estimate to size a Bloom filter at a target false-positive rate. genomics/v1 10.1002/cpz1.442
skills.summary: Estimates the number of distinct (non-erroneous) k-mers in short-read data from ntCard k-mer frequency histograms, by subtracting singleton counts from the estimated total F0 per k-mer size, and uses the largest estimate to size a Bloom filter at a target false-positive rate.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Reads have not yet been histogrammed by ntCard — the estimation requires k-mer frequency histograms (from an upstream ntCard/ntHits step), not raw FASTQ alone. The downstream tool does not accept Bloom filter sizing in suffix notation (e.g. ABySS-Bloom b=200M), or the analysis uses alignment-based polishing tools like Pilon or Racon that do not use Bloom filters. K-mer sizes other than the protocol's descending set are used without re-histogramming, since n must be recomputed per k.

skills.description: Use when you need a unique pairwise alignment (with error-type counts) between two equal-ish-length DNA barcodes so that insertions, deletions and substitutions can be weighted independently, e.g. to compute ProDiv for demultiplexing.
skills.name: dna-sequence-edit-distance-dynamic-programming
skills.search_text: dna-sequence-edit-distance-dynamic-programming Use when you need a unique pairwise alignment (with error-type counts) between two equal-ish-length DNA barcodes so that insertions, deletions and substitutions can be weighted independently, e.g. to compute ProDiv for demultiplexing. When only a plain edit-distance value (not error-type counts) is needed — edlib's built-in distance suffices without backtracking counts When barcodes are not short equal-length DNA sequences; the paper's probability-divergence model is defined for short DNA sequences used as nanopore barcodes, not long genomic reads When error types cannot be assumed independent — ProDiv is defined under the assumption that insertion, deletion, and substitution of each base occur independently during sequencing http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Implements edit-distance dynamic programming to align two short DNA sequences and count matches m, insertions i, deletions d, and substitutions s, which are then fed into PRO's probability-divergence formula ProDiv(X,Y) = pm^m * pd^d * (ps/3)^s * (pi/4)^i with pd = ps = pi = (1-pm)/3 for barcode demultiplexing. genomics/v1 10.1016/j.fmre.2024.04.014

skills.when_to_use_negative: When only a plain edit-distance value (not error-type counts) is needed — edlib's built-in distance suffices without backtracking counts When barcodes are not short equal-length DNA sequences; the paper's probability-divergence model is defined for short DNA sequences used as nanopore barcodes, not long genomic reads When error types cannot be assumed independent — ProDiv is defined under the assumption that insertion, deletion, and substitution of each base occur independently during sequencing

skills.description: Use when reproducing or extending GutUDB THERAPY-module analyses: counting curated drug-disease interactions by category, or assessing whether a specific drug (e.g., cisplatin for colon cancer) shows strong connectivity in an integrated drug-disease-gene graph.
skills.name: drug-disease-gene-network-reconstruction
skills.search_text: drug-disease-gene-network-reconstruction Use when reproducing or extending GutUDB THERAPY-module analyses: counting curated drug-disease interactions by category, or assessing whether a specific drug (e.g., cisplatin for colon cancer) shows strong connectivity in an integrated drug-disease-gene graph.
