Reads are short Illumina reads — invMap targets long noisy PacBio/Oxford Nanopore reads that can span SV breakpoints The task is generic co-linear alignment with no interest in inversion structural variants, where standard mappers suffice Available RAM is below 16G when mapping to large reference genomes, which invMap requires http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_3577 A seed-anchoring and dynamic-programming chaining strategy used by invMap to locate the aligned region of long noisy PacBio/Oxford Nanopore reads against a reference genome, followed by non-linear-to-linear anchor transformation to expose inversion chains. genomics/v1 10.1093/bioinformatics/btad726
skills.summary: A seed-anchoring and dynamic-programming chaining strategy used by invMap to locate the aligned region of long noisy PacBio/Oxford Nanopore reads against a reference genome, followed by non-linear-to-linear anchor transformation to expose inversion chains.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Reads are short Illumina reads — invMap targets long noisy PacBio/Oxford Nanopore reads that can span SV breakpoints The task is generic co-linear alignment with no interest in inversion structural variants, where standard mappers suffice Available RAM is below 16G when mapping to large reference genomes, which invMap requires

skills.description: Use when segmenting ultra-long nucleotide sequences for multiple sequence alignment: MEMs have been found via suffix array and must be filtered (colinearity, size, coverage c) and chained into partial chains for downstream segmentation.
skills.name: dynamic-programming-chaining
skills.search_text: dynamic-programming-chaining Use when segmenting ultra-long nucleotide sequences for multiple sequence alignment: MEMs have been found via suffix array and must be filtered (colinearity, size, coverage c) and chained into partial chains for downstream segmentation. MEMs have not yet been found — this skill filters and chains existing MEMs, it does not do suffix-array MEM discovery Input is protein or already-aligned data — FMAlign2 targets ultra-long nucleotide (DNA) FASTA input A single global chain over all sequences is desired — this skill intentionally replaces FMAlign's global-chain search with partial chains http://edamontology.org/topic_0080 Reconstructs FMAlign2's Step 2: filtering suffix-array-derived MEMs with global/local dynamic programming (colinearity, MEM size, sequence-coverage threshold c) and augmenting them with striped Smith–Waterman (SSW) similar substrings to form partial chains instead of FMAlign's global chains. genomics/v1 10.1093/bioinformatics/btae014
skills.summary: Reconstructs FMAlign2's Step 2: filtering suffix-array-derived MEMs with global/local dynamic programming (colinearity, MEM size, sequence-coverage threshold c) and augmenting them with striped Smith–Waterman (SSW) similar substrings to form partial chains instead of FMAlign's global chains.
skills.when_to_use_negative: MEMs have not yet been found — this skill filters and chains existing MEMs, it does not do suffix-array MEM discovery Input is protein or already-aligned data — FMAlign2 targets ultra-long nucleotide (DNA) FASTA input A single global chain over all sequences is desired — this skill intentionally replaces FMAlign's global-chain search with partial chains

skills.description: Use when correcting long noisy reads (Nanopore R9/R10 or PacBio CLR) from a diploid genome while preserving heterozygote alleles that a vanilla POA consensus would collapse away.
skills.name: dynamic-programming-consensus-generation
skills.search_text: dynamic-programming-consensus-generation Use when correcting long noisy reads (Nanopore R9/R10 or PacBio CLR) from a diploid genome while preserving heterozygote alleles that a vanilla POA consensus would collapse away. Data are Nanopore duplex or PacBio HiFi reads — the paper reports the method achieves only mediocre performance on these high-accuracy data The goal is a consensus/variant call on an existing assembly rather than error-corrected reads — Medaka pileup-based consensus or Clair3 SNP calling is the appropriate alternative Heterozygosity rate is very low — the method cannot distinguish small sequencing errors from heterozygote alleles in such regions http://edamontology.org/topic_0196 PECAT-style haplotype-aware consensus generation: build a partial-order alignment (POA) graph from raw long reads, score supporting reads against the template read at heterozygous dominant branches, re-weight selected same-haplotype supports, and emit a corrected consensus read by dynamic programming. genomics/v1 10.1038/s41467-024-47349-7
skills.summary: PECAT-style haplotype-aware consensus generation: build a partial-order alignment (POA) graph from raw long reads, score supporting reads against the template read at heterozygous dominant branches, re-weight selected same-haplotype supports, and emit a corrected consensus read by dynamic programming.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Data are Nanopore duplex or PacBio HiFi reads — the paper reports the method achieves only mediocre performance on these high-accuracy data The goal is a consensus/variant call on an existing assembly rather than error-corrected reads — Medaka pileup-based consensus or Clair3 SNP calling is the appropriate alternative Heterozygosity rate is very low — the method cannot distinguish small sequencing errors from heterozygote alleles in such regions

skills.description: Use when you have a single-cell isoform expression matrix and a percentile correlation matrix, and need to identify modules of co-expressed isoforms across cell types without hard-coding a cluster count.
skills.name: dynamic-tree-cut-module-detection
skills.search_text: dynamic-tree-cut-module-detection Use when you have a single-cell isoform expression matrix and a percentile correlation matrix, and need to identify modules of co-expressed isoforms across cell types without hard-coding a cluster count. You have gene-level (not isoform-level) expression data and want conventional gene co-expression modules rather than isoform co-usage modules You need a fully automated, parameter-free clustering — this pipeline is explicitly semi-automated and includes manual cluster merges Your goal is differential isoform usage (DIU/coDIU) detection itself rather than the upstream module detection that feeds it http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Semi-automated detection of isoform co-expression modules by running the dynamicTreeCut hybrid algorithm on a percentile correlation matrix of single-cell isoform expression, followed by correlation-based filtering, metatranscript-based cluster merging, and recursive assignment of unclustered isoforms. Used by acorde to partition mouse neural isoforms into cell type-specific co-usage modules. genomics/v1 10.1038/s41467-022-29497-w
skills.summary: Semi-automated detection of isoform co-expression modules by running the dynamicTreeCut hybrid algorithm on a percentile correlation matrix of single-cell isoform expression, followed by correlation-based filtering, metatranscript-based cluster merging, and recursive assignment of unclustered isoforms. Used by acorde to partition mouse neural isoforms into cell type-specific co-usage modules.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You have gene-level (not isoform-level) expression data and want conventional gene co-expression modules rather than isoform co-usage modules You need a fully automated, parameter-free clustering — this pipeline is explicitly semi-automated and includes manual cluster merges Your goal is differential isoform usage (DIU/coDIU) detection itself rather than the upstream module detection that feeds it

skills.description: Use when you have PacBio CCS BAMs with kinetic tags (fi, ri, fp, rp) and need per-read '+'/'-' calls distinguishing dZ-DNA from canonical DNA, e.g. in metagenomes or mixed dZ/canonical samples.
skills.name: dz-dna-read-classification
skills.search_text: dz-dna-read-classification Use when you have PacBio CCS BAMs with kinetic tags (fi, ri, fp, rp) and need per-read '+'/'-' calls distinguishing dZ-DNA from canonical DNA, e.g. in metagenomes or mixed dZ/canonical samples. Site-specific single-nucleotide Z/A discrimination is the goal — use the k11-mixed-AZ model (-k 11) base-calling module instead, which records per-base Z probability Quantifying Z fractions at individual loci in hybrid (partially substituted) samples — the SVM is optimized for fully substituted dZ-genomes and misses hybrid reads with diluted kinetic signatures Input reads lack PacBio kinetic signals (e.g. ONT data or CCS generated without --keep-kinetics) http://edamontology.org/topic_0654 http://edamontology.org/topic_3168 Classifies individual PacBio HiFi (CCS) reads as dZ-DNA-positive ('+') or canonical ('-') using Z-Calling's k21 MLP base-caller followed by the k21ReadClassifier SVM, enabling detection of dZ-DNA molecules in mixed samples. genomics/v1 10.1038/s42003-026-09849-8
skills.summary: Classifies individual PacBio HiFi (CCS) reads as dZ-DNA-positive ('+') or canonical ('-') using Z-Calling's k21 MLP base-caller followed by the k21ReadClassifier SVM, enabling detection of dZ-DNA molecules in mixed samples.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Site-specific single-nucleotide Z/A discrimination is the goal — use the k11-mixed-AZ model (-k 11) base-calling module instead, which records per-base Z probability Quantifying Z fractions at individual loci in hybrid (partially substituted) samples — the SVM is optimized for fully substituted dZ-genomes and misses hybrid reads with diluted kinetic signatures Input reads lack PacBio kinetic signals (e.g. ONT data or CCS generated without --keep-kinetics)

skills.description: Use when quantifying how Z (2,6-diaminopurine) incorporation perturbs PacBio HiFi PW/IPD kinetics relative to canonical A, using sequence-matched k-mer contexts with exactly one A/Z target base per window.
skills.name: dz-vs-canonical-sequence-matched-comparison
skills.search_text: dz-vs-canonical-sequence-matched-comparison Use when quantifying how Z (2,6-diaminopurine) incorporation perturbs PacBio HiFi PW/IPD kinetics relative to canonical A, using sequence-matched k-mer contexts with exactly one A/Z target base per window. Goal is production Z/A base calling or dZ-DNA read classification with the pre-trained models (z-calling-base with k21/k11 models, or the SVM read classifier) rather than feature-importance analysis Context k-mer windows contain multiple adjacent A/Z bases — the paper explicitly excludes these to avoid interference among adjacent A/Zs Input BAMs lack kinetic tags (fi, ri, fp, rp) because CCS was run without --keep-kinetics, or reads fail the Median_PW/Median_IPD >=0.3 quality filter http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 Compares PacBio kinetic signals (pulse width, inter-pulse duration) between matched dZ-DNA and canonical-DNA reads on 21-mer contexts centered on a single A/Z target base, controlling sequence context (fixed central 3-mer) to isolate Z-induced kinetic shifts and quantify them via Random Forest feature importance. genomics/v1 10.1038/s42003-026-09849-8
skills.summary: Compares PacBio kinetic signals (pulse width, inter-pulse duration) between matched dZ-DNA and canonical-DNA reads on 21-mer contexts centered on a single A/Z target base, controlling sequence context (fixed central 3-mer) to isolate Z-induced kinetic shifts and quantify them via Random Forest feature importance.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Goal is production Z/A base calling or dZ-DNA read classification with the pre-trained models (z-calling-base with k21/k11 models, or the SVM read classifier) rather than feature-importance analysis Context k-mer windows contain multiple adjacent A/Z bases — the paper explicitly excludes these to avoid interference among adjacent A/Zs Input BAMs lack kinetic tags (fi, ri, fp, rp) because CCS was run without --keep-kinetics, or reads fail the Median_PW/Median_IPD >=0.3 quality filter

skills.description: Use when you have a raw gene-by-sample RNA-seq count matrix and must call differentially expressed genes between mutant and wild-type conditions using edgeR TMM normalization plus a negative-binomial GLM with likelihood-ratio tests.
skills.name: edger-negative-binomial-differential-expression-testing
skills.search_text: edger-negative-binomial-differential-expression-testing Use when you have a raw gene-by-sample RNA-seq count matrix and must call differentially expressed genes between mutant and wild-type conditions using edgeR TMM normalization plus a negative-binomial GLM with likelihood-ratio tests. The question concerns methylation status of SMRT reads (methylated vs non-methylated motif sites) rather than gene expression — use SMALR's SMsn or SMp protocols instead. Input is already a normalized expression matrix or population-level consensus methylation calls rather than a raw gene-by-sample count matrix. There are no biological replicates (e.g., only a single wild-type sample), since the GLM contrast here depends on multiple clonal wild-type isolates. http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Differential-expression testing of RNA-seq gene count matrices with edgeR's negative-binomial generalized linear model, used here to quantify transcriptome changes in H. pylori J99 methyltransferase mutants (HPXZ1401, HPXZ1398) against five clonal wild-type isolates. genomics/v1 10.1038/ncomms8438
skills.summary: Differential-expression testing of RNA-seq gene count matrices with edgeR's negative-binomial generalized linear model, used here to quantify transcriptome changes in H. pylori J99 methyltransferase mutants (HPXZ1401, HPXZ1398) against five clonal wild-type isolates.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The question concerns methylation status of SMRT reads (methylated vs non-methylated motif sites) rather than gene expression — use SMALR's SMsn or SMp protocols instead. Input is already a normalized expression matrix or population-level consensus methylation calls rather than a raw gene-by-sample count matrix. There are no biological replicates (e.g., only a single wild-type sample), since the GLM contrast here depends on multiple clonal wild-type isolates.

skills.description: Use when checking whether short (~20–100 nt) Nanopore rapid-barcoding or adapter sequences occur in assembled contigs or read sets despite sequencing errors, e.g. screening GenBank assemblies for barcode contamination.
skills.name: edit-distance-approximate-matching
skills.search_text: edit-distance-approximate-matching Use when checking whether short (~20–100 nt) Nanopore rapid-barcoding or adapter sequences occur in assembled contigs or read sets despite sequencing errors, e.g. screening GenBank assemblies for barcode contamination. Reads are already demultiplexed and trimmed and you only need downstream analysis — no fuzzy barcode search is needed Queries are longer than Sassy's intended range (it works well for patterns up to length ~1000, best at 20–100 nt DNA) You need exact matching only — edit-distance tolerance would inflate counts with spurious near-matches http://edamontology.org/topic_0102 Fuzzy (edit-distance) search of short Nanopore barcode and flank sequences against FASTA assemblies or reads, using Sassy-accelerated approximate matching as implemented in Barbell, to detect barcode contamination in public NCBI records. genomics/v1 10.1093/bioinformatics/btag349
skills.summary: Fuzzy (edit-distance) search of short Nanopore barcode and flank sequences against FASTA assemblies or reads, using Sassy-accelerated approximate matching as implemented in Barbell, to detect barcode contamination in public NCBI records.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Reads are already demultiplexed and trimmed and you only need downstream analysis — no fuzzy barcode search is needed Queries are longer than Sassy's intended range (it works well for patterns up to length ~1000, best at 20–100 nt DNA) You need exact matching only — edit-distance tolerance would inflate counts with spurious near-matches

skills.description: Use when evaluating whether a barcode-matching method recovers long-read cellular barcodes as accurately as an exact edit-distance baseline or a competing tool on simulated hybrid LR-SR scRNA-seq datasets.
skills.name: edit-distance-benchmark-comparison
skills.search_text: edit-distance-benchmark-comparison Use when evaluating whether a barcode-matching method recovers long-read cellular barcodes as accurately as an exact edit-distance baseline or a competing tool on simulated hybrid LR-SR scRNA-seq datasets. The goal is real-data performance characterization rather than controlled benchmarking against a published reference table The input barcodes come from a non-10x scRNA-seq platform without a fixed sequence adjacent to the barcode in the LR template UMI-level matching between SR and LR data is required, since scTagger does not yet support it http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 Benchmarks cellular barcode matching accuracy across a trie-based method (scTagger, e=2), an exact dynamic-programming brute-force baseline (edlib v1.3.9), and an alternative tool (FLAMES, commit #18fb83c) by classifying each long read as match, ambiguous, mismatch, or skip and comparing category percentages against published Table 3 values. genomics/v1 10.1016/j.isci.2022.104530
skills.summary: Benchmarks cellular barcode matching accuracy across a trie-based method (scTagger, e=2), an exact dynamic-programming brute-force baseline (edlib v1.3.9), and an alternative tool (FLAMES, commit #18fb83c) by classifying each long read as match, ambiguous, mismatch, or skip and comparing category percentages against published Table 3 values.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is real-data performance characterization rather than controlled benchmarking against a published reference table The input barcodes come from a non-10x scRNA-seq platform without a fixed sequence adjacent to the barcode in the LR template UMI-level matching between SR and LR data is required, since scTagger does not yet support it

skills.description: Use when reads carry short barcodes embedded between known flanking sequences (e.g. ONT kit B3 flanks 'GGTGCTG'/'TTAACCT' around a 24-bp barcode) and the corrupted barcode s' must be located in each FASTQ read before demultiplexing by probability divergence.
skills.name: edit-distance-flank-localization
skills.search_text: edit-distance-flank-localization Use when reads carry short barcodes embedded between known flanking sequences (e.g. ONT kit B3 flanks 'GGTGCTG'/'TTAACCT' around a 24-bp barcode) and the corrupted barcode s' must be located in each FASTQ read before demultiplexing by probability divergence. The reads are already-extracted, corrupted barcodes that only need classification — that is PRO's demultiplexing step (PRO-dex, probability divergence), not flank localization. The library preparation does not ligate flanking sequences around the barcode (no flank motifs to anchor the extraction), so there is nothing to align. Data are PacBio reads — the article states no tests on PacBio data have been performed, so extraction behavior is unvalidated there. http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Extracts corrupted barcodes from nanopore reads by aligning the flanking sequences with the edlib Python library (semiglobal edit distance, Dm = min{Df, Db}) and excising the interval between the two flank alignments, as used in PRO's demultiplexing procedure. genomics/v1 10.1016/j.fmre.2024.04.014
skills.summary: Extracts corrupted barcodes from nanopore reads by aligning the flanking sequences with the edlib Python library (semiglobal edit distance, Dm = min{Df, Db}) and excising the interval between the two flank alignments, as used in PRO's demultiplexing procedure.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The reads are already-extracted, corrupted barcodes that only need classification — that is PRO's demultiplexing step (PRO-dex, probability divergence), not flank localization. The library preparation does not ligate flanking sequences around the barcode (no flank motifs to anchor the extraction), so there is nothing to align. Data are PacBio reads — the article states no tests on PacBio data have been performed, so extraction behavior is unvalidated there.

skills.description: Use when comparing assembled long-read consensus sequences (e.g. MinION rDNA amplicons) against a high-accuracy reference consensus and you need a single per-sequence error metric for accuracy/coverage sweeps.
skills.name: edit-distance-sequence-comparison
skills.search_text: edit-distance-sequence-comparison Use when comparing assembled long-read consensus sequences (e.g. MinION rDNA amplicons) against a high-accuracy reference consensus and you need a single per-sequence error metric for accuracy/coverage sweeps. Input is a bulk-sample metabarcoding feature table or abundance matrix — the article notes long rDNA amplicon sequencing is not yet reliable for bulk sample analysis, and edit distance to a single reference consensus is meaningless there You need alignment with quality-score weighting or homopolymer-aware error modeling — Edlib computes unweighted Levenshtein distance only Reads still carry barcodes and primers — trim with MiniBar -T first, otherwise the untrimmed ends inflate the measured edit distance http://edamontology.org/topic_3168 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Quantifies sequence similarity between DNA consensus sequences (e.g. Nanopore rDNA consensus vs. Illumina-derived reference consensus) using Levenshtein edit distance computed with the Edlib library, expressing distances as percent error relative to consensus length. genomics/v1 10.1093/gigascience/giz006
skills.summary: Quantifies sequence similarity between DNA consensus sequences (e.g. Nanopore rDNA consensus vs. Illumina-derived reference consensus) using Levenshtein edit distance computed with the Edlib library, expressing distances as percent error relative to consensus length.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is a bulk-sample metabarcoding feature table or abundance matrix — the article notes long rDNA amplicon sequencing is not yet reliable for bulk sample analysis, and edit distance to a single reference consensus is meaningless there You need alignment with quality-score weighting or homopolymer-aware error modeling — Edlib computes unweighted Levenshtein distance only Reads still carry barcodes and primers — trim with MiniBar -T first, otherwise the untrimmed ends inflate the measured edit distance

skills.description: Use when long reads from hybrid LR-SR scRNA-seq (e.g., 10x Genomics split-pool libraries) contain a fixed adapter sequence adjacent to the cellular barcode and you must locate and score that locus per read by edit distance.
skills.name: edit-distance-sequence-scoring
skills.search_text: edit-distance-sequence-scoring Use when long reads from hybrid LR-SR scRNA-seq (e.g., 10x Genomics split-pool libraries) contain a fixed adapter sequence adjacent to the cellular barcode and you must locate and score that locus per read by edit distance. The long-read template lacks a fixed sequence adjacent to the barcode (non-10x platforms) — scTagger support is conditional on a fixed sequence next to the barcode Barcode segments are already extracted and you only need to build the barcode whitelist or match barcodes (use extract_sr_bc / extract_sr_bc_from_lr / match_trie instead) You need to match UMI sequences between SR and LR data — that is not supported by this method http://edamontology.org/topic_0080 Scores approximate occurrences of a fixed short sequence (the Illumina adapter CTACACGACGCTCTTCCGATCT) against every long read by edit distance, using edlib glocal alignment to locate the barcode-adjacent segment in hybrid scRNA-seq long reads. This is the scTagger extract_lr_bc stage that precedes trie-based barcode matching. genomics/v1 10.1016/j.isci.2022.104530
skills.summary: Scores approximate occurrences of a fixed short sequence (the Illumina adapter CTACACGACGCTCTTCCGATCT) against every long read by edit distance, using edlib glocal alignment to locate the barcode-adjacent segment in hybrid scRNA-seq long reads. This is the scTagger extract_lr_bc stage that precedes trie-based barcode matching.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The long-read template lacks a fixed sequence adjacent to the barcode (non-10x platforms) — scTagger support is conditional on a fixed sequence next to the barcode Barcode segments are already extracted and you only need to build the barcode whitelist or match barcodes (use extract_sr_bc / extract_sr_bc_from_lr / match_trie instead) You need to match UMI sequences between SR and LR data — that is not supported by this method

skills.description: Use when demultiplexing dual-indexed Oxford Nanopore reads with MiniBar and you need to set or vary the barcode (-e) and primer (-E) edit-distance tolerances to balance read yield against misassignment.
skills.name: edit-distance-tolerance-parameterization
skills.search_text: edit-distance-tolerance-parameterization Use when demultiplexing dual-indexed Oxford Nanopore reads with MiniBar and you need to set or vary the barcode (-e) and primer (-E) edit-distance tolerances to balance read yield against misassignment. Reads are not dual-indexed Nanopore amplicons (e.g. single-index Illumina data) — MiniBar's dual barcode-plus-primer matching at both read ends does not apply The goal is consensus calling or downstream phylogenetic analysis of already-binned reads rather than tuning demultiplexing stringency You need exact barcode matching or mismatch-tolerant schemes other than Levenshtein/edit distance, which is what the Edlib-backed matcher implements http://edamontology.org/topic_0080 http://edamontology.org/topic_3168 Tunes the barcode and primer edit-distance thresholds (MiniBar's -e and -E flags) when demultiplexing dual-indexed Nanopore rDNA amplicon reads, trading read yield against misassignment. The article shows per-specimen read recovery rising steeply with the barcode edit distance (mean 355/647/1,051 reads at -e 2/3/4 with -E 11). genomics/v1 10.1093/gigascience/giz006
skills.summary: Tunes the barcode and primer edit-distance thresholds (MiniBar's -e and -E flags) when demultiplexing dual-indexed Nanopore rDNA amplicon reads, trading read yield against misassignment. The article shows per-specimen read recovery rising steeply with the barcode edit distance (mean 355/647/1,051 reads at -e 2/3/4 with -E 11).
skills.when_to_use_negative: Reads are not dual-indexed Nanopore amplicons (e.g. single-index Illumina data) — MiniBar's dual barcode-plus-primer matching at both read ends does not apply The goal is consensus calling or downstream phylogenetic analysis of already-binned reads rather than tuning demultiplexing stringency You need exact barcode matching or mismatch-tolerant schemes other than Levenshtein/edit distance, which is what the Edlib-backed matcher implements

skills.description: Use when assigning cell barcodes to ONT/PacBio single-cell reads from 10x Genomics 5'-anchored cDNA libraries, where sequencing error and variable barcode/UMI placement demand error-tolerant motif search before whitelist alignment.
skills.name: edlib-edit-distance-sequence-matching
skills.search_text: edlib-edit-distance-sequence-matching Use when assigning cell barcodes to ONT/PacBio single-cell reads from 10x Genomics 5'-anchored cDNA libraries, where sequencing error and variable barcode/UMI placement demand error-tolerant motif search before whitelist alignment. Data are short-read (Illumina) 10x libraries where barcode and UMI sit in a fixed R1 position — direct whitelist matching without softclip motif search suffices The goal is downstream UMI deduplication rather than barcode detection — for that, nanoranger.R collapses UMIs with starcode at Levenshtein distance 3 since UMIs have no whitelist http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 Use edlib's Levenshtein-distance approximate matching to locate 10x Genomics barcode-UMI motifs in long-read 5' softclips, tolerating the elevated error rate of ONT/PacBio reads. It is the motif-detection front end of the nanoranger cell-barcode assignment pipeline. genomics/v1 10.1038/s41467-023-44137-7
skills.summary: Use edlib's Levenshtein-distance approximate matching to locate 10x Genomics barcode-UMI motifs in long-read 5' softclips, tolerating the elevated error rate of ONT/PacBio reads. It is the motif-detection front end of the nanoranger cell-barcode assignment pipeline.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Data are short-read (Illumina) 10x libraries where barcode and UMI sit in a fixed R1 position — direct whitelist matching without softclip motif search suffices The goal is downstream UMI deduplication rather than barcode detection — for that, nanoranger.R collapses UMIs with starcode at Levenshtein distance 3 since UMIs have no whitelist

skills.description: Use when predicted proteins from coding genes absent from a reference GTF annotation (e.g. novel-prot.fa from an add-ncbi-annotation run) need homolog/paralog assignment and functional descriptions to recover missing genes.
skills.name: eggnog-functional-annotation-intersection
skills.search_text: eggnog-functional-annotation-intersection Use when predicted proteins from coding genes absent from a reference GTF annotation (e.g. novel-prot.fa from an add-ncbi-annotation run) need homolog/paralog assignment and functional descriptions to recover missing genes. The organism lacks an assembled genome and an NCBI GTF annotation, since the workflow depends on reconciled genomic coordinates and a reference annotation (per the article's scope statement) The proteins already carry gene names and functional descriptions in the reference annotation, so homology-based recovery of missing genes is unnecessary A full multi-hit homology search is needed rather than a single best hit per query, since -max_target_seqs 1 suppresses secondary paralog matches outside the 90-100% same-locus rule http://edamontology.org/topic_0080 http://edamontology.org/topic_0621 Assigns gene names and functional descriptions to novel predicted coding proteins by intersecting a blastp hit table (single best hit against the UniProt Gallus gallus proteome, taxid 9031) with eggNOG-mapper functional annotations, and classifies hits as single-copy homologs vs paralogs (90-100% homology within <0.5 Mb loci). genomics/v1 10.1093/gigascience/giac099
skills.summary: Assigns gene names and functional descriptions to novel predicted coding proteins by intersecting a blastp hit table (single best hit against the UniProt Gallus gallus proteome, taxid 9031) with eggNOG-mapper functional annotations, and classifies hits as single-copy homologs vs paralogs (90-100% homology within <0.5 Mb loci).
skills.when_to_use_negative: The organism lacks an assembled genome and an NCBI GTF annotation, since the workflow depends on reconciled genomic coordinates and a reference annotation (per the article's scope statement) The proteins already carry gene names and functional descriptions in the reference annotation, so homology-based recovery of missing genes is unnecessary A full multi-hit homology search is needed rather than a single best hit per query, since -max_target_seqs 1 suppresses secondary paralog matches outside the 90-100% same-locus rule

skills.description: Use when full-length circRNA isoform structures from isocirc.out (blockType/blockStarts/blockSize with readCount) must be compared to GTF exon coordinates to classify internal alternative splicing and EIciRNA retained introns.
skills.name: eicircrna-retained-intron-identification
skills.search_text: eicircrna-retained-intron-identification Use when full-length circRNA isoform structures from isocirc.out (blockType/blockStarts/blockSize with readCount) must be compared to GTF exon coordinates to classify internal alternative splicing and EIciRNA retained introns. skills.name: energy-delay-product-computation
skills.search_text: energy-delay-product-computation Use when a benchmarking source reports per-read (or per-operation) execution time and energy consumption separately for multiple platforms and the analysis goal is a normalized efficiency comparison via EDP and derived ratio fields. The source reports only throughput or total-job timings without paired per-read energy measurements — EDP cannot be recomputed without both latency and energy The comparison is between runs on the same platform (e.g., sigfish-haru vs. sigfish-cpu on the Kria KV260) where a raw speed ratio alone is sufficient Measurements are total-workflow rather than per-read, unless they are first normalized to a per-read basis http://edamontology.org/topic_0605 Recompute energy-delay product (EDP) as per-read latency (ms) × per-read energy (mJ) from reported benchmark measurements, and derive cross-platform ratios (e.g., HARU on Xilinx FPGA EDP ≈0.987 vs. 36-core Intel Xeon Gold server ≈644.94, a ~650x EDP gap). skills.description: Use when judging how complete a hybrid-scaffolded eukaryotic genome assembly is, e.g. comparing contig count and N50 (npScarf 19 contigs / 913 Kb on S. cerevisiae W303) against competitor scaffolders via QUAST.
skills.name: eukaryotic-genome-completeness-evaluation
skills.search_text: eukaryotic-genome-completeness-evaluation Use when judging how complete a hybrid-scaffolded eukaryotic genome assembly is, e.g. comparing contig count and N50 (npScarf 19 contigs / 913 Kb on S. cerevisiae W303) against competitor scaffolders via QUAST. The sample is prokaryotic/bacterial — the completeness statistic is described as stable for bacterial genomes (up to 20 largest contigs > 20 Kb), so eukaryotic-scale evaluation logic and the circularized-mitochondrial check do not apply. Input is already a finished or reference-complete assembly and no competitor scaffolds exist to compare — QUAST-vs-next-best-method reasoning adds nothing. Nanopore data are raw signal without base-calling and no real-time base-caller (e.g. Nanocall, DeepNano) is available, so the streaming scaffold feed cannot be produced. http://edamontology.org/topic_0196 http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Evaluates the completeness of a real-time hybrid-scaffolded eukaryotic assembly by comparing contig number and N50 against the next best scaffolding method, and by checking hallmarks such as a circularized mitochondrial contig. Applied to S. cerevisiae W303, where npScarf achieved 19 contigs with N50 913 Kb versus 108 contigs (N50 600 Kb) for Nanocorr. genomics/v1 10.1038/ncomms14515
skills.summary: Evaluates the completeness of a real-time hybrid-scaffolded eukaryotic assembly by comparing contig number and N50 against the next best scaffolding method, and by checking hallmarks such as a circularized mitochondrial contig. Applied to S. cerevisiae W303, where npScarf achieved 19 contigs with N50 913 Kb versus 108 contigs (N50 600 Kb) for Nanocorr.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The sample is prokaryotic/bacterial — the completeness statistic is described as stable for bacterial genomes (up to 20 largest contigs > 20 Kb), so eukaryotic-scale evaluation logic and the circularized-mitochondrial check do not apply. Input is already a finished or reference-complete assembly and no competitor scaffolds exist to compare — QUAST-vs-next-best-method reasoning adds nothing. Nanopore data are raw signal without base-calling and no real-time base-caller (e.g. Nanocall, DeepNano) is available, so the streaming scaffold feed cannot be produced.

skills.description: Reference for nanopore direct RNA pipelines using Nanopolish eventalign output where per-k-mer signal samples must be reordered to 5'–3' before building fixed-length (5 × 20 = 100) 9-mer feature vectors for deep-learning modification callers.
skills.name: eventalign-signal-orientation-flipping
skills.search_text: eventalign-signal-orientation-flipping Reference for nanopore direct RNA pipelines using Nanopolish eventalign output where per-k-mer signal samples must be reordered to 5'–3' before building fixed-length (5 × 20 = 100) 9-mer feature vectors for deep-learning modification callers. If signals were generated by a tool that already emits 5'–3'-ordered k-mer samples (e.g. non-Nanopolish resquiggling), an unconditional flip may invert correct ordering. If the downstream model does not use overlapping 5-mer windows around a central modified base (different context size), the 9-mer assembly and flip are unnecessary. http://edamontology.org/topic_3168 Preprocessing step for nanopore direct RNA data in which per-5-mer signal lists from Nanopolish eventalign (produced in 3'–5' order) are flipped to 5'–3' orientation before concatenating signals from overlapping 5-mers, so that 9-mer contexts are correctly assembled for CHEUI m6A/m5C model input. genomics/v1 10.1038/s41467-024-47953-7
skills.summary: Preprocessing step for nanopore direct RNA data in which per-5-mer signal lists from Nanopolish eventalign (produced in 3'–5' order) are flipped to 5'–3' orientation before concatenating signals from overlapping 5-mers, so that 9-mer contexts are correctly assembled for CHEUI m6A/m5C model input.
skills.when_to_use_negative: If signals were generated by a tool that already emits 5'–3'-ordered k-mer samples (e.g. non-Nanopolish resquiggling), an unconditional flip may invert correct ordering. If the downstream model does not use overlapping 5-mer windows around a central modified base (different context size), the 9-mer assembly and flip are unnecessary.

skills.description: Use when analyzing frequency-dependent selection between two behavioral strategies (hawk vs. dove), where the user supplies an initial hawk frequency and a payoff matrix for hawk-hawk, hawk-dove, and dove-dove interactions.
skills.name: evolutionary-game-dynamics-simulation
skills.search_text: evolutionary-game-dynamics-simulation Use when analyzing frequency-dependent selection between two behavioral strategies (hawk vs. dove), where the user supplies an initial hawk frequency and a payoff matrix for hawk-hawk, hawk-dove, and dove-dove interactions. The model of interest is frequency-independent selection on phenotypic traits or gene frequencies under drift/migration rather than strategy-based game dynamics The analysis targets more than two competing strategies or asymmetric games not expressible as a 2x2 hawk-dove payoff matrix The user is less adept in R and only needs a prebuilt interactive web interface rather than a scripted simulation Simulates frequency-dependent evolutionary game dynamics (e.g., the hawk-dove game) by iteratively computing per-strategy expected payoffs from a user-specified payoff matrix and updating strategy frequencies via relative fitness, as implemented in the learnPopGen R package. genomics/v1 10.1002/ece3.5412
skills.summary: Simulates frequency-dependent evolutionary game dynamics (e.g., the hawk-dove game) by iteratively computing per-strategy expected payoffs from a user-specified payoff matrix and updating strategy frequencies via relative fitness, as implemented in the learnPopGen R package.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The model of interest is frequency-independent selection on phenotypic traits or gene frequencies under drift/migration rather than strategy-based game dynamics The analysis targets more than two competing strategies or asymmetric games not expressible as a 2x2 hawk-dove payoff matrix The user is less adept in R and only needs a prebuilt interactive web interface rather than a scripted simulation

skills.description: Use when you need to quantify which pipeline stage dominates runtime (e.g., sDTW vs preprocessing vs I/O) to justify or evaluate hardware acceleration on a specific dataset such as SARS-CoV-2 BLOW5 nanopore reads.
skills.name: execution-time-percentage-analysis
skills.search_text: execution-time-percentage-analysis Use when you need to quantify which pipeline stage dominates runtime (e.g., sDTW vs preprocessing vs I/O) to justify or evaluate hardware acceleration on a specific dataset such as SARS-CoV-2 BLOW5 nanopore reads. The goal is end-to-end throughput benchmarking (e.g., reads/second or the reported 2.5x/85x speedups) rather than a per-stage percentage breakdown of where time is spent The pipeline being profiled is not a staged squiggle-mapping workflow (sDTW/preprocessing/I-O) — a single monolithic step has no meaningful per-stage share to attribute The dataset is not representative (timing shares like the >98% sDTW figure were reported for the complete SARS-CoV-2 dataset; shares may differ substantially on other read sets) http://edamontology.org/topic_0102 http://edamontology.org/topic_3168 http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Profiles a nanopore Read Until pipeline (e.g., sigfish/sigfish-haru sDTW squiggle mapping) by instrumenting wall-clock time around each stage — sDTW alignment, signal preprocessing, and file I/O — and reports each stage's share of total runtime as a percentage. This reveals computational bottlenecks such as sDTW dominating >98% of software-only runtime versus <64% with the HARU FPGA accelerator. genomics/v1 10.1093/gigascience/giad046
skills.summary: Profiles a nanopore Read Until pipeline (e.g., sigfish/sigfish-haru sDTW squiggle mapping) by instrumenting wall-clock time around each stage — sDTW alignment, signal preprocessing, and file I/O — and reports each stage's share of total runtime as a percentage. This reveals computational bottlenecks such as sDTW dominating >98% of software-only runtime versus <64% with the HARU FPGA accelerator.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is end-to-end throughput benchmarking (e.g., reads/second or the reported 2.5x/85x speedups) rather than a per-stage percentage breakdown of where time is spent The pipeline being profiled is not a staged squiggle-mapping workflow (sDTW/preprocessing/I-O) — a single monolithic step has no meaningful per-stage share to attribute The dataset is not representative (timing shares like the >98% sDTW figure were reported for the complete SARS-CoV-2 dataset; shares may differ substantially on other read sets)

skills.description: Use when validating de novo variant calls from whole-exome sequencing trios, where capture-region boundaries bias callability and DNVs must be split into high vs low confidence classes.
skills.name: exome-capture-interval-buffering
skills.search_text: exome-capture-interval-buffering Use when validating de novo variant calls from whole-exome sequencing trios, where capture-region boundaries bias callability and DNVs must be split into high vs low confidence classes. Input data is WGS-only with no exome capture-region BED file — the ±10 bp/50 bp interval buffering step is specific to WES capture boundaries Only VCFs are available without BAM/CRAM files — HAT-FLEX is the caller-agnostic drop-in alternative, and mpileup read counting cannot be performed The data is PacBio HiFi long-read WGS, which the Hare v1.2 workflow does not cover (use Tortoise instead) http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 A WES follow-up method from the HAT workflow that trims exome capture regions to ±10 bp around a 50 bp buffered exon boundary to define high-confidence callable windows, then labels trio DNVs high/low confidence using Samtools mpileup read counts in child and parents. genomics/v1 10.1093/bioinformatics/btad775
skills.summary: A WES follow-up method from the HAT workflow that trims exome capture regions to ±10 bp around a 50 bp buffered exon boundary to define high-confidence callable windows, then labels trio DNVs high/low confidence using Samtools mpileup read counts in child and parents.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input data is WGS-only with no exome capture-region BED file — the ±10 bp/50 bp interval buffering step is specific to WES capture boundaries Only VCFs are available without BAM/CRAM files — HAT-FLEX is the caller-agnostic drop-in alternative, and mpileup read counting cannot be performed The data is PacBio HiFi long-read WGS, which the Hare v1.2 workflow does not cover (use Tortoise instead)

skills.description: Use when a published exon list must be intersected with a genome annotation to verify exon categories (e.g. strictly second-first vs 'diverse') before computing upfi/dofi ratios or Fupfi distributions.
skills.name: exon-annotation-interval-matching
skills.search_text: exon-annotation-interval-matching Use when a published exon list must be intersected with a genome annotation to verify exon categories (e.g. strictly second-first vs 'diverse') before computing upfi/dofi ratios or Fupfi distributions. The input is already a per-transcript exon-type table derived from the annotation — re-matching exons would be redundant. The analysis targets novel unannotated exons or de novo splicing junctions absent from the GTF, which cannot be typed by interval matching against Ensembl. The goal is quantification of splicing order itself (upfi/dofi counts), for which Insplico — not annotation matching — is the tool. http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 Match user-supplied or study-defined exon sets (e.g. Kim et al.'s 17,273 second-first exons) against an Ensembl GTF annotation to classify each exon by its exon type across transcripts (second-first, second-last, internal, or 'diverse'), which is essential for reconciling AISO profiles between Insplico quantification and published re-analyses. genomics/v1 10.1093/nar/gkad244
skills.summary: Match user-supplied or study-defined exon sets (e.g. Kim et al.'s 17,273 second-first exons) against an Ensembl GTF annotation to classify each exon by its exon type across transcripts (second-first, second-last, internal, or 'diverse'), which is essential for reconciling AISO profiles between Insplico quantification and published re-analyses.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is already a per-transcript exon-type table derived from the annotation — re-matching exons would be redundant. The analysis targets novel unannotated exons or de novo splicing junctions absent from the GTF, which cannot be typed by interval matching against Ensembl. The goal is quantification of splicing order itself (upfi/dofi counts), for which Insplico — not annotation matching — is the tool.

skills.description: Use when a de novo exon or splice-graph prediction (EXFI, ChopStitch, GMAP) must be quantitatively scored against a reference GFF3 annotation and assessed for downstream usability via mappability.
skills.name: exon-annotation-recovery-metrics
skills.search_text: exon-annotation-recovery-metrics Use when a de novo exon or splice-graph prediction (EXFI, ChopStitch, GMAP) must be quantitatively scored against a reference GFF3 annotation and assessed for downstream usability via mappability. No reference genome or GFF3 annotation exists for the target species — coordinate-based precision/recall and genomic mappability cannot be computed at all Predictions are still raw GFA1 splice graph nodes and have not been extracted into exon coordinate sets comparable to BED/GFF3 intervals The question is SNP/indel genotyping suitability (quality and distance filtering of variants) rather than exon recovery benchmarking http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Benchmarks predicted exon sets (from EXFI, ChopStitch, or GMAP) against reference GFF3 annotations by computing precision, recall, and F1 from coordinate overlaps, and mappability from BWA MEM alignments of predicted exons back to the genomic reference. genomics/v1 10.1002/ece3.6587
skills.summary: Benchmarks predicted exon sets (from EXFI, ChopStitch, or GMAP) against reference GFF3 annotations by computing precision, recall, and F1 from coordinate overlaps, and mappability from BWA MEM alignments of predicted exons back to the genomic reference.
skills.when_to_use_negative: No reference genome or GFF3 annotation exists for the target species — coordinate-based precision/recall and genomic mappability cannot be computed at all Predictions are still raw GFA1 splice graph nodes and have not been extracted into exon coordinate sets comparable to BED/GFF3 intervals The question is SNP/indel genotyping suitability (quality and distance filtering of variants) rather than exon recovery benchmarking

skills.description: Use when you have per-exon AISO measurements (upfi/dofi counts, Fupfi) plus extracted intron-exon features and want to reveal monotonic or non-monotonic feature–Fupfi relationships, e.g. reproducing Figure 6 of the Insplico study.
skills.name: exon-binning-stratified-feature-analysis
skills.search_text: exon-binning-stratified-feature-analysis Use when you have per-exon AISO measurements (upfi/dofi counts, Fupfi) plus extracted intron-exon features and want to reveal monotonic or non-monotonic feature–Fupfi relationships, e.g. reproducing Figure 6 of the Insplico study. You only have long-read RNA-seq without the 5'/3' bias correction module applied — uncorrected long-read biases will distort Fupfi bins relative to short-read patterns You need AISO information beyond the introns directly flanking the exon of interest — short reads barely provide splicing-order information beyond flanking introns The goal is per-exon (not population-level) AISO inference or quantification of AISO itself — use Insplico's AISO quantification, not this binning/plotting skill http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 http://edamontology.org/topic_2269 Stratifies exons into five equal subsets per intron-exon feature (splice-site strengths, intron/exon lengths, branch point-to-AG distance), computes mean Fupfi per bin in R, and plots binned relationships with ggplot2 to expose universal genomic features associated with adjacent-intron splicing order (AISO) across species. genomics/v1 10.1093/nar/gkad244
skills.summary: Stratifies exons into five equal subsets per intron-exon feature (splice-site strengths, intron/exon lengths, branch point-to-AG distance), computes mean Fupfi per bin in R, and plots binned relationships with ggplot2 to expose universal genomic features associated with adjacent-intron splicing order (AISO) across species.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You only have long-read RNA-seq without the 5'/3' bias correction module applied — uncorrected long-read biases will distort Fupfi bins relative to short-read patterns You need AISO information beyond the introns directly flanking the exon of interest — short reads barely provide splicing-order information beyond flanking introns The goal is per-exon (not population-level) AISO inference or quantification of AISO itself — use Insplico's AISO quantification, not this binning/plotting skill

skills.description: Use when a raw PacBio Iso-Seq/lrCaptureSeq isoform annotation (transcript FASTA, abundance table, GFF, ORF FASTA) must be converted into a curated isoform catalog by removing isoforms with fewer than 4 exon segments, truncated transcripts, or the bottom 5% least-abundant isoforms per gene.
skills.name: exon-count-threshold-filtering
skills.search_text: exon-count-threshold-filtering Use when a raw PacBio Iso-Seq/lrCaptureSeq isoform annotation (transcript FASTA, abundance table, GFF, ORF FASTA) must be converted into a curated isoform catalog by removing isoforms with fewer than 4 exon segments, truncated transcripts, or the bottom 5% least-abundant isoforms per gene. Input is short-read RNA-seq data, which cannot resolve full-length sequences of multi-kilobase transcripts and therefore lacks the isoform-level annotation these filters require The goal is off-target transcript removal or database saving/loading (process_db, saveRDS/readRDS steps), which are separate workflow stages rather than exon-count/abundance filtering Isoforms smaller than ~4.5 kb or very rare transcripts are the target of interest, since the size-selection protocol and filtering intentionally remove short and rare isoforms http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 An IsoPops-based filtering procedure for lrCaptureSeq isoform catalogs that drops low-quality and low-confidence isoforms using a minimum non-contiguous exon-segment count (exon_min_count = 4), a per-isoform abundance floor, and truncation removal, reducing 8287 pre-filter isoforms to a curated catalog of ~4116 isoforms across 30 targeted genes. genomics/v1 10.1038/s41467-020-17009-7
skills.summary: An IsoPops-based filtering procedure for lrCaptureSeq isoform catalogs that drops low-quality and low-confidence isoforms using a minimum non-contiguous exon-segment count (exon_min_count = 4), a per-isoform abundance floor, and truncation removal, reducing 8287 pre-filter isoforms to a curated catalog of ~4116 isoforms across 30 targeted genes.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is short-read RNA-seq data, which cannot resolve full-length sequences of multi-kilobase transcripts and therefore lacks the isoform-level annotation these filters require The goal is off-target transcript removal or database saving/loading (process_db, saveRDS/readRDS steps), which are separate workflow stages rather than exon-count/abundance filtering Isoforms smaller than ~4.5 kb or very rare transcripts are the target of interest, since the size-selection protocol and filtering intentionally remove short and rare isoforms

skills.description: Use when reconstructing exons from a de novo transcriptome against a WGS-derived Bloom filter (e.g. k=25 genome_k25_m100M_l1.bloom) and you must merge positive k-mers, remove Bloom-filter false-positive exons, and trim splice-site overlaps into a GFA1 graph.
skills.name: exon-merging-and-false-positive-filtering
skills.search_text: exon-merging-and-false-positive-filtering Use when reconstructing exons from a de novo transcriptome against a WGS-derived Bloom filter (e.g. k=25 genome_k25_m100M_l1.bloom) and you must merge positive k-mers, remove Bloom-filter false-positive exons, and trim splice-site overlaps into a GFA1 graph. A reference genome and GFF3 annotation are already available — a splice-aware aligner such as GMAP can extract IEB coordinates directly from alignments There is no assembled transcriptome — EXFI requires a transcriptome assembly plus raw WGS reads, not raw RNA-Seq reads alone The goal is read-level sequence classification or host/contamination screening — use biobloomcategorizer directly instead of the exon reconstruction pipeline http://edamontology.org/topic_0080 http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 EXFI's build_splice_graph post-detection logic: after transcriptomic k-mers are scored against a WGS Bloom filter, consecutive positive k-mers overlapping by k-1 bases are merged into a draft exome, short false-positive exons are removed, and overlapping exon pairs are relaxed-merged or GU/AG-polished before writing a GFA1 splice graph. genomics/v1 10.1002/ece3.6587
skills.summary: EXFI's build_splice_graph post-detection logic: after transcriptomic k-mers are scored against a WGS Bloom filter, consecutive positive k-mers overlapping by k-1 bases are merged into a draft exome, short false-positive exons are removed, and overlapping exon pairs are relaxed-merged or GU/AG-polished before writing a GFA1 splice graph.
skills.when_to_use_negative: A reference genome and GFF3 annotation are already available — a splice-aware aligner such as GMAP can extract IEB coordinates directly from alignments There is no assembled transcriptome — EXFI requires a transcriptome assembly plus raw WGS reads, not raw RNA-Seq reads alone The goal is read-level sequence classification or host/contamination screening — use biobloomcategorizer directly instead of the exon reconstruction pipeline

skills.description: Use when you have aligned RNA-seq (short or long reads) around user-specified exons and need to label each exon's AISO class (upfi/dofi) or quantify Fupfi for cross-sample consistency, conservation, or spliceosomal-disruption analyses.
skills.name: exon-splicing-order-classification-fupfi-thresholds
skills.search_text: exon-splicing-order-classification-fupfi-thresholds Use when you have aligned RNA-seq (short or long reads) around user-specified exons and need to label each exon's AISO class (upfi/dofi) or quantify Fupfi for cross-sample consistency, conservation, or spliceosomal-disruption analyses. The goal is differential transcript-level splicing (PSI/PIR of alternative exons) rather than the relative splicing order of the two introns flanking a single exon — Insplico targets AISO specifically. Exons lack a clear adjacent upstream/downstream intron pair (first/last exons, single-exon transcripts) or the flanking introns exceed quantifiable limits, since informative upfi/dofi reads cannot be defined. Only very short reads or short paired-end fragments are available for long exons — read length and fragment size limit the maximum exon length quantifiable with short reads. http://edamontology.org/topic_3523 http://edamontology.org/topic_3320 Classifies individual exons into adjacent-intron splicing-order (AISO) categories — upfi (upstream intron first), dofi (downstream intron first), or unclassified — using Insplico-quantified upfi/dofi/bus/bos read counts and the fraction of upstream-first informative reads (Fupfi) with fixed thresholds. genomics/v1 10.1093/nar/gkad244
skills.summary: Classifies individual exons into adjacent-intron splicing-order (AISO) categories — upfi (upstream intron first), dofi (downstream intron first), or unclassified — using Insplico-quantified upfi/dofi/bus/bos read counts and the fraction of upstream-first informative reads (Fupfi) with fixed thresholds.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is differential transcript-level splicing (PSI/PIR of alternative exons) rather than the relative splicing order of the two introns flanking a single exon — Insplico targets AISO specifically. Only very short reads or short paired-end fragments are available for long exons — read length and fragment size limit the maximum exon length quantifiable with short reads.

skills.search_text: exon-structure-clustering-by-umi-support Use when full-length Nanopore scRNA-seq reads (10x-barcoded, UMI-annotated) must be collapsed into discrete isoform models and candidate novel isoforms must be supported by a minimum number of UMIs. Input reads are not UMI/cell-barcode-annotated long reads (e.g. raw fastq or short-read-only data) — CollapseModel relies on per-UMI grouping of Nanopore SAM records The goal is gene-level or isoform-level count matrices from already-validated transcriptomes (use IsoformMatrix, Steps 4a/4b, instead of novel isoform discovery) No external short-read data or CAGE/polyA reference resources are available, so novel isoforms cannot satisfy the juncCo/cageCo/polyaCo validation step http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Clusters Nanopore long reads into transcript isoform models by grouping SAM records per cell barcode and UMI according to exon makeup, then filters candidate novel isoforms by UMI-based evidence thresholds in the Sicelore CollapseModel step. genomics/v1 10.1038/s41467-020-17800-6

skills.description: Use when single-cell long-read (Nanopore) molecule consensus alignments must be assigned to annotated Gencode isoforms via strict exonic-structure matching to build isoform-level UMI count matrices per cell.
skills.name: exon-structure-transcript-assignment
skills.search_text: exon-structure-transcript-assignment Use when single-cell long-read (Nanopore) molecule consensus alignments must be assigned to annotated Gencode isoforms via strict exonic-structure matching to build isoform-level UMI count matrices per cell. You want novel isoform discovery or novel junction reconstruction — STRICT full-match assignment only recovers known Gencode transcripts (use Sicelore CollapseModel / step 7 instead). Input is raw Nanopore FASTQ rather than UMI-consensus molecules — barcode/UMI assignment, error correction and consensus generation must happen first (Steps 1–4b). Ambiguous multi-transcript assignments should be retained (e.g. gene-level-only quantification) — set AMBIGUOUS_ASSIGN accordingly or use a non-strict METHOD, as STRICT discards reads not fully matching one annotated isoform. http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Assigns single-cell Nanopore UMI molecules to known Gencode transcript isoforms by requiring a full exon-structure match between aligned consensus reads and annotated transcripts, then emits gene-, isoform- and junction-level UMI count matrices via Sicelore's IsoformMatrix. genomics/v1 10.1038/s41467-020-17800-6
skills.summary: Assigns single-cell Nanopore UMI molecules to known Gencode transcript isoforms by requiring a full exon-structure match between aligned consensus reads and annotated transcripts, then emits gene-, isoform- and junction-level UMI count matrices via Sicelore's IsoformMatrix.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You want novel isoform discovery or novel junction reconstruction — STRICT full-match assignment only recovers known Gencode transcripts (use Sicelore CollapseModel / step 7 instead). Input is raw Nanopore FASTQ rather than UMI-consensus molecules — barcode/UMI assignment, error correction and consensus generation must happen first (Steps 1–4b). Ambiguous multi-transcript assignments should be retained (e.g. gene-level-only quantification) — set AMBIGUOUS_ASSIGN accordingly or use a non-strict METHOD, as STRICT discards reads not fully matching one annotated isoform.

skills.name: family-wise-error-rate-correction
skills.search_text: family-wise-error-rate-correction Use when running many association tests (e.g. 68 SVs × 228 quantitative traits in a mixed-model GWAS) and you need trait-specific significance cutoffs at a 5% family-wise error rate instead of a single genome-wide P-value. You have very few tests or a single pre-specified hypothesis, where a simple Bonferroni correction or uncorrected threshold suffices and permuting trait values adds no value Your variant set includes SVs below the reliability threshold of the study (minor allele count <5), which were excluded from the mixed-model GWAS You need to call or filter structural variants themselves — that is handled upstream by the SURVIVOR consensus pipeline, not by this significance-correction step http://edamontology.org/topic_0625 Permutation-based trait-specific significance thresholds that control the 5% family-wise error rate in mixed-model GWAS. In the Jeffares et al. S. pombe study this was applied to associate 68 structural variants (plus 139,396 SNPs and 22,058 indels) with quantitative traits using LDAK. genomics/v1 10.1038/ncomms14061
skills.summary: Permutation-based trait-specific significance thresholds that control the 5% family-wise error rate in mixed-model GWAS. In the Jeffares et al. S. pombe study this was applied to associate 68 structural variants (plus 139,396 SNPs and 22,058 indels) with quantitative traits using LDAK.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You have very few tests or a single pre-specified hypothesis, where a simple Bonferroni correction or uncorrected threshold suffices and permuting trait values adds no value Your variant set includes SVs below the reliability threshold of the study (minor allele count <5), which were excluded from the mixed-model GWAS You need to call or filter structural variants themselves — that is handled upstream by the SURVIVOR consensus pipeline, not by this significance-correction step

The analysis only needs basecalled sequences (FASTQ/BAM), which can be pulled directly from SRA without downloading the source FAST5 archives The dataset's raw signal is stored in POD5 format rather than FAST5; use a converter such as blue-crab to reach SLOW5/BLOW5 instead http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_3168 Acquire raw nanopore signal data (FAST5 archives) from SRA via direct S3 links to sra-pub-src, then extract them for downstream signal-level analysis such as basecalling with guppy and visualization with Squigualiser. This skill bridges public archive deposition and signal-level workflows that require FAST5 input rather than FASTQ alone. genomics/v1 10.1093/bioinformatics/btae501

skills.description: Use when building a combined human-genome-plus-HLA reference for long-read (nanopore/PacBio) alignment in the HLAminer protocol, or when HLA allele FASTA headers must be reduced to allele names before concatenation.
skills.name: fasta-concatenation-reheadering
skills.search_text: fasta-concatenation-reheadering Use when building a combined human-genome-plus-HLA reference for long-read (nanopore/PacBio) alignment in the HLAminer protocol, or when HLA allele FASTA headers must be reduced to allele names before concatenation. The reference already exists as GCA_000001405.15_GRCh38_genomic.chr-only-noChr6-HLA-I_II_GEN.fa.gz in a validated deposit (Zenodo doi 10.5281/zenodo.14751276 / bcgsc.ca downloads) — reuse it instead of rebuilding. The task is short-read HLAminer prediction via HPTASR/HPRA against the IMGT/HLA allele database only, not whole-genome long-read alignment, which does not require the concatenated genome reference. Prepares the single FASTA reference used for HLAminer long-read alignments by reheadering IMGT/HLA allele genomic FASTA files to allele names only, concatenating them with the GRCh38 chromosome-only genome lacking chr6, and compressing everything into one .fa.gz. genomics/v1 10.1002/cpz1.70124
skills.summary: Prepares the single FASTA reference used for HLAminer long-read alignments by reheadering IMGT/HLA allele genomic FASTA files to allele names only, concatenating them with the GRCh38 chromosome-only genome lacking chr6, and compressing everything into one .fa.gz.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The reference already exists as GCA_000001405.15_GRCh38_genomic.chr-only-noChr6-HLA-I_II_GEN.fa.gz in a validated deposit (Zenodo doi 10.5281/zenodo.14751276 / bcgsc.ca downloads) — reuse it instead of rebuilding. The task is short-read HLAminer prediction via HPTASR/HPRA against the IMGT/HLA allele database only, not whole-genome long-read alignment, which does not require the concatenated genome reference.

skills.description: Use when long reads (PacBio, Oxford Nanopore, raw or error-corrected) must be converted into synthetic mate-pair FASTQ libraries with defined insert sizes for scaffolding or library parameter estimation.
skills.name: fasta-read-pair-simulation
skills.search_text: fasta-read-pair-simulation Use when long reads (PacBio, Oxford Nanopore, raw or error-corrected) must be converted into synthetic mate-pair FASTQ libraries with defined insert sizes for scaffolding or library parameter estimation. The input is already short-read Illumina mate-pair or paired-end data — no simulation/extraction is needed and real insert-size distributions should be estimated from the aligned reads directly. Long reads are too short to span the requested insert sizes — since the insert size is restricted to the actual long-read size, no pairs will be produced at that insert size; use smaller D or longer reads. Gap-size estimation requiring true insert-size distributions from commercial long-range technologies (10X Genomics, DOVETAIL Genomics), where linking information comes from a range of insert sizes and read-pair orientation may be unknown — synthetic libraries are comparatively easier but not equivalent. http://edamontology.org/topic_0196 http://edamontology.org/topic_0102 Extracts synthetic mate-pair libraries from long-read (FASTA/FASTQ) sequences in the Fast-SG style: forward/reverse 200 bp reads are excised at user-specified insert sizes so short-read algorithms can exploit long-range linking information without an aligner. genomics/v1 10.1093/gigascience/giy048
skills.summary: Extracts synthetic mate-pair libraries from long-read (FASTA/FASTQ) sequences in the Fast-SG style: forward/reverse 200 bp reads are excised at user-specified insert sizes so short-read algorithms can exploit long-range linking information without an aligner.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is already short-read Illumina mate-pair or paired-end data — no simulation/extraction is needed and real insert-size distributions should be estimated from the aligned reads directly. Long reads are too short to span the requested insert sizes — since the insert size is restricted to the actual long-read size, no pairs will be produced at that insert size; use smaller D or longer reads. Gap-size estimation requiring true insert-size distributions from commercial long-range technologies (10X Genomics, DOVETAIL Genomics), where linking information comes from a range of insert sizes and read-pair orientation may be unknown — synthetic libraries are comparatively easier but not equivalent.

skills.description: Use when de novo assembled contigs (e.g. no-target.contigs.fasta or re-assembly.contigs.fasta from Canu) must be matched to known viral references so each unique top hit can be written as a reference FASTA for consensus building.
skills.name: fasta-reference-sequence-emission
skills.search_text: fasta-reference-sequence-emission Use when de novo assembled contigs (e.g. no-target.contigs.fasta or re-assembly.contigs.fasta from Canu) must be matched to known viral references so each unique top hit can be written as a reference FASTA for consensus building. The pipeline run is intended to detect novel/unknown viruses — ViMOP only detects known virus species, so no database top hit exists to emit Large DNA viruses with extensive repetitive regions (e.g. mpox), where the reference-guided assembly may yield inaccurate draft genomes Reads rather than contigs need classifying or filtering — Centrifuge-based filtering acts on reads, not on contig-to-reference assignment http://edamontology.org/topic_0080 http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Emits one per-contig virus reference FASTA (e.g. AB627954.reference.fasta) into the ViMOP consensus output directory by selecting the highest-scoring BLAST hit from the ViMOP_DB virus reference database, enabling downstream reference-guided consensus assembly. genomics/v1 10.1093/bioinformatics/btaf687
skills.summary: Emits one per-contig virus reference FASTA (e.g. AB627954.reference.fasta) into the ViMOP consensus output directory by selecting the highest-scoring BLAST hit from the ViMOP_DB virus reference database, enabling downstream reference-guided consensus assembly.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The pipeline run is intended to detect novel/unknown viruses — ViMOP only detects known virus species, so no database top hit exists to emit Large DNA viruses with extensive repetitive regions (e.g. mpox), where the reference-guided assembly may yield inaccurate draft genomes Reads rather than contigs need classifying or filtering — Centrifuge-based filtering acts on reads, not on contig-to-reference assignment

skills.description: Use when reads have undergone methylation-sensitive base conversion (e.g. EMseq/APOBEC C-to-T) and must be aligned against a reference that has been identically converted, requiring FASTA-wide base substitution.
skills.name: fasta-sequence-manipulation
skills.search_text: fasta-sequence-manipulation Use when reads have undergone methylation-sensitive base conversion (e.g. EMseq/APOBEC C-to-T) and must be aligned against a reference that has been identically converted, requiring FASTA-wide base substitution. The reference must remain unconverted, e.g. when preparing to call methylation with sambamba mpileup against the original 'ref' or when aligning native (non-base-converted) nanopore reads with nanopolish The task is read-level conversion rather than reference conversion — convert_reads.py handles the *_CT.fq.gz and *_GA.fq.gz outputs instead http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_3295 Programmatically transform nucleotide sequences in a reference-genome FASTA — here, converting every C to T and G to A with pysam so base-converted nanoEM long reads can align to a mirrored reference while preserving sequence names and coordinate space. genomics/v1 10.1093/nar/gkab397
skills.summary: Programmatically transform nucleotide sequences in a reference-genome FASTA — here, converting every C to T and G to A with pysam so base-converted nanoEM long reads can align to a mirrored reference while preserving sequence names and coordinate space.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The reference must remain unconverted, e.g. when preparing to call methylation with sambamba mpileup against the original 'ref' or when aligning native (non-base-converted) nanopore reads with nanopolish The task is read-level conversion rather than reference conversion — convert_reads.py handles the *_CT.fq.gz and *_GA.fq.gz outputs instead

skills.description: Use when preparing raw FASTA protein sequences (e.g. PDB-derived DBP/non-DBP benchmark sets) for descriptor extraction and you must remove sequences shorter than 50 residues or containing ambiguous 'X' residues.

skills.search_text: fasta-sequence-quality-filtering Use when preparing raw FASTA protein sequences (e.g. PDB-derived DBP/non-DBP benchmark sets) for descriptor extraction and you must remove sequences shorter than 50 residues or containing ambiguous 'X' residues. Input is already a feature table or .mat workspace (e.g. DDE594.mat, PSSM_DBT_594.mat) — filtering operates on raw FASTA sequences, not on encoded feature matrices Sequences are nucleotide or non-protein FASTA records — the 50-residue and 'X'-residue criteria are defined for the 20 standard amino acids You need sequences shorter than 50 residues preserved, e.g. when studying short peptides outside the iDBP-DEP DBP/non-DBP benchmark scope http://edamontology.org/topic_0080 Quality filtering of FASTA protein sequences prior to feature encoding in the iDBP-DEP pipeline: deposited PDB1075, PDB594 and PDB186 benchmark sequences are loaded from ~/Data feature-data directories and sequences shorter than 50 residues or containing the ambiguous residue 'X' are excluded before DDE/PSSM feature extraction. genomics/v1 10.1002/minf.202000006

skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a feature table or .mat workspace (e.g. DDE594.mat, PSSM_DBT_594.mat) — filtering operates on raw FASTA sequences, not on encoded feature matrices Sequences are nucleotide or non-protein FASTA records — the 50-residue and 'X'-residue criteria are defined for the 20 standard amino acids You need sequences shorter than 50 residues preserved, e.g. when studying short peptides outside the iDBP-DEP DBP/non-DBP benchmark scope

skills.description: Use when you need a per-dataset base-count denominator (e.g., FASTQ datasets like snail, banana, hs1, hs4) to normalize compressed stream sizes into bits-per-base, or to reconcile stream contributions against total compressed size.
skills.name: fastq-base-count-accounting
skills.search_text: fastq-base-count-accounting Use when you need a per-dataset base-count denominator (e.g., FASTQ datasets like snail, banana, hs1, hs4) to normalize compressed stream sizes into bits-per-base, or to reconcile stream contributions against total compressed size. The FASTQ encodes data compressed by a tool that also compresses read identifiers or quality scores, since a sequence-only base count would not cover the full archive size The input is already a bits-per-base table or the compressed archive has not been decomposed into its individual streams http://edamontology.org/topic_0080 http://edamontology.org/topic_3168 Counts the number of bases in FASTQ read files and uses that denominator to convert compressed stream byte sizes into bits-per-base contributions (e.g., for NanoSpring's consensus, error, and lone-read streams), enabling fair cross-dataset comparison of compression breakdowns. genomics/v1 10.1038/s41598-023-29267-8
skills.summary: Counts the number of bases in FASTQ read files and uses that denominator to convert compressed stream byte sizes into bits-per-base contributions (e.g., for NanoSpring's consensus, error, and lone-read streams), enabling fair cross-dataset comparison of compression breakdowns.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The FASTQ encodes data compressed by a tool that also compresses read identifiers or quality scores, since a sequence-only base count would not cover the full archive size The input is already a bits-per-base table or the compressed archive has not been decomposed into its individual streams
