The task concerns somatic/oncogenicity classification of tumor variants (PCGR's VICC/CGC/ClinGen and AMP/ASCO/CAP frameworks) rather than germline ACMG/AMP classification of cancer predisposition variants The reference set consists of ClinVar variants without the minimum two-star review status, so concordance estimates would not be comparable to the curated two-star calibration The goal is running CPSR's classification on a single patient sample to produce a report, not optimizing or evaluating the underlying score thresholds http://edamontology.org/topic_2640 Calibrates the five score-to-classification cut-offs of CPSR's point-based ACMG/AMP variant classification logic against curated ClinVar assertions in cancer predisposition genes, and quantifies per-class concordance between the automated scores and ClinVar review-starred classifications. genomics/v1 10.1002/ijc.33749
skills.summary: Calibrates the five score-to-classification cut-offs of CPSR's point-based ACMG/AMP variant classification logic against curated ClinVar assertions in cancer predisposition genes, and quantifies per-class concordance between the automated scores and ClinVar review-starred classifications.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The task concerns somatic/oncogenicity classification of tumor variants (PCGR's VICC/CGC/ClinGen and AMP/ASCO/CAP frameworks) rather than germline ACMG/AMP classification of cancer predisposition variants The reference set consists of ClinVar variants without the minimum two-star review status, so concordance estimates would not be comparable to the curated two-star calibration The goal is running CPSR's classification on a single patient sample to produce a report, not optimizing or evaluating the underlying score thresholds

skills.description: Use when timing or throughput tables for an imaging workflow are available and you must compute per-embryo (or per-object) acquisition cost and a speedup ratio versus a single-pass imaging baseline.
skills.name: screening-throughput-estimation
skills.search_text: screening-throughput-estimation Use when timing or throughput tables for an imaging workflow are available and you must compute per-embryo (or per-object) acquisition cost and a speedup ratio versus a single-pass imaging baseline. Input is raw image data rather than acquisition timing/throughput tables — object detection and imaging, not cost modeling, is needed The workflow being evaluated is a true single-pass acquisition with no low-resolution detection pass, so no two-pass timing table exists to normalize Embryo/object density per slide is unknown, making per-object cost normalization impossible http://edamontology.org/topic_3383 Derive a per-sample imaging cost and speedup factor for a multi-pass high-content screening workflow by normalizing acquisition timing data (e.g., ~20 min per 100 detected Drosophila embryos at ~300 embryos/slide in the two-pass OpenHiCAMM workflow) against a single-pass full-slide 20× baseline (3,000–6,500 images), and validating the result against the paper's reported >10-fold speedup. genomics/v1 10.1016/j.isci.2018.03.017
skills.summary: Derive a per-sample imaging cost and speedup factor for a multi-pass high-content screening workflow by normalizing acquisition timing data (e.g., ~20 min per 100 detected Drosophila embryos at ~300 embryos/slide in the two-pass OpenHiCAMM workflow) against a single-pass full-slide 20× baseline (3,000–6,500 images), and validating the result against the paper's reported >10-fold speedup.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw image data rather than acquisition timing/throughput tables — object detection and imaging, not cost modeling, is needed The workflow being evaluated is a true single-pass acquisition with no low-resolution detection pass, so no two-pass timing table exists to normalize Embryo/object density per slide is unknown, making per-object cost normalization impossible

skills.description: Use when a pipeline needs a ground-truth simulated scRNA-seq count matrix (known DE vs non-DE genes, zero inflation, within-sample correlation) to validate gene-level or gene-set testing methods.
skills.name: scrna-seq-count-simulation
skills.search_text: scrna-seq-count-simulation Use when a pipeline needs a ground-truth simulated scRNA-seq count matrix (known DE vs non-DE genes, zero inflation, within-sample correlation) to validate gene-level or gene-set testing methods. The goal is analyzing real scRNA-seq data — twosigma's count_matrix input expects observed non-negative integer counts and performs no normalization, so simulated matrices are only for method validation The analysis requires the ad hoc random-effect screening (adhoc.twosigma) to be evaluated on empirical residual structure — simulated data with imposed variance components would not be an independent test A different count model is required (e.g. hurdle/log-scale models like MAST or SCDE-style simulations) — this function generates only zero-inflated negative binomial data with random effects http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 Simulates zero-inflated negative binomial scRNA-seq count matrices with individual-level random effects using the simulate_zero_inflated_nb_random_effect_data function from the twosigma R package, so that TWO-SIGMA/TWO-SIGMA-G workflows can be exercised on data with known DE and non-DE gene labels and controlled drop-out and overdispersion. genomics/v1 10.1002/gepi.22361
skills.summary: Simulates zero-inflated negative binomial scRNA-seq count matrices with individual-level random effects using the simulate_zero_inflated_nb_random_effect_data function from the twosigma R package, so that TWO-SIGMA/TWO-SIGMA-G workflows can be exercised on data with known DE and non-DE gene labels and controlled drop-out and overdispersion.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is analyzing real scRNA-seq data — twosigma's count_matrix input expects observed non-negative integer counts and performs no normalization, so simulated matrices are only for method validation The analysis requires the ad hoc random-effect screening (adhoc.twosigma) to be evaluated on empirical residual structure — simulated data with imposed variance components would not be an independent test A different count model is required (e.g. hurdle/log-scale models like MAST or SCDE-style simulations) — this function generates only zero-inflated negative binomial data with random effects

skills.description: Use when assembling a moderate-size (~860 Mbp) eukaryotic genome from uncorrected Oxford Nanopore reads using a curated set of unique 285 bp seed sequences, where standard long-read assemblers are computationally prohibitive.
skills.name: seed-based-genome-assembly-layout
skills.search_text: seed-based-genome-assembly-layout Use when assembling a moderate-size (~860 Mbp) eukaryotic genome from uncorrected Oxford Nanopore reads using a curated set of unique 285 bp seed sequences, where standard long-read assemblers are computationally prohibitive. Your goal is a fully polished, chromosome-scale reference: TULIP produces a candidate assembly that likely omits large repetitive and (sub)telomeric regions and needs downstream Racon/Pilon correction and optical-mapping validation You have no pre-selected unique seed set: strict requirements are unique numeric seed identifiers (excluding 0), identical seed lengths, and 'not too repetitive' sequences, otherwise graph untangling becomes very slow Your assembly problem is small enough that Canu or similar downstream assemblers are affordable — TULIP exists to split large problems into manageable subsets and adds fragmentation when seeds do not fortuitously bridge mergeable scaffolds http://edamontology.org/topic_0196 http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Reproduces the TULIP seed-based assembly of the European eel genome by aligning 873058-fragment 285 bp seeds against four nanopore read sets with chemistry-tuned BWA MEM settings, then running tulipseed.perl and tulipbulb.perl to order seeds into scaffolds and bundle seed/read sequence, yielding 2366 scaffolds (431 bp–8.7 Mbp) with ~7.4 read alignments per seed link. genomics/v1 10.1038/s41598-017-07650-6
skills.summary: Reproduces the TULIP seed-based assembly of the European eel genome by aligning 873058-fragment 285 bp seeds against four nanopore read sets with chemistry-tuned BWA MEM settings, then running tulipseed.perl and tulipbulb.perl to order seeds into scaffolds and bundle seed/read sequence, yielding 2366 scaffolds (431 bp–8.7 Mbp) with ~7.4 read alignments per seed link.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Your goal is a fully polished, chromosome-scale reference: TULIP produces a candidate assembly that likely omits large repetitive and (sub)telomeric regions and needs downstream Racon/Pilon correction and optical-mapping validation You have no pre-selected unique seed set: strict requirements are unique numeric seed identifiers (excluding 0), identical seed lengths, and 'not too repetitive' sequences, otherwise graph untangling becomes very slow Your assembly problem is small enough that Canu or similar downstream assemblers are affordable — TULIP exists to split large problems into manageable subsets and adds fragmentation when seeds do not fortuitously bridge mergeable scaffolds

skills.search_text: seed-match-chaining-nanopore-signals Use when mapping raw nanopore signals (FAST5/POD5/SLOW5/BLOW5) to a reference and you need to chain seed-match anchors into candidate mappings, or when verifying the f(i) chain-score DP recurrence (Section 2.2, Equation 3) against a manual trace. skills.search_text: segmentation-mask-border-extraction-and-dilation Use when comparing predicted cell segmentation masks (e.g., MIRIAM, Mesmer, Voronoi outputs) against manually annotated membranes on multiplexed tissue images and you need a border-based DSC/JSC agreement metric rather than whole-mask overlap. Input data lacks ground-truth fusion annotations — metrics cannot be computed without a known truth set The analysis goal is detecting fusions in real (non-simulated) tumor data, where sensitivity/specificity cannot be directly estimated and experimental validation (e.g., ~86% validation rate reported for TAGET) is the appropriate check http://edamontology.org/topic_0080 http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 Scores every gene-fusion call from a long-read caller (e.g., TAGET, SQANTI, JAFFAL) against simulated Iso-seq ground truth and computes sensitivity, specificity, and F-score per dataset, as done in the TAGET benchmark of ten simulated Iso-seq datasets with 300 fusions each. genomics/v1 10.1038/s41467-023-41649-0
skills.summary: Scores every gene-fusion call from a long-read caller (e.g., TAGET, SQANTI, JAFFAL) against simulated Iso-seq ground truth and computes sensitivity, specificity, and F-score per dataset, as done in the TAGET benchmark of ten simulated Iso-seq datasets with 300 fusions each.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input data lacks ground-truth fusion annotations — metrics cannot be computed without a known truth set The analysis goal is detecting fusions in real (non-simulated) tumor data, where sensitivity/specificity cannot be directly estimated and experimental validation (e.g., ~86% validation rate reported for TAGET) is the appropriate check

skills.description: Use when evaluating a joint tumor/control somatic SV caller against a naive baseline, or when only single-sample germline SV callers (Sniffles2, cuteSV, Delly, SVIM) are available for paired long-read data.
skills.name: separate-detection-and-subtraction-sv-filtering
skills.search_text: separate-detection-and-subtraction-sv-filtering Use when evaluating a joint tumor/control somatic SV caller against a naive baseline, or when only single-sample germline SV callers (Sniffles2, cuteSV, Delly, SVIM) are available for paired long-read data. When a joint tumor/control caller such as nanomonsv is available — the paper shows the subtraction approach yields more false positives because germline SVs can pass the threshold in the tumor and narrowly miss it in the matched control When calling somatic SVs at low tumor purity or low sequence yield — the subtraction baseline loses precision/recall relative to nanomonsv at 10–20x coverage and 20% tumor purity in NanoSim simulations http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 A baseline somatic SV-calling strategy in which a long-read SV caller is run independently on the tumor and matched-control BAMs and tumor calls overlapping control calls (with a margin, e.g. 200 bp) are subtracted. It is used by the nanomonsv paper as a comparison baseline that nanomonsv outperforms. genomics/v1 10.1093/nar/gkad526
skills.summary: A baseline somatic SV-calling strategy in which a long-read SV caller is run independently on the tumor and matched-control BAMs and tumor calls overlapping control calls (with a margin, e.g. 200 bp) are subtracted. It is used by the nanomonsv paper as a comparison baseline that nanomonsv outperforms.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When a joint tumor/control caller such as nanomonsv is available — the paper shows the subtraction approach yields more false positives because germline SVs can pass the threshold in the tumor and narrowly miss it in the matched control When calling somatic SVs at low tumor purity or low sequence yield — the subtraction baseline loses precision/recall relative to nanomonsv at 10–20x coverage and 20% tumor purity in NanoSim simulations

skills.description: Use when preprocessing raw sRNA-seq (FASTQ/FASTA) libraries for small RNA discovery and you need to discard reads outside the miRNA/siRNA size window or below a minimum count threshold.
skills.name: sequence-length-abundance-thresholding
skills.search_text: sequence-length-abundance-thresholding Use when preprocessing raw sRNA-seq (FASTQ/FASTA) libraries for small RNA discovery and you need to discard reads outside the miRNA/siRNA size window or below a minimum count threshold. Input is already a filtered FASTA set past the Wbench Filter step — instead restart the pipeline with -s|--step 2 (Filter Genome & miRBase) to avoid re-filtering The read type falls outside the 18–26 nt window (e.g. piRNA- or rRNA-focused analyses) — the hard-coded sRNA size defaults would discard the targets Quality control is the goal — miRPursuit explicitly notes fastqc-based QC is not yet implemented http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 http://edamontology.org/topic_0080 A filtering step from miRPursuit's Wbench Filter stage that reduces raw sRNA FASTA reads by length (18–26 nt), abundance (min_abundance=5), low complexity, invalid reads, and t/rRNA contamination before genome mapping and miRNA identification. genomics/v1 10.1002/1873-3468.12746
skills.summary: A filtering step from miRPursuit's Wbench Filter stage that reduces raw sRNA FASTA reads by length (18–26 nt), abundance (min_abundance=5), low complexity, invalid reads, and t/rRNA contamination before genome mapping and miRNA identification.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a filtered FASTA set past the Wbench Filter step — instead restart the pipeline with -s|--step 2 (Filter Genome & miRBase) to avoid re-filtering The read type falls outside the 18–26 nt window (e.g. piRNA- or rRNA-focused analyses) — the hard-coded sRNA size defaults would discard the targets Quality control is the goal — miRPursuit explicitly notes fastqc-based QC is not yet implemented

skills.name: sequence-motif-logo-visualization
skills.search_text: sequence-motif-logo-visualization Use when you have a set of genomic or transcriptomic modification sites (e.g. CHEUI-diff m5C calls) and need to verify biological plausibility by checking enrichment of a known sequence motif around the modified positions. The modification type has no known sequence-context motif (logo would show no interpretable pattern and provide no validation signal) Input is raw nanopore signal or FAST5 files rather than a curated list of called sites — motif analysis must follow modification calling and annotation, not precede it http://edamontology.org/topic_0099 http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 Generate and inspect sequence logos (e.g. with WebLogo) around predicted RNA modification sites to confirm expected sequence-context motifs, such as the 5'-m5CNGGG-3' motif enriched at NSUN2-dependent m5C sites in HeLa DRS data. genomics/v1 10.1038/s41467-024-47953-7
skills.summary: Generate and inspect sequence logos (e.g. with WebLogo) around predicted RNA modification sites to confirm expected sequence-context motifs, such as the 5'-m5CNGGG-3' motif enriched at NSUN2-dependent m5C sites in HeLa DRS data.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The modification type has no known sequence-context motif (logo would show no interpretable pattern and provide no validation signal) Input is raw nanopore signal or FAST5 files rather than a curated list of called sites — motif analysis must follow modification calling and annotation, not precede it

skills.description: Use when aligning ultra-long (billion-base) nucleotide FASTA datasets that were segmented by partial-chain MEM detection and the resulting subset blocks must be combined into one seamless multiple sequence alignment.
skills.name: sequence-profile-alignment-and-refinement
skills.search_text: sequence-profile-alignment-and-refinement Use when aligning ultra-long (billion-base) nucleotide FASTA datasets that were segmented by partial-chain MEM detection and the resulting subset blocks must be combined into one seamless multiple sequence alignment. Sequences are short or few, so the overhead of MEM-based segmentation and parallel subMSA is unnecessary — a standard MSA tool alone suffices. Input is protein sequences — FMAlign2 targets nucleotide (DNA) alignment. You need a single fixed alignment backend and cannot supply FASTA-in/FASTA-out commands; FMAlign2 requires the MSA tool to accept and emit FASTA. http://edamontology.org/topic_0080 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 FMAlign2's Step 3 module: after partial-chain segmentation of ultra-long nucleotide sequences, segmented subMSA blocks are aligned in parallel by a pluggable backend (MAFFT, Clustal Omega, HAlign3, or HAlign4), and unmatched fragments are stitched into the backbone via sequence-profile alignment with gap-based refinement during block concatenation. genomics/v1 10.1093/bioinformatics/btae014
skills.summary: FMAlign2's Step 3 module: after partial-chain segmentation of ultra-long nucleotide sequences, segmented subMSA blocks are aligned in parallel by a pluggable backend (MAFFT, Clustal Omega, HAlign3, or HAlign4), and unmatched fragments are stitched into the backbone via sequence-profile alignment with gap-based refinement during block concatenation.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Sequences are short or few, so the overhead of MEM-based segmentation and parallel subMSA is unnecessary — a standard MSA tool alone suffices. Input is protein sequences — FMAlign2 targets nucleotide (DNA) alignment. You need a single fixed alignment backend and cannot supply FASTA-in/FASTA-out commands; FMAlign2 requires the MSA tool to accept and emit FASTA.

skills.description: Use when constructing splice-site training/testing datasets where each example must be a fixed 400-nt sequence window around a true or false acceptor or donor site before one-hot encoding.
skills.name: sequence-region-extraction
skills.search_text: sequence-region-extraction Use when constructing splice-site training/testing datasets where each example must be a fixed 400-nt sequence window around a true or false acceptor or donor site before one-hot encoding. The downstream model or task requires a sequence window length other than 400 nt, since the CNNSplice constructed dataset permits a Sequence Length of 400 The input is already a fixed-length, one-hot-encoded sequence matrix ready for CNN training rather than raw splice-site annotations on a genome The goal is splice-site model training/testing rather than dataset construction (use train.py/test.py directly instead) http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 Extracts fixed-length 400-nt genomic sequence regions centered on splice sites (acceptor/donor) so that every example conforms to the Sequence Length of 400 constraint imposed by CNNSplice's CNN models. genomics/v1 10.1016/j.csbj.2023.05.031
skills.summary: Extracts fixed-length 400-nt genomic sequence regions centered on splice sites (acceptor/donor) so that every example conforms to the Sequence Length of 400 constraint imposed by CNNSplice's CNN models.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The downstream model or task requires a sequence window length other than 400 nt, since the CNNSplice constructed dataset permits a Sequence Length of 400 The input is already a fixed-length, one-hot-encoded sequence matrix ready for CNN training rather than raw splice-site annotations on a genome The goal is splice-site model training/testing rather than dataset construction (use train.py/test.py directly instead)

skills.description: Use when a per-window read alignment pile has been turned into a POA variation graph and sequencing-error-induced nodes/edges must be pruned iteratively before reading off the corrected subread's alignment path.
skills.name: sequence-to-graph-realignment-iteration
skills.search_text: sequence-to-graph-realignment-iteration Use when a per-window read alignment pile has been turned into a POA variation graph and sequencing-error-induced nodes/edges must be pruned iteratively before reading off the corrected subread's alignment path. Cycle-2 haplotype-aware consensus derivation: consensus sequences are derived from the constructed variation graphs by dynamic programming without re-pruning the graph Very large datasets where VeChat's longer runtimes and higher peak memory usage make it computationally unattractive versus consensus-based correctors Input is not raw noisy long reads (VeChat is a self-correction method for raw TGS reads, not a polishing step for finished assemblies) http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Iterative prune-and-realign cycle for ad-hoc variation graphs built by POA: edges lacking sufficient directional Confidence(e) and Support(e) from a frequent itemset model are removed, the target subread is re-aligned, and the cycle repeats until the graph retains only true sequential phenomena. genomics/v1 10.1038/s41467-022-34381-8
skills.summary: Iterative prune-and-realign cycle for ad-hoc variation graphs built by POA: edges lacking sufficient directional Confidence(e) and Support(e) from a frequent itemset model are removed, the target subread is re-aligned, and the cycle repeats until the graph retains only true sequential phenomena.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Cycle-2 haplotype-aware consensus derivation: consensus sequences are derived from the constructed variation graphs by dynamic programming without re-pruning the graph Very large datasets where VeChat's longer runtimes and higher peak memory usage make it computationally unattractive versus consensus-based correctors Input is not raw noisy long reads (VeChat is a self-correction method for raw TGS reads, not a polishing step for finished assemblies)

skills.description: Use when benchmarking a long-read ARG profiling or taxonomic classification pipeline's sensitivity to sequencing depth, requiring matched subsets of reads spanning low (1–2×) to high (32×) coverage.
skills.name: sequencing-depth-downsampling
skills.search_text: sequencing-depth-downsampling Use when benchmarking a long-read ARG profiling or taxonomic classification pipeline's sensitivity to sequencing depth, requiring matched subsets of reads spanning low (1–2×) to high (32×) coverage. When evaluating a method at a single sequencing depth with no interest in the coverage-performance curve — a single run suffices When the goal is de novo discovery of ARG genomic contexts in understudied environments rather than depth-benchmarked detection (assembly-/binning-based approaches may be preferred per the article) When taxonomic composition varies between samples, since differences would confound the coverage effect being measured http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_3697 Systematically downsamples simulated or real Nanopore metagenomic reads to a ladder of expected coverages (1×, 2×, 4×, 8×, 16×, 32×) so that detection-performance of ARG profiling methods can be compared as a function of sequencing depth. genomics/v1 10.1038/s41467-025-57088-y
skills.summary: Systematically downsamples simulated or real Nanopore metagenomic reads to a ladder of expected coverages (1×, 2×, 4×, 8×, 16×, 32×) so that detection-performance of ARG profiling methods can be compared as a function of sequencing depth.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When evaluating a method at a single sequencing depth with no interest in the coverage-performance curve — a single run suffices When the goal is de novo discovery of ARG genomic contexts in understudied environments rather than depth-benchmarked detection (assembly-/binning-based approaches may be preferred per the article) When taxonomic composition varies between samples, since differences would confound the coverage effect being measured

skills.description: Use when you have a high-coverage dRNA-seq dataset (e.g. PromethION human reads, SRA BioProject PRJNA995902) and need to quantify how sequencing depth affects m6A tool performance (hits, F1, AUPRC).
skills.name: sequencing-depth-saturation-analysis
skills.search_text: sequencing-depth-saturation-analysis Use when you have a high-coverage dRNA-seq dataset (e.g. PromethION human reads, SRA BioProject PRJNA995902) and need to quantify how sequencing depth affects m6A tool performance (hits, F1, AUPRC). When the dataset has low coverage and cannot be meaningfully subsampled to multiple depths (e.g. the oligos, yeast or mouse datasets used for the main benchmark rather than the high-throughput PromethION human data). When the goal is to compare tools at a single fixed depth rather than characterize performance as a function of sequencing depth. When assessing the 'relaxed' threshold regime specifically — this skill fixes filtering at the 'default' threshold set so F1 is comparable across depths. http://edamontology.org/topic_0085 http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 Reproduces the NanOlympicsMod coverage-saturation analysis, in which a high-depth human PromethION dRNA-seq dataset is subsampled to 25%, 50%, 75% and 100% of reads to quantify how sequencing depth affects the number of m6A hits called, default-condition F1 scores, and AUPRC for each of the benchmarked m6A detection tools. genomics/v1 10.1093/bib/bbae001
skills.summary: Reproduces the NanOlympicsMod coverage-saturation analysis, in which a high-depth human PromethION dRNA-seq dataset is subsampled to 25%, 50%, 75% and 100% of reads to quantify how sequencing depth affects the number of m6A hits called, default-condition F1 scores, and AUPRC for each of the benchmarked m6A detection tools.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the dataset has low coverage and cannot be meaningfully subsampled to multiple depths (e.g. the oligos, yeast or mouse datasets used for the main benchmark rather than the high-throughput PromethION human data). When the goal is to compare tools at a single fixed depth rather than characterize performance as a function of sequencing depth. When assessing the 'relaxed' threshold regime specifically — this skill fixes filtering at the 'default' threshold set so F1 is comparable across depths.

skills.search_text: sequencing-error-injection-simulation Use when benchmarking tandem-repeat decomposition accuracy against a known ground truth, e.g. simulating (AC)m(AG)n-style mosaic TRs with substitution error injection before scoring predictions. Input is already real sequencing data without ground-truth mosaic repeat annotations — the simulation provides no benefit there; use realdata/realdata.fasta workflows instead The goal is detecting tandem repeats de novo in a genome rather than benchmarking decomposer accuracy under controlled error rates http://edamontology.org/topic_0654 http://edamontology.org/topic_3524 Generates synthetic FASTA datasets of mosaic tandem repeats with substitution errors injected at controlled rates (0/1/3/5/10/15%) so that decomposers like uTR, RepeatMasker, and TRF can be scored against known ground-truth patterns. genomics/v1 10.1093/bioinformatics/btad185
skills.summary: Generates synthetic FASTA datasets of mosaic tandem repeats with substitution errors injected at controlled rates (0/1/3/5/10/15%) so that decomposers like uTR, RepeatMasker, and TRF can be scored against known ground-truth patterns.

skills.name: sequencing-error-metrics-tabulation
skills.search_text: sequencing-error-metrics-tabulation Use when comparing simulated nanopore read quality across simulators (e.g. seq2squiggle vs squigulator) on R10.4.1 datasets and you need median match rate and median PHRED score per organism/mode. Input is real sequencing data rather than simulator output — the metric ranges (match rate 91.91–95.29, PHRED 11.61–13.67) only serve as simulator benchmark expectations, not real-data quality targets The task is signal generation itself (noise/duration sampler tuning) rather than tabulating downstream basecalling error metrics http://edamontology.org/topic_0102 http://edamontology.org/topic_3168 Benchmark nanopore read simulators (seq2squiggle vs squigulator) by tabulating per-organism, per-mode basecalling error metrics — median match rate, mismatch/insertion/deletion rates, and median PHRED score — from dorado basecalls of simulated squiggle signals aligned with minimap2. genomics/v1 10.1093/bioinformatics/btae744
skills.summary: Benchmark nanopore read simulators (seq2squiggle vs squigulator) by tabulating per-organism, per-mode basecalling error metrics — median match rate, mismatch/insertion/deletion rates, and median PHRED score — from dorado basecalls of simulated squiggle signals aligned with minimap2.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is real sequencing data rather than simulator output — the metric ranges (match rate 91.91–95.29, PHRED 11.61–13.67) only serve as simulator benchmark expectations, not real-data quality targets The task is signal generation itself (noise/duration sampler tuning) rather than tabulating downstream basecalling error metrics

skills.description: Use when raw PacBio CLR read sets (e.g., yeast pseudo-diploid, NWC metagenome, Microbial 10-plex) must be corrected and their residual sequencing error rate computed to reproduce or compare against published correction benchmarks.
skills.name: sequencing-error-rate-benchmarking
skills.search_text: sequencing-error-rate-benchmarking Use when raw PacBio CLR read sets (e.g., yeast pseudo-diploid, NWC metagenome, Microbial 10-plex) must be corrected and their residual sequencing error rate computed to reproduce or compare against published correction benchmarks. Input reads are Oxford Nanopore rather than PacBio CLR — the reported validation values (0.089%/0.101%/0.236%) are specific to PacBio datasets and will not reproduce Reads are already corrected or consensus-polished, so residual error-rate benchmarking against raw-read correction results is meaningless Small exploratory datasets where VeChat's higher runtimes and peak memory usage on large files (needing --split/HPC splitting) are not warranted http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 Benchmarks long-read error-correction performance by running correction tools (VeChat and competitors) on real PacBio CLR datasets and quantifying residual error rates (read accuracy/QV) against published values from the VeChat paper. genomics/v1 10.1038/s41467-022-34381-8
skills.summary: Benchmarks long-read error-correction performance by running correction tools (VeChat and competitors) on real PacBio CLR datasets and quantifying residual error rates (read accuracy/QV) against published values from the VeChat paper.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input reads are Oxford Nanopore rather than PacBio CLR — the reported validation values (0.089%/0.101%/0.236%) are specific to PacBio datasets and will not reproduce Reads are already corrected or consensus-polished, so residual error-rate benchmarking against raw-read correction results is meaningless Small exploratory datasets where VeChat's higher runtimes and peak memory usage on large files (needing --split/HPC splitting) are not warranted

skills.description: Use when generating error-tolerant DNA barcode kits for nanopore sequencing and you need to translate a target sequencing error rate and tolerated error count into PRO's probability-divergence threshold t.
skills.name: sequencing-error-threshold-calibration
skills.search_text: sequencing-error-threshold-calibration Use when generating error-tolerant DNA barcode kits for nanopore sequencing and you need to translate a target sequencing error rate and tolerated error count into PRO's probability-divergence threshold t. Input is already a validated barcode kit (e.g., official ONT kits EXP-NBD104, SQK-16S024, EXP-PBC096) — demultiplex with PRO-dex instead of calibrating a generation threshold The sequencing platform is PacBio with a different error profile — the article states no tests on PacBio data have been performed, so the error-rate conversion is unvalidated there Flanking sequences used in library preparation are similar to candidate barcodes — threshold calibration does not fix extraction failures; such candidates must be removed by semiglobal-alignment edit distance <= 1 before generation http://edamontology.org/topic_0654 http://edamontology.org/topic_3168 Calibrates the probability-divergence threshold t used by PRO's farthest-point sampling by converting the nanopore sequencing error rate p and the number of errors k the kit must tolerate into a divergence cutoff for barcode candidate filtering. genomics/v1 10.1016/j.fmre.2024.04.014
skills.summary: Calibrates the probability-divergence threshold t used by PRO's farthest-point sampling by converting the nanopore sequencing error rate p and the number of errors k the kit must tolerate into a divergence cutoff for barcode candidate filtering.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a validated barcode kit (e.g., official ONT kits EXP-NBD104, SQK-16S024, EXP-PBC096) — demultiplex with PRO-dex instead of calibrating a generation threshold The sequencing platform is PacBio with a different error profile — the article states no tests on PacBio data have been performed, so the error-rate conversion is unvalidated there Flanking sequences used in library preparation are similar to candidate barcodes — threshold calibration does not fix extraction failures; such candidates must be removed by semiglobal-alignment edit distance <= 1 before generation

skills.name: sequencing-fastq-input-handling
skills.search_text: sequencing-fastq-input-handling Use when raw nanopore sequencing data in FASTQ format must be imported into Galaxy (e.g., from a GigaDB dataset) and characterized before downstream long-read assembly or AMR analysis. Input data is already basecalled, filtered, or provided as alignment files (e.g., BAM) rather than raw nanopore FASTQ reads The analysis goal is short-read data handling — NanoGalaxy focuses on long-read Oxford Nanopore data A numeric QC threshold decision is required: the paper reports no QC cutoff values, so acceptance is structural completeness of the report, not threshold passing http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_3168 Handles raw Oxford Nanopore FASTQ read files as the entry point for NanoGalaxy long-read analyses, covering upload into Galaxy and initial quality assessment (e.g., with NanoPlot) before assembly or AMR workflows. genomics/v1 10.1093/gigascience/giaa105
skills.summary: Handles raw Oxford Nanopore FASTQ read files as the entry point for NanoGalaxy long-read analyses, covering upload into Galaxy and initial quality assessment (e.g., with NanoPlot) before assembly or AMR workflows.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input data is already basecalled, filtered, or provided as alignment files (e.g., BAM) rather than raw nanopore FASTQ reads The analysis goal is short-read data handling — NanoGalaxy focuses on long-read Oxford Nanopore data A numeric QC threshold decision is required: the paper reports no QC cutoff values, so acceptance is structural completeness of the report, not threshold passing
